source: WaniKani API v2 subjects + Sou Matome N3 kanji list

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: This radical consists of a single, horizontal stroke. What's the biggest, single, horizontal stroke? That's the <radical>ground</radical>. Look at the ground, look at this radical, now look at the ground again. Kind of the same, right?

This little radical is a <radical>drop</radical>, maybe of water or some other liquid. Notice how it's only one drop? Sometimes radicals and kanji will have more than one drop in them, but don't let that throw you off.

This is a <radical>person</radical>. They're standing with their arms down at their sides and their legs spread out, which kind of makes them look like a torso with a pair of legs. Think of 人 as highlighting the bipedal nature of people. Walking on two legs? Probably a person.

This looks like an enclosure of sorts — that's why it's a <radical>prison</radical>. Imagine a tiny prisoner curled up inside, staring off into space, completely convinced they're trapped forever. Ironically this prison is actually wide open. They're just so consumed with self-pity that they haven't realized they've been free to leave all along.
This radical looks like a <radical>cross</radical>. I mean, just look at it. Two bars going through each other = a cross!
A big, gaping, square hole represents someone opening their giant <radical>mouth</radical> to tell you something stupid.

At first this looks like a cross in the ground, but it's actually something growing in the <radical>dirt</radical>. It's a little sprout, already rocking three leaves. And it's all thanks to that dirt! When you see this radical, think about how amazing it is that things just, like, grow in the dirt.
This is a <radical>mountain</radical>. See the big peak in the middle and the smaller ones on either side? This totally looks like a mountain.

Since there are no circles in Japanese characters, sometimes rectangles or squares have to make do. In this case, this big rectangle is the <radical>sun</radical>. The middle line is a cloud, moving across the sun. Picture it, but don't actually look at the sun and burn your eyes!
Do you see the <radical>tree</radical> in here? It has branches, and then it has the foliage coming down diagonally from it, spreading out like a tree would. That's why this radical is a tree.

This is the <radical>sword</radical> radical. The ノ part is the curvy sword, while the rest is a samurai bowing deeply, like 90 degrees, as he holds that sword — probably before a sword fight. By the way, don't confuse this with the power radical (力). See the difference? In the sword radical (刀), the ノ doesn't pierce through the bowing samurai. (Lucky for him.)

You know those big steel girders that are used for the frame of big buildings? This is like the end of one of those, and has a very distinct shape, just like this radical. These girders are used in construction, which is why this radical means <radical>construction</radical>. Funny thing is, you use these girders to put together buildings just like you're going to use this radical to put together kanji!

This is the outline of a <radical>head</radical>. A really square head, admittedly, but try to imagine it facing to the right. The left side is the back of the head, and the barb-like part on the right shows the curve of the chin. See the head?

Remember the guy from the big radical? This is him again, but this time he's so big his head is touching <radical>heaven</radical>. He's looking up and has his arms stretched open toward heaven, and his big hair is poking into those heavenly clouds.

This is the radical for <radical>water</radical>. It's the water radical because it kind of looks like water coming out of a faucet and splashing everywhere. See how it flows off in different directions too? Very water-like! As water-like as a radical can be, anyway…

This is the <radical>king</radical> radical. Picture this king sitting on his solid, squarish throne. The top stroke is the high back of the throne. The cross in the middle is his body, with his arms spread out on the arm rests. The bottom stroke is the ground. See him sitting there now, looking all dignified. Talk about a kingly king.

In Japan rice paddies are made up of square fields with irrigation lines going between them. See the four rice paddies with water flowing between and around them? That's why this radical is <radical>rice paddy</radical>.

Add a drop of the sun to something and it will turn it <radical>white</radical>. The sun is really strong, so even a single drop will burn anything white. Why do you think so many beaches are white? Even the drops of sunblock you use to stop the sun's rays is white. So when you think of sun drops, think white.

See the iris in the middle of the eyeball? Remember that there are no round things in kanji, so square things take their place. That makes this a pretty realistic, square <radical>eye</radical>. You just have to squint with your real eyes a bit.

A leaf growing out of a… mouth?? Look again and see the mouth is actually made of <radical>stone</radical>. The leaf here was just growing out of a crack on the side. Makes this stone mouth sculpture look kinda elegant, if you ask me. And obviously leaves don't grow on mouths, so whenever you see a leaf on a mouth, remember it's gotta be stone.

This L-shaped radical is the <radical>lion</radical> radical, because "L" is for "Lion." It also looks like a lion's mouth being opened really, really wide. Imagine a lion opening its mouth to yawn. It looks like this radical!

This radical looks like a <radical>spoon</radical>! Well, a spoon that's been bent a lot by an angry person or a psychic. Go grab a spoon and try to bend it into this shape. Then hold on to it so you'll never forget that this is the spoon radical!

This is the radical for <radical>winter</radical>. It looks like a skier going downhill (to the left), with their skis out in front and their poles out behind them. And when do people ski? In winter!

You could also remember this as looking like the evening radical but with an extra long stroke, since the evenings are long in winter. It gets dark early in winter, you know?
This is a <radical>canopy</radical>. See the cloth draping down and the little point at the middle holding it up? You could sit under here and enjoy a bright summer day without getting any sun!

This looks like a long index finger bent at the bottom, with several other stubby fingers growing out of it on either side. That makes it the <radical>fingers</radical> radical. A bit creepy, but imagine how easily you could grip something or scratch your back with fingery fingers like these. Pretty nice, right?

This is also a lot like the hand radical (手) but smaller. And what are the smaller parts of a hand? The fingers! You can remember it that way too, if you want.

Take a good look at this one. It kind of looks like a <radical>heart</radical>. Not the heart emoji kind, but a real-deal beating heart. Basically, there's a lump in the middle (the heart), and three lines that make up the arteries. Okay, so it's not the most anatomically correct heart, but just look at those floppy arteries going in and out, doing their thing and keeping you alive. What's not to love?

This radical technically means person (like 人), but we're going to shift the meaning a little bit. It's kind of like the person radical, but it's taller and skinnier, standing above the others and raising its fist to lead them. That's why this is a <radical>leader</radical>, not a regular person.

Sure, this <radical>forehead</radical> is a bit square, but that's because it's the top part of the head (冂) radical. This is just the forehead part of that! You can even imagine this as the forehead of Frankenstein's monster, since his forehead was pretty square too.

Also, don't confuse this for a roof. You know this is a forehead and not a roof because this doesn't have a cute little chimney sticking out of the top. Foreheads definitely don't have chimneys.
This is a <radical>roof</radical> ー a flat roof with a little chimney sticking out. How cute!

This radical looks like a person with a long dress running behind them. That's because they're all dressed up to go to a <radical>ceremony</radical>. You usually have to wear a long dress (or something formal) if you're going to a big ceremony, right? So when you see this radical, think of all the different ceremonies you might have to go to in your life and what you'll need to wear.
See how tall the stalks are with little bushy things at the top? It kind of looks like <radical>bamboo</radical>, if you use your imagination.

In some poop you find something small. You lean in, carefully pull it out, and realize it's a <radical>thread</radical>. What's that doing there? Well, it came from a cat, and cats love to eat thread when you aren't looking. And floss and hoodie strings and mouse tails… But this time, just thread.

See the little things sticking out of the ground? Those little things are pretty little <radical>flowers</radical>.

You could also see this as a little flower crown, especially since this radical almost always appears at the top of a kanji.

This eye has legs, since you have to let your eyes run over something in order to <radical>see</radical> it. That's why those eyes need legs — to see. They're wandering eyes, they want to see the world!!

This radical looks like a <radical>shellfish</radical>. What looks like the eye radical is its long spiral shell. The bottom part that looks like fins is its little legs poking out, helping the shellfish move around.

Fun fact: A long time ago people used shellfish shells as currency, so this radical often shows up in kanji related to money and commerce.

This is the <radical>foot</radical> radical. See the person doing a flying dragon kick to the right? What do they hit the target with? Obviously their foot. Imagine that foot coming straight at your face. At that point, your only hope is that it's clean. Nobody wants a foot to the face, especially not a filthy foot.

This is the radical for <radical>rice</radical>. Specifically raw rice, like the grain that grows out of the ground when rice is raw and fresh. When rice is particularly ripe, it'll kind of look like this at the top of the stalks. See the long leaves and the little rice tufts at the top? That's why this radical is "rice."

There's something draped over that stick. It's a <radical>towel</radical>! It's the kind of towel you clean with, so it's sort of old and crusty, which is why it holds its square shape even when it's hanging on the stick like that.

A single drop (丶) is just water. But as soon as there are three, rising higher and higher, you know what's coming. A <radical>tsunami</radical>! Think of those drops as wave crests. Three whole tsunami waves, stacking up? That's a big tsunami.
This radical is a <radical>scooter</radical>. See the handlebars and the little light? And there's a platform at the bottom you can stand or sit on (if it's one of those nice motorized scooters).

This is the radical for <radical>axe</radical>, since it looks like one. The two horizontal strokes are the head, the long left line is the whole edge of its blade, and the vertical line in the middle is its short handle. Kind of a strange axe, I admit, but an axe is an axe.
See the <radical>cliff</radical>? It's facing to the left. What do you think this cliff is jutting out over? Maybe an ocean, or a valley? Cliffs love to jut out over things like that.
There are a bunch of lines coming out of a mouth. Think of them as speech lines in a little speech bubble. Those lines represent the things you <radical>say</radical>.

Underneath that hat are two bars of <radical>gold</radical>, but under those there are some spikes. This is some kind of trap for people who try to take your gold. And why else would you make a trap? Everyone wants to protect their gold.

See the <radical>mustache</radical> going around the mouth? Man, I wish I could grow a sweet mustache like this. (Sure, the mustache looks a lot like the head radical here, but just imagine it as a mustache this time!)

Remember the radical for drop (of liquid)? Looks like it's shattered into two pieces here, which means it must be <radical>ice</radical> now. You know, since a drop could only break in two after turning into ice.

This is the <radical>cow</radical> radical. It kind of looks like the long face of a cow, right? You can think of that top horizontal line as its horns. Seeing it yet? It's got a little tuft of hair on its head, and some kind of accessory on the horn to your left, so this is a very stylish cow.

(Did you know both male and female cows can have horns? I didn't either, but it's true. So please don't write in telling us we can't call this thing a cow — we don't want any beef.)

This is a <radical>knife</radical>. See the sharp edge on the left and the tapered tip on top? And there's a little handle at the bottom for the... well, the handle. Be careful you don't cut yourself on this knife!

This is a little triangle that's almost completely closed off. When you want to be alone, you hide in a place where you can be in <radical>private</radical>. That's why this is the private radical. You're closing yourself off to the rest of the world, with just a little peephole.

A (modified) prison radical containing a person radical. What does a person experience in prison? <radical>Lack</radical>. Prison is all about lack — lack of freedom, lack of the comforts of home, lack of privacy, lack of conversation. Yep, the life of a person in prison is defined by lack.

The radicals ground and big make up this radical. There's a big guy on the ground... who is that big guy? Embarrassingly, it's your <radical>husband</radical>. Feel the shame that he got knocked down on the ground. By what? Who? How? (It doesn't matter.)

Don't confuse this with 未 (jet), though. See how 未 has a little tail at the end? That's because jets and other planes have tails, while husbands don't. At least I'd sure hope yours doesn't.

Flowers that grow out of the ground of a rice paddy after you bury fins there will grow <radical>yellow</radical>. Why? Because yellow is the color of a fish's soul, so planting flowers over their fins will turn them into a nice, pretty yellow.

The king is hovering a drop of water over his head. He's acquired the ability to manipulate water at will, making him the <radical>master</radical> of all water! If you think about how all life depends on water, that really makes him the master of everything…
This looks like a <radical>hook</radical>, like the kind a pirate would wear. The flat line shows where the hand was cut off, and the hook is right above, ready to take its place. Yarrrr.

This is the <radical>snake</radical> radical. See the head at the top with its long skinny body stretching down from it?

Don't confuse this with 己 (oneself) — the snake has an extra line behind its head to connect to the rest of its body.

Stick a table on top of a stool and you end up with a very dangerous <radical>weapon</radical>. Imagine hitting someone with this thing! Or, even better, imagine making someone sit on it. They'd be crushed mentally and emotionally and whatnot. Now that's a scary weapon.

This radical is made up of two slightly different versions of the spoon radical. Look closely at these two spoons. <radical>Compare</radical> their differences, like the different angles in the bends of the spoons. It's like one of those "spot the difference" games where you compare two similar pictures. But this time it's with spoons.

Most of this radical is just the rice radical, but the top part is something coming to cut the rice from its stalk. That, my friend, is the <radical>sickle</radical>. See how the rice is still there? That's because it's in motion. The sickle is literally doing the cutting RIGHT NOW! (And don't confuse this with the grain 禾 radical!)

This radical looks like a <radical>horse</radical>. See the long, thick neck with the mane flowing to the right? What might look like a wing is actually the horse's four legs and its tail hanging down.

Don't confuse this radical with the bird radical (鳥). They look similar, but this one doesn't have the little feather sticking out of the top of its head!

You have a roof on top of what looks like a volcano. What's the roof covering? It's definitely covering the hole at the top. I guess someone thought if they built a roof on the hole, none of the lava could come out. But isn't there a hole in the chimney? Guess their theory had some holes in it… Oh no, now lava is coming through the hole. RUN!!! RUN!!!!!!!!

This radical looks like a curvy letter B. What does B stand for? <radical>Building</radical>! This radical often shows up in kanji related to gatherings or to places where people come together… like buildings.

In winter, your mouth longs for a <radical>kiss</radical>. You know, because your lips get cold and you want someone to warm them up. How do you think that whole mistletoe thing got started? Cold winter mouths, longing for a kiss. So just imagine the top part of this radical as some winter mistletoe (or holly leaves, since that's probably easier), and the bottom part as a kissy mouth.

Do you see the handles on the top and the barb on the bottom? It's a <radical>jackhammer</radical>. How can you tell? The two diagonal lines on the side show the motion of the jackhammer going up and down really fast, doing what jackhammers do. BBBHHRZHHHHRHHRZHZHHZH JUJUJUJUJU.

See the two fists gripping the two vertical bars? They probably belong to a <radical>criminal</radical>, since criminals get put behind bars. It also looks like the bar on the left has been bent, like the criminal is trying to escape. Oh no…

This radical already looks like a <radical>gate</radical>, right? A high gate with pillars on either side and two small gate doors, way up at the top for some reason. Worst gate ever in terms of security, but definitely still a gate.

This looks like a tree with something tied around its middle, holding it tight. If you untied that middle part you'd realize it's actually a bunch of little trees (aka twigs and sticks) tied in a <radical>bundle</radical>!

You're lost, but you've come across a signpost that says "<radical>correct</radical>" in all directions. "Correct," "correct," "correct," it says. No matter which way you go, it's the correct way! What a relief!

You could also use the mnemonic you learned with the kanji: There is a line on the ground so you stop, making a giant sign pop up that says CORRECT! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you.
You spot a wispy shape flanked by ethereal orbs of flame. Don't be scared — this is just a friendly little <radical>soul</radical> on its way to get reincarnated into a new body.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>hundred</radical>.
This is the <radical>turkey</radical> radical. It kinda looks like a turkey facing to the left, with big tail feathers fanning out behind it. See it? You can practically hear this thing gobble!

This is the <radical>face</radical> radical, because it looks kind of like a face. See the flat brow on top? Imagine some eyes under it, a blocky nose in the middle, and some big ol’ cheeks on either side. It's a little bit square, but that's just what a face looks like when you take away the head and you're left with nothing but a face.

Everyone used a slide (丿) to escape the many little cages (匚) you tried to boil (灬) them in, leaving you with <radical>nothing</radical>. Absolutely nothing inside those boiling cages. Which, to be honest, serves you right. Anyone who pulls a stunt like that deserves… nothing. Nothing at all.

This radical is pretty complicated, but not much looks like this radical, so you're in luck. This looks like a giant flying airship of some kind. See the propellers on the back as it moves to the left? Just imagine a kind of steampunk airship like this flying through the air. That's why this radical is <radical>fly</radical> — because it's flying.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>fault</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember the kanji's meaning mnemonic, here's the gist: That slide is your husband's only <kanji>fault</kanji>. He spends all day sliding down it like a madman, which is why his hair sticks straight up on top. Maybe that's another fault… It's also a way to remember this is 失 (fault), not 矢 (arrow).

This is the <radical>restaurant</radical> radical. Do you see the moody light fixture shining down on a steel cloche, itself sitting atop a table covered with a white tablecloth? C'mon, you've gotta treat yourself to a nice dinner here and there!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>both</radical>.

Poor turtles. We don't like them here. This is a <radical>turtle shell</radical>. See the shell with just a tail remaining? It's the only thing we didn't remove off the turtle. It's just a shell with a tail, so basically it's just a turtle shell.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>line up</radical>.

If you pick up your sword (刀) and see a drop (丶) of blood, it might mean you accidentally grabbed it by the <radical>blade</radical>. Blades are sharp, so be careful when you handle them — you don't want to get drops of blood everywhere.

See all the arms sticking out of this radical? Those are for hanging lots of coats and things on, because this is a <radical>coat rack</radical>. Kind of a weird coat rack, but definitely a coat rack.

If you're wearing a hat and have dirt on your mouth, chances are you're staying in a <radical>cottage</radical>. That's because cottages are usually in the countryside, which means you're likely spending time out in the garden, with a hat on and dirt all over your mouth. You know, your average cottage experience. And hey, this radical even kind of looks like a cottage.
Can you see the <radical>horns</radical>? You could put these horns on anything. Donkeys, people, monkeys, and so on. That's exactly what we'll be doing when we learn kanji that have horns too.

On the top part of the head (冂) radical, there is a horn radical with one extra spike in the middle. This is a horned helmet with one extra spike. Who were famous for having horned helmets like that? The Vikings! That's why this radical is called <radical>Viking</radical>.
See the <radical>squid</radical> shape here? There's its pointy head, its eyes, and its tentacles (two, anyway). Pretty squid-like if you ask me!

There's a canopy with a grid-like frame near the top. It's a <radical>yurt</radical> with a window! Yurts are those dome-shaped huts nomads use. Once you've set up a canopy with a window frame, you've basically built one. Imagine gazing out that window, kicking back in your yurt. Yurt sweet yurt!
This is the <radical>comb</radical> radical. Look at all those little things sticking out. You could easily use this to comb your hair.

Someone shoved horns onto your husband and said he has to fight for them now. They turned him into a <radical>gladiator</radical>! Now your husband has to fight for their amusement. Are you not entertained?!

P.S. You know this is a gladiator, not a viking, because the horns are on the gladiator's shoulder pads instead of his helmet, and his helmet has a big crest on it.

example.jp: ここに駐車しないでください。
example.furigana: ここにちゅうしゃしないでください。
example.en: Please do not park here.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>horse</radical> is your <radical>master</radical> and you are merely a <kanji>resident</kanji> in his house. How did this horse become your master? Those aren’t questions a resident should ask! Know your place, resident!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To prove yourself a worthy <kanji>resident</kanji> of the horse master’s house, you must capture <reading>Chew</reading>bacca (ちゅう). Your horse master collects rare creatures, and Chewbacca is his latest desire. If you wish to remain a resident of the house, you must capture Chewbacca.

compounds.meaning: does not exist, do not have, gone

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>nothing</radical> radical and the <kanji>nothing</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Woah!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Nothing</kanji> can <reading>moo</reading> (む) quite like a cow can moo. Cows are the best at going moo. That’s a fact.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> hits these <radical>flowers</radical> they'll <radical>both</radical> become <kanji>full</kanji> of water. Tsunamis carry a lot of water, definitely enough to make both of these flowers full.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you stare at the <kanji>full</kanji> flowers, you decide to write a <reading>man</reading>ga (まん) about them. Your head is full of manga ideas!

kanji.kunyomi: むかう / むける / むこう
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> hits your <radical>mustache</radical>. Where did it come from? "Ah, it came from over <kanji>yonder</kanji>," you say, <kanji>facing</kanji> that way.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Who shot this drop at you from over <kanji>yonder</kanji>? You look over yonder, and see a figure. It is <reading>こう</reading>いち.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Killing two <radical>tree</radical>s with a <radical>jackhammer</radical> is expressly <kanji>prohibit</kanji>ed. Don't get me wrong, you can rip up one tree with your jackhammer, but not two.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The person who decided to <kanji>prohibit</kanji> jackhammering two trees is the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. He's the only person who's able to prohibit certain things, so it had to be him.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>gate</radical> of <radical>horns</radical> will take you to <radical>heaven</radical>. These horns are <kanji>related</kanji> and <kanji>connected</kanji> to heaven in some way.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: They are <kanji>related</kanji> and <kanji>connected</kanji> to heaven because these are the horns that Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) made from his enemies. God said he could come into heaven if he made a gate of horns, so that's what he did.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A psychic <radical>leader</radical> kneels to the <radical>ground</radical>, picks up a <radical>thread</radical>, and instantly makes a <kanji>connection</kanji> with the person that it came from. This leader is very powerful, so even a thread is enough for them to make a psychic connection with the person who was wearing it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you develop this psychic <kanji>connection</kanji> with the owner of the thread, you can tell that they're currently eating a <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lion</radical> harvesting <radical>rice</radical> uses an <radical>axe</radical> to <kanji>cut off</kanji> the tops of the stalks. The lion is roaming the rice fields using his axe to harvest the rice. He does so by cutting off the part of the rice stalks he needs.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The lion will <kanji>cut off</kanji> rice stalks until <reading>dawn</reading> (だん). But at the first light of dawn, it will run and hide in the shade of the trees, cut off from the rice.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>tree</radical> marked with a <radical>yellow</radical> X on the <kanji>side</kanji> of the house is going to get cut down. You’ve marked it with a yellow X so the hired help knows which tree to cut down. There are a lot of trees on the side of the house, but the tree marked with a yellow X is the only one in danger of causing damage to your roof in the event of a storm.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Wait, that woman with the chainsaw is <reading>Yoko</reading> (よこ) Ono! Yes, the same Yoko Ono who’s married to John Lennon of the Beatles. What’s she doing chopping down trees on the <kanji>side</kanji> of your house? Who can say. Silly Yoko.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Take your <radical>fingers</radical>, put them on this <radical>turtle shell</radical>, and <kanji>push</kanji> push push! Push the turtle right on out of there.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're trying to <kanji>push</kanji> this turtle out so you can use the shell for your new <reading>o</reading>bi (お). You keep seeing other people wearing turtle shell patterns on their obi, but you're going to go a step further. You're going to MAKE your obi out of actual turtle shells! You just have to push this darn turtle out first.

compounds.meaning: a ceremony to begin the school term

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
A good <radical>ceremony</radical> is under <radical>construction</radical> for a long time. You can't just make up a new ceremony on the spot. A ceremony is done a certain way because that's the way it's always been done. In short, to build a ceremony, you have to create a <kanji>ritual</kanji> first. Then, the ritual can be constructed into a bigger, more lavish <kanji>ceremony</kanji>.

This kanji also means <kanji>equation</kanji> for some reason. Just think of a ceremony that involves doing math and solving equations. How strange would that be? Pretend you're at this ceremony.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: So, you're at a <kanji>ritual</kanji>, but not just any old ritual. This is a full-blown <kanji>ceremony</kanji> and it's incredibly <reading>chic</reading> (しき). Imagine just how chic it is. Give it a shot — I'll let you come up with the chicness this time (it's good practice).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: To your <radical>leader</radical>, you <radical>say</radical>: "<kanji>Believe</kanji> and <kanji>trust</kanji> in me." The leader doesn't think you can handle your duties, so you have to say this to him. You want him to believe and trust that you're responsible. You can handle this task.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you face your leader and say "<kanji>Believe</kanji> and <kanji>trust</kanji> in me," you kneel down on each <reading>shin</reading> (しん). You have shin splints, so it hurts a bit, but you do it anyway to show how serious you are.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>mouth</radical> in the <radical>ground</radical> (in our case, it's a hatch), and inside is some kind of <radical>prison</radical> you can't quite get to. If you've ever seen Lost, this will sound familiar... on the hatch, there's actually a series of <kanji>number</kanji>s that you don't understand.
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
"You want to know the <kanji>number</kanji> to the hatch?" yells an old voice from inside. You say "yes," and the voice gives you the numbers and you're in! You go down into the prison, where there is one prisoner: Grandpa <reading>ごう</reading>いち.

Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.

kanji.kunyomi: たしか / たしかめる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You take a <radical>stone</radical> to the <radical>forehead</radical> of a <radical>turkey</radical>. It is <kanji>certain</kanji> that you will damage it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're killing this turkey, and you need to make sure he's dead for <kanji>certain</kanji>. The reason you need to make sure this turkey is dead is because of the <reading>cock</reading> (かく) in your life. Male chickens get really jealous when turkeys are around.

kanji.kunyomi: みとめる / したためる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever people <radical>say</radical> to you will be carved by a <radical>blade</radical> into your <radical>heart</radical>. Sounds cruel, but it's a way to make you <kanji>recognize</kanji> their power.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Having their words carved into your heart makes you <kanji>recognize</kanji> the authority of many people. But the only one you could ever truly <kanji>acknowledge</kanji>, is <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (にん).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fly</radical> radical and the <kanji>fly</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Awesome!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you <kanji>fly</kanji>, you generate a lot of <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) because you're moving so fast through the atmosphere. Normally this heat would be a nuisance, but you're a superhero so it doesn't bother you. This is actually the reason you're able to fly — you're a superhero and super resistant to heat.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>criminal</radical> has done an <kanji>injustice</kanji> on the world or other people. Being a criminal is a <kanji>negative</kanji> thing, and even if it was just a <kanji>mistake</kanji>, it was still a crime.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you commit an <kanji>injustice</kanji>, you'll know because <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) fills your body. Maybe you've never done any kind of big thing, but when you make a <kanji>mistake</kanji> your face fills with heat and you turn red!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>viking</radical> with a <radical>mouth</radical> <radical>towel</radical> is a totally <kanji>normal</kanji> thing. It's <kanji>ordinary</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: It's <kanji>normal</kanji> for a viking to have a mouth towel, but your sloppy farmhand friend <reading>Joe</reading>(じょう) has a mouth towel too. That's a habit that's only <kanji>normal</kanji> for vikings, so why does he have one?

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Look at a <radical>building</radical> and <radical>compare</radical> the <radical>white</radical> parts. Each of those white parts is a <kanji>floor</kanji>. Multi-<kanji>story</kanji> buildings have tons of different floors that you can see from the outside.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: One <kanji>floor</kanji> is just all <reading>kay</reading>aks (かい). You're looking at this building, and every other <kanji>story</kanji> is normal, but that one floor is kayak after kayak after kayak.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Cut this <radical>comb</radical> up with your <radical>weapon</radical> and turn it into the <kanji>steps</kanji> for some <kanji>stairs</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You slowly work to create these <kanji>stairs</kanji>, you have to slice up a lot of combs, and at <reading>dawn</reading> (だん) they are done!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: With the <radical>bamboo</radical> from that <radical>tree</radical>, your trained <radical>eye</radical> can tell it'll make an excellent <kanji>box</kanji>. Boxes made from bamboo trees are very sturdy and fashionable. You have an eye for fashion as well, you see.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Now you can use that <kanji>box</kanji> to store all your <reading>ha</reading>rd<reading>co</reading>re (はこ) punk vinyl records. You're a real connoisseur, so you know that hardcore music should only ever be kept in bamboo boxes.

kanji.kunyomi: あぶない / あやうい
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There is a <radical>prison</radical> on a <radical>cliff</radical> surrounded by <radical>snake</radical>s. Now that's a <kanji>dangerous</kanji> place. If you try to escape the prison you either fall to your death off the cliff or get bitten/squeezed to death by the snakes. Can you think of anything more dangerous than this? I can't.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Lucky for you, even though you're stuck in this <kanji>dangerous</kanji> place, there is hope. There is a <reading>key</reading> (き). All dangerous prisons have a key. You just have to find and steal it so you can avoid the cliffs and snakes!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Going into a <radical>building</radical> made by a <radical>squid</radical> is <kanji>risky</kanji>. First of all, squids only have tentacles, no bones, and they make all of their buildings out of risky materials like kelp and sharp coral.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: "It's too <kanji>risky</kanji>, leave me!" the squid cries. "I'll save you, underwater citizen! Nothing is too risky for <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai!" The building is collapsing on the squid, the risk is so great, but Ken the samurai dives in and saves him!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> have nothing to do when you're at your <radical>cottage</radical> except <kanji>throw away</kanji> things. Your cottage is for vacation. And vacation means being as lazy as possible. But you certainly don't want to live in filth, so you have to throw away your trash at least.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The number one thing you <kanji>throw away</kanji> while in your cottage is your <reading>su</reading>it (す). Suits just don't fit the cottage vibe, man.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You can use a long piece of <radical>thread</radical> during <radical>white</radical> <radical>water</radical> rafting as a safety <kanji>line</kanji>. Sure it's thin, but if someone goes overboard even a line of thread is better than nothing. Throw them a line and drag them back aboard!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The person who threw you that <kanji>line</kanji> of thread is actually a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん). How kind of him. After you are safe you hop on the centaur's back and ride around to get the wind to dry you off.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>face</radical> radical and the <kanji>face</kanji> kanji are the same! But this isn't just a face like the one you're looking at your computer/phone with. It's the <kanji>surface</kanji> kind of face too!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>face</kanji> you're looking at, that has a lot of <kanji>surface</kanji> area, belongs to <reading>men</reading> (めん). Not a single man, but all men put together. It's hundreds of thousands of men's faces in a row.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>line up</radical> your body with the <radical>sun</radical> and everything looks <kanji>normal</kanji>.  The sun is lined up behind you, and you’re looking at all the things the sun has lit up. Everything looks normal.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Soon you see something that doesn’t look so <kanji>normal</kanji>. It’s a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ), a jester. Dressed all in fool’s garb, this fool is dancing up towards you with a ridiculously unsettling grin on his face.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>kiss</radical> <kanji>each</kanji> and <kanji>every</kanji> one of your best pals to show them how much you love and care for them. You kiss each friend right on the mouth.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Actually, <kanji>each</kanji> and <kanji>every</kanji> one of your best pals is of the <reading>cock</reading> (かく) variety. By that, I mean each of them is a rooster. Imagine kissing each cock on its beak.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Ice</radical> is what you're <radical>lack</radical>ing, so the <kanji>next</kanji> thing you need to do is go to the store and see if they have any. Nope, no ice. So, now you go to the next store. Is there ice here? Nope. Next!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading じ, we used the word "Jesus" - Finally, when you're at the last store in existence, you decide it's time to pray to <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ), asking for a miracle. He comes down from the heavens with ice in his hands.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>soul</radical> of a <radical>person</radical> has a <radical>hook</radical> that can make them <kanji>pleasant</kanji>. When you see, hear, or feel something pleasant, can't you feel that hook pressing into the middle of your body?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If you want to feel this <kanji>pleasant</kanji> feeling just look at a <reading>kay</reading>ak (かい). Kayaks are the most pleasant boats in the world. Feel that pleasant feeling in your chest just from reading about kayaks in this mnemonic right now.

kanji.kunyomi: はやい / はやす / はやめる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You jump on your <radical>scooter</radical> with a big <radical>bundle</radical> to go as <kanji>fast</kanji> as you can! You have a bundle of pizzas in here, and they need to be delivered as fast as you can get them there!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You were going so <kanji>fast</kanji>, you only put on <reading>sock</reading>s (そく). So now you're barreling down the street at top speeds in just your sad, white socks.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: While riding on your <radical>scooter</radical>, you grow a <radical>mustache</radical> on top of the <radical>mustache</radical> you already have in order to <kanji>surpass</kanji> the people around you. You're in a scooter race and your mustache is the only thing keeping you in the lead, but someone else has a mustache too! So you grow another mustache to surpass them once again!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Suddenly, something else manages to <kanji>surpass</kanji> you all. It's a <reading>ca</reading>r (か)! A car with two mustaches is also riding on a scooter and going way faster than you.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You look at some <radical>gold</radical> and notice a <radical>fault</radical> in it. You scrape at the fault and see that it's just sprayed with gold paint. It's not gold, it's (comparatively) worthless <kanji>iron</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Do you know that movie, <reading>Tetsu</reading>o (てつ) the <kanji>Iron</kanji> Man? We talked about it on Tofugu a while back. It’s one of the wackiest Japanese movies of all time. If you don’t know about Tetsuo the Iron Man, you should definitely look it up (if you aren't averse to horror/violent films). Tetsuo is one of the most insane movies in the history of ever.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Try to use your <radical>fingers</radical> to <radical>spoon</radical> out some of the <radical>sun</radical> and you'll come back with just one <kanji>finger</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Don't worry, you aren't the only one out there with just one <kanji>finger</kanji>, <reading>shee</reading>p (し) only have one finger too. I mean, they're hooves, which are really just a single animal finger. It's just big and kind of flat.

kanji.kunyomi: さだめる / さだまる / さだかに
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You build a <radical>roof</radical> over your <radical>coat rack</radical> because you <kanji>determine</kanji> that this is the best way to protect your coats from the elements.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Why did you <kanji>determine</kanji> your coat rack needed a roof? Because your coat pockets are full of <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots! You can't afford to let your tater tots get rained on, so you determined they needed to be properly sheltered with a roof.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: In a <radical>yurt</radical> you use a <radical>towel</radical> as a <kanji>seat</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Something about using a towel for a <kanji>seat</kanji> is very <reading>sexy</reading> (せき) to you. Probably because you associate it with sexy people using towel seats on the beach.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A giant <radical>cross</radical> with a <radical>mouth</radical> stands above you. "I am <kanji>reason</kanji>!" it says to you. It is the Cross of Reason.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>reason</kanji> that this Cross of Reason exists is to combat the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう) of the world, who just bring chaos into everything.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have to <radical>sickle</radical> the <radical>rice paddy</radical> today because it's your <kanji>turn</kanji>. This kanji also means <kanji>number in a series</kanji>, which is a lot like a turn. For example, you're number 3, so your turn will be number 3.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>turn</kanji>-based rice sickle system is a contest as well! But, you are disappointed to find out that you have been <reading>ban</reading>ned (ばん) from the game because of the performance enhancing steroids you've been taking.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>hole</radical> leading to the <radical>private</radical> <radical>heart</radical> of your house is the <kanji>window</kanji>. Or maybe it's just the window to your soul, and not your house. Like the poetry people say.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You realize that a ton of people are looking into your <kanji>window</kanji> and seeing all your private things. This makes you <reading>mad</reading> (まど)! What right do they have to know your private thoughts and desires?!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>shellfish</radical> has a <radical>knife</radical> in his <kanji>side</kanji>. It's fine though, don't worry — if anything, it makes him look more battle-hardened and leader-like.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Who stuck this knife in the shellfish leader's <kanji>side</kanji>? Sir <reading>Gawa</reading>in (がわ), knight of the Round Table. He mistook him for the Green Knight and stabbed him in the side before realizing his mistake.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you've been walking all day, your <radical>foot</radical> is the last thing anyone would want to <radical>kiss</radical>, especially after wandering barefoot down a <kanji>road</kanji>. Your feet are filthy, sweaty, and stinky. Nobody is going to want to kiss those feet.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What was this person walking down again? Oh, that's right – a <reading>ro</reading>ad (ろ). They were walking down a filthy road.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>restaurant</radical> says, "<kanji>Halt</kanji>!" to everyone who wants to come in. The leader looks them up and down. Stares into their eyes. And then, maybe, they may go into the restaurant to eat.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: People only <kanji>halt</kanji> because they want this restaurant's world famous <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots. Which is probably why there is a leader out front making sure only people who can really appreciate the tater tots can get in to eat them.

kanji.kunyomi: ととのえる / ととのう

compounds.meaning: numbered ticket (issued at cinemas, etc. to indicate the order in which people may enter)

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bundle</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> is the <radical>correct</radical> way to <kanji>arrange</kanji> things. Just make sure you <kanji>organize</kanji> it all before winter comes, or it'll be too late.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But the most important things to <kanji>arrange</kanji> and <kanji>organize</kanji> are your <reading>sa</reading>bers (せい). You have an extensive saber collection that you simply must organize before winter arrives.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gladiator</radical> in front of you draws his <radical>sword</radical>. He points the sword at your chest and right when you think everything is about to end, you realize he's pointing the sword at the <kanji>ticket</kanji> in your hand.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The gladiator happily marks your <kanji>ticket</kanji> with his blade, when <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai pushes past you. He holds up his own sword, challenging the gladiator, who just shakes his head and points at your ticket again.

kanji.kunyomi: あらわれる / あらわす
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> can <radical>see</radical> the <kanji>present time</kanji> for what it really is. The future isn't important. The past isn't important. The present is when everything <kanji>appear</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: At the <kanji>present time</kanji> the king is <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). The time has finally come for him to get serious, and as they say, there's no time like the present.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: As you dig under the <radical>ground</radical> you discover a <radical>head</radical> resting near a <radical>mountain</radical>, which are <kanji>both</kanji> strange things to find beneath the earth.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But, you dig too deep and water flows into where you are. Your only hope is a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat floating off in the distance.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>husband</radical> marries a <radical>husband</radical> while the <radical>sun</radical> goes down and the men <kanji>replace</kanji> their solitary lives with one of everlasting companionship. Instead of one husband and one wife, we have two husbands here. They shed their lives of bachelorhood and replace it with one of monogamy.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After the ceremony, the husband and his husband get in a <reading>ca</reading>r (か) and drive off into the sunset. They’ll never be able to <kanji>replace</kanji> this memory with anything. Truly it is the happiest day of these husbands’ lives.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of a <radical>hundred</radical> <radical>forehead</radical>s in the <radical>heart</radical> of <radical>winter</radical> is <kanji>superior</kanji> at being <kanji>gentle</kanji>. These hundred foreheads are sensitive, especially in the heart of winter, so the leader must be very gentle. Not just any kind of gentle though—the superior kind of gentle that will keep a hundred foreheads following.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You need to be <kanji>superior</kanji> because all of these foreheads belong to <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう). They don't know how to take care of themselves, though they try to convince you they can. They're too young to know any better.

compounds.meaning: sit on the floor Japanese style

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Under a <radical>canopy</radical>, there are two <radical>person</radical>s on the <radical>dirt</radical>. What do they do there? They <kanji>sit</kanji>. The people use the dirt under the canopy as a <kanji>seat</kanji> for their butts.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Who decided people have to <kanji>sit</kanji> like this? The C<reading>za</reading>r (ざ). The Czar wants to be above everyone, so he makes them sit on the dirt under canopies while he goes around on horseback or something, towering over them as they sit.

kanji.kunyomi: おりる / ふる / くだる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Inside the <radical>building</radical> is the <radical>Winter</radical> <radical>Cow</radical>. You need to see it, so you go inside. It is deep down in there, and you'll have to <kanji>descend</kanji> to reach it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>descend</kanji> to the bottom and there it is, the Winter Cow. You walk up to the cow, and it swings its head back to see you. Instead of a cow's face, it's <reading>こう</reading>いち's face.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

This word is generally added to the end of a number, as in 三号 ("number 3"). It can also go together with other words to give things like train car numbers, as in ２号車 ("car 2"), and room numbers. When used on its own, it indicates the edition number of magazines and the like.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji all alone, but it uses the on'yomi reading. This is probably because you'll usually see this word attached to other things, like numbers. This shows the edition or number of an item. So, even though it's alone, it's usually used like jukugo, which is why the reading for this one is the same as the reading you learned when you learned the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>yonder</kanji>, which is like "over there." This is the verb version of "yonder." That being said, "to yonder" isn't really a thing, so you have to think of what happens when you "look yonder." This word means <vocabulary>to turn toward</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary>. You're looking yonder, but you have to turn towards said yonder to look that way.

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to be suitable</vocabulary>, as in a good fit for a job, role, or situation. After all, you turn toward the things you're most suitable for, right?
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You turn <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> a new direction and look out into the distance. There is a single cow out there. It turns to face you too, and says <reading>moo</reading> (む).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 向く means "to face" or "to turn towards", and this verb is related. This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. It's when someone turns or points something. That something doesn't just turn on its own. So this verb means <vocabulary>to turn something towards</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to point something at</vocabulary>.

In order to remember that this word means "to turn something towards," focus on the け. You have a bottle of ketchup in your hands and you're turning it toward your worst enemy to spray them. Picture yourself pointing the ketchup toward them.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is the same as 向く which you learned in a previous level. As long as you know that one you should be able to learn this one's reading as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 向 means <kanji>yonder</kanji>, and this is its noun version, meaning <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

向こう is used when speaking generally about something distant from yourself, whether it's a place, as in 向こうの山 (the mountain <vocabulary>over that way</vocabulary>), or a person, as in 向こうの人 (the person on the <vocabulary>other side</vocabulary>). Sometimes, it can even be used for time, like 向こう一週間 (the next week ahead).
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that with 向く, but here's a mnemonic for you in case you forgot:

<vocabulary>Over there</vocabulary>, a cow is saying <reading>moo</reading> (む). It's way over there, though, so you can't see or hear it. Kinda makes you wonder: if a cow moos way over there and no one's around to listen, did it really moo at all?

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>number in a series</kanji> plus a <kanji>number</kanji>. You know what happens when two kanji with basically the same meaning get combined into one by now, right? It just turns out to be the same meaning, basically. This word means <vocabulary>number</vocabulary>, and it's used in contexts like phone numbers, exam numbers, and serial numbers.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 向く and 向ける by now. They mean "to face" and "to turn toward." This has a similar idea. When you add 向け to something imagine you're turning it, aiming it at someone. It's aimed at them, meaning it's <vocabulary>made for</vocabulary> them. Turn a book toward someone, now it's <vocabulary>aimed at</vocabulary> them, it's made for them. See the connection?
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 向く so work off of that word to be able to read this one.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Please note that this word refers to "the side of something." Not "the left side," for example. That would be 左側.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this vocab is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, lucky you!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Someone yells out "NEXT!" because the first thing didn't work on you. That was a single guillotine. Now they are going to try <reading>two gui</reading>llotines (つぎ) and see how that works on your thick neck. NEXXXXT!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This also works for "train lines" as well. You'll see this attached onto the ends of names describing them.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the same for this vocab word. Enjoy it!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>line</kanji> that runs on a <kanji>road</kanji> is a <vocabulary>railroad track</vocabulary>. First you have to get into your mind that the "line" in question is a railway line. Then, what railway line runs on a road and what kind of road is it? It's a <vocabulary>railroad track</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Just like the meaning of the kanji (<kanji>fast</kanji>) this adjective also means <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Remember how 早い means "early"? If you are early to something, it probably means you moved <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary> to get there. These two words share a reading (and have similar meanings, in a way, as well!).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. The only difference is that this word can mean <vocabulary>finger</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>toe</vocabulary>. What are toes but small, walking fingers?
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

What do you use your <vocabulary>finger</vocabulary> for the most? For pointing, of course! Imagine going up to people and saying, "What will <reading>you be</reading> (ゆび) when you grow up?" Point your finger at the next person, "What will you be?" Keep going until you're just saying, "You be? You be?" with your finger out.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>finger</kanji>. So, if you "to finger" something, what are you doing? You're pointing. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to point</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You are pointing at something in fear. It is a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). Thing is, you're pointing at this saw with a missing finger. It just cut off your finger and you're freaking out, trying to point with a bloody non-finger.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>determine</kanji> and use your <kanji>finger</kanji> to point at someone or something, you're going <vocabulary>to appoint</vocabulary> them. Just imagine yourself determining who's the best for the job then pointing with your finger. That is who you will appoint. The する on the end makes it a verb, so <vocabulary>指定</vocabulary> would be "appointment" or "designation" or something along those lines. Cool how する works.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji refers to a <kanji>floor</kanji> (as in the "fifth floor"). This word represents the version that comes after a number, shown with a 〜. Essentially, this has the same meaning as the kanji you learned, making it nice and easy.

Note that floor-counting systems can vary across different countries. In Japan the ground floor is generally called 一階, with the floors above being 二階, 三階, and so on.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Don't type in the 〜 or you'll get it wrong!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>believe</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to believe</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 信 is しん no matter what! See, if you believe, good things will happen. You should be able to read this.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>believe</kanji> in the <kanji>number</kanji>s, there will be no traffic because the <vocabulary>traffic light</vocabulary> will be functioning properly. Traffic lights are based all off of traffic data and numbers. You just have to believe and hope it all works out in terms of these traffic lights.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. In fact, this kanji's on'yomi AND kun'yomi are しき, so you can never go wrong.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>arrange</kanji>, and the verb version also means <vocabulary>to arrange</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put in order</vocabulary>. This has to do with putting things in their rightful place, getting affairs in order, or even preparing equipment.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Everything in your room has finally been <vocabulary>put in order</vocabulary>. Just as you finish, you hear a crash and turn to see your dog has jumped up onto your desk. "<reading>Toto no</reading> (ととの)!" you yell as he knocks everything over. Guess you have  <vocabulary>to arrange</vocabulary>  it all over again. Dammit Toto.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: ゴミ means "garbage." Add a <kanji>box</kanji> to it and you have a garbage box aka a <vocabulary>garbage can</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>garbage bin</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kun'yomi reading, the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to pay attention to the rendaku though. はこ changes to ばこ.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>dangerous</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>dangerous</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Someone is in danger! It's poor old <reading>abe</reading> (あぶ) Lincoln. You try to save him, yelling out 危ないよ！！！！, but he gets shot in the back of the head anyways.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>dangerous</kanji> and <kanji>risky</kanji> is probably pretty <vocabulary>risky</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>dangerous</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>unsafe</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 関 means <kanji>related</kanji>. So, when you add する to it you make it a verb. Now it means <vocabulary>to be related to</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>connection</kanji> <kanji>related</kanji> to another <kanji>connection</kanji> obviously has some kind of <vocabulary>connection</vocabulary>, at least between all those meanings.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Both</kanji> <kanji>side</kanji>s is <vocabulary>both sides</vocabulary>. Which side? Both sides.

両側 typically refers to both sides in a physical sense, like saying there are houses on both sides of the street or handrails on both sides of a staircase.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The first kanji takes the on'yomi reading and the second takes the kun'yomi reading. Luckily you know both of them already!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
You've learned the <reading>がわ</reading> as the reading for this kanji, but when its used on its own as a vocabulary word, it is read as <reading>そば</reading>. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

Having a <reading>sober</reading>(そば) person by your <vocabulary>side</vocabulary> is important when you're drunk. 

Think of other vocabulary words that use <reading>がわ</reading>. In these words, <kanji>側</kanji> is a suffix, so it will have another kanji that comes before it.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the on you learned with the kanji. Have a seat and relax.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The particle に here is a clue that this word is an adverb. An adverb describes actions, so what's a <kanji>normal</kanji> action? It's one you're <vocabulary>always</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>constantly</vocabulary>, doing. That's what makes it normal!
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn. In order to learn it, think of this:

I <vocabulary>always</vocabulary> <reading>tune</reading> (つね) my violin, but today I didn't tune it. So, now I sound terrible. Imagine how terrible my untuned violin sounds, compared to how it always sounds.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>nothing</kanji>, so when you have nothing, you are <vocabulary>without</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

When you are <vocabulary>without</vocabulary> you don't have anything to eat either, so you end up <reading>gnashi</reading>ng (なし) your teeth together instead.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When an <kanji>injustice</kanji> to what's <kanji>normal</kanji> is being committed, that makes it an <vocabulary>emergency</vocabulary>! 

Although it's less common, this can also be used as a な adjective. In that case, it means <vocabulary>extreme</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>unusual</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sit</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike the kanji reading, so let's use a separate mnemonic to remember this. Just imagine yourself going <vocabulary>to sit</vocabulary> down. You sit down, and the ground collapses below you and you fall. When you land, you find yourself in a nasty, stinking <reading>sewer</reading> (すわ). It is so gross. Taste the sewage in your mouth. Smell it. Feel gross. You shouldn't have sat down on that spot, it was looking awfully dangerous, now that you think about it.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sit</kanji> <kanji>seat</kanji> is probably going to be a <vocabulary>seat</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>prohibition</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to prohibit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to forbid</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji means <kanji>related</kanji>. As a verb, this often means <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be related</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to be connected</vocabulary>. Basically, things that have to do with being related to something else.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:  

Ever heard of the "<reading>Kaw Kaw</reading> (かか) Crow Gang"? They are bad news, always eating from garbage and squawking "kaw kaw" ... You don't want <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> with them.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: When something is moving towards <kanji>emergency</kanji> (非常), it is something that is <vocabulary>very</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>extremely</vocabulary> bad. Like, <vocabulary>exceedingly</vocabulary> so. It's nuts.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from the word 非常, which you hopefully know okay by now!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Here we have <kanji>nothing</kanji>, followed by the verb なる. A verb that means "become nothing"? That'll be <vocabulary>to be gone</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to run out</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be lost</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary>.

This can be translated in various ways depending on the situation, but just remember that it always refers to something changing from being there, to not being there.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading, which you learned with 無し, so you should be good to go.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is an adverb, but it has the same meaning (basically) as the kanji. It means <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary>, and it can also mean <vocabulary>surely</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary> weird. To remember the reading for this word, just think how you're certain that if you s<reading>tash</reading> (たし) the treasure, nobody will find it here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>fly</kanji>, and the verb vocab version is also <vocabulary>to fly</vocabulary>. In addition to flying, the verb also means <vocabulary>to jump</vocabulary>. Just think of jumping as being some sort of... smaller version of flying, and this'll make sense.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: When you try <vocabulary>to fly</vocabulary>, the main thing holding you back is your <reading>toe</reading> (と). It's like forty pounds and holds you down.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>cut off</kanji>. What happens when you do the action of cutting someone off? You're going <vocabulary>to refuse</vocabulary> them whatever it is they want.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Deciding <vocabulary>to refuse</vocabulary> something unfortunately starts a <reading>coat war</reading> (like a pillow fight, but everyone hits each other with coats instead of pillows). Coats to the ready, and let the coat war commence!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word ends with a う sound so you can guess it's a verb. The kanji means <kanji>nothing</kanji>, and the best way to end up with nothing is either <vocabulary>to lose something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get rid of</vocabulary> it.

無くす is a broad word that can be used both when you unintentionally lose something, like 財布を無くしちゃった (I lost my wallet), and when you deliberately do away with something, as in 戦争を無くす (eliminate war).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi, which you already learned when you learned the word 無し.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Just be sure to make <kanji>certain</kanji> that you <kanji>recognize</kanji> him. We need <vocabulary>confirmation</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>verification</vocabulary>, so make certain again, please.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>recognize</kanji> or <kanji>acknowledge</kanji>, so the verb also means <vocabulary>to acknowledge</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to recognize</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to perceive</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to admit</vocabulary>, among others.

This can be used to mean recognizing somebody or something visually, as well as in the sense of "to acknowledge" or "to admit". So you can use this verb to recognize someone's presence, achievements, marriage, or your own defeat. That said, you'll usually see 認める in the sense of "to acknowledge".
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The only thing you could ever truly <vocabulary>acknowledge</vocabulary> is <reading>meat</reading> (みと). Meat is the only thing in your life that has any authority over you. That's how much you love meat.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, though it's kind of like an add-on for other words in a sense, which makes it behave like jukugo, I think. Don't confuse this with 各々 though. That one does use the kun'yomi reading, which is strange when you consider this one doesn't. Every kanji has its own "perks" I suppose.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Like with 確か, which means <kanji>certain</kanji>, this is the verb version of that. So when you "do certain" you are going <vocabulary>to make sure of</vocabulary> something or you're going <vocabulary>to verify</vocabulary> something.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This one is kun'yomi followed by okurigana. If you remember the reading you learned with 確かに, you should know this one!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>surpass</kanji>, but this verb is intransitive, meaning we’re not focussing on who did the action, but on the action itself. So this means <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary>, as in “the storm passed”, <vocabulary>to be over</vocabulary> as in “winter’s over”, or <vocabulary>to be too much</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

In order for the storm <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary> you’re going to have to <reading>sue</reading> (す) it. Sadly storms won’t pass unless you take legal action these days.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 飛ぶ is to fly? Well this word is for when you make some thing fly. So, this word is <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to send something flying</vocabulary>. It also means <vocabulary>to skip over something</vocabulary>, such as someone's turn or a question on a test.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is just like 飛ぶ, so if you know that reading you're close. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember the second part:

You can use your strength <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary>, and that something is a <reading>bus</reading> (ばす). You're that buff!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is where the <kanji>bus</kanji> (バス) halts. It's the <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>gentle</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>gentle</vocabulary> (but also <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>warm hearted</vocabulary>).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What do people who are <vocabulary>gentle</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary> say when someone asks of them a favor? Always "<reading>yessir</reading>" (やさ). Always, always "yessir"!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>cut off</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary>.

This is often used metaphorically to describe cutting off things that tie us down mentally or societally. This includes ending bad habits, so it also means <vocabulary>to quit doing something</vocabulary>.

Don't confuse this with 断る which means "to refuse." You know this is to cut off because of the つ, which hints that you have had <reading>two</reading> (つ) too many chocolates, and it's time to cut you off.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: URGH! The reading isn't even the same as 断る, how frustrating. <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary> is read as たつ. Instead of eating too many chocolates and getting cut off, maybe you're eating too many tater <reading>tots</reading> (たつ). Don't eat so many of those, it's unhealthy. You have <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary> tater tots from your diet so you don't get fat.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>present time</kanji> is the time you're <vocabulary>actually</vocabulary> in. You aren't <vocabulary>really</vocabulary> in any other time, because that's not how time works!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>appear</kanji>, so this word means <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to emerge</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Some kind of paranormal entity starts <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary> in front of you. "You… <reading>are a wa</reading>lrus (あらわ)!" you scream, terrified. Yes, it seems a ghostly walrus has appeared before you. It has come from beyond the grave to warn you that the Crabigator will get you if you don't do your reviews!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 確認 is confirmation. When that's a verb, you have <vocabulary>to confirm</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to verify</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help immensely if you know the word 確認 already as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>descend</kanji>, but this verb vocab word is <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary>, as in, to get off the train, or to get out of the car. If you think about trains back in the day, you had to descend down to the platform to get out of them, which is how this word became what it is. You know that this word is the "to get off" word because once you get off the train, you enter the <reading>real</reading> (りる) world, where hardships are real and not as comfy as the train.

Figuratively, this word also means <vocabulary>to step down</vocabulary>, as in "to give up" or "to resign” from something. For example, you can say ニュース番組を降りる (to step down from a news program) or ゲームを降りる (to drop out of a game).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike anything you've seen with this kanji. Just think about how you have <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary> at <reading>O</reading>-station. None of the other letters are your stop. Just <reading>O</reading>-Station (お).
