vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 過ぎる is <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary>. When you pass what is needed, what are you left with? Just this word: <vocabulary>too much</vocabulary>. This can also mean <vocabulary>after</vocabulary>, as in "after 5pm", and <vocabulary>past</vocabulary>, as in "past sixty".
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 過ぎる. Know that and you know <vocabulary>too much</vocabulary>. Dial it down to get 過ぎ.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>connection</kanji>. This is a verb, so one meaning is <vocabulary>to be connected</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to be related</vocabulary>. Basically things that have to do with being connected with something else.

Does this all sound familiar? In fact, this is another way to write 関わる, which you already learned! The two have exactly the same meaning, but this version is a bit less common.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. It's exactly the same as the reading for 関わる, so here's a reminder of that mnemonic to help you:

Remember the "<reading>Kaw Kaw</reading> (かか) Crow Gang"? They are bad news, always eating from garbage and squawking "kaw kaw"... You don't want <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> with them.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This is the verb version of the kanji <kanji>superior</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>to surpass</vocabulary>. Someone who is superior is always going to surpass and <vocabulary>to excel</vocabulary> beyond others. That's what makes them so superior in the first place!

This is a formal word that is often used in writing or formal speech.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: If you want to surpass everyone, you have to be super good (すぐ) at stuff. Like, super good at everything. Not pretty good, not really good — super good. Only then can you surpass all the others.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>replace</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to replace</vocabulary>. You know that you're doing the replacing because of the <reading>air</reading> (える). You're replacing the air as quickly as you can because if you don't you wouldn't be able to breathe in this small room.

替える means to replace something with another item of the same kind or equivalent, rather than changing its state. Wondering how it differs from 代える? While 代える stresses that you’re using someone or something “in place of another,” 替える simply indicates the act of swapping one thing for another similar thing.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the transitive version of 現れる (to appear), so rather than something appearing on its own, you're making it appear. So this word means <vocabulary>to show</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to reveal</vocabulary>, but it's usually used in set phrases like 姿を現す (to show up) or 正体を現す (to reveal one's true nature).
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with 現れる, but here's a mnemonic to help you:

The monster under your bed decides <vocabulary>to show</vocabulary> you its true form. "You… <reading>are a wa</reading>lrus (あらわ)?" you ask, shocked. Evidently, the monster under your bed was actually just a walrus who got in one day when you left the window open. You feel silly for being scared of it for so long, but you're glad it finally showed itself to you.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 降りる means "to get off." This is when you're helping something else descend down from something, not when you yourself are getting down. So it means <vocabulary>to take down</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lower</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading, which you already learned. Go you!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>replace</kanji>, and this word means <vocabulary>to be replaced</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be substituted</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to be switched</vocabulary>.

Wondering about the difference between 代わる and 替わる? 代わる is used when someone or something takes the place of another, like filling in for a sick coworker. Whereas 替わる is used when things or situations switch places or are replaced with something new, like when talking about generations changing or a new governmental cabinet taking over.

This verb is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You'll sometimes see it with the particle を, though, because the を is showing a "path" rather than a direct object in this case. For example, 席を替わる (to switch seats) indicates your location is moving from one seat to another. Likewise, 電話を替わる indicates that a call is being handed off to another person.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
過ぎる means "to pass," and 過ごす is <vocabulary>to pass time</vocabulary>.

過ごす refers to how you live through or experience your time. So it usually needs some extra context when you use it, like what you do while passing time, who you pass it with, or what was it like. Check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as  過ぎる. If you know it, it's OK <vocabulary>to pass time</vocabulary> relaxing for a bit! If you don’t know it, maybe it's good <vocabulary>to spend time</vocabulary> reviewing…

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Coins? Bills? <kanji>Both</kanji> can be <kanji>replace</kanji>d if you want to <vocabulary>change money</vocabulary> at this <vocabulary>money exchange</vocabulary>. Just don’t do your <vocabulary>currency exchange</vocabulary> at the airport — the rates aren’t so great.

You'll probably see this word the most in arcades where you can go to the 両替 machine and get coins to feed your crane game addiction.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading here is a bit weird. Instead of just being か (it changes to が for the rendaku), it is がえ. Just think that if you want change exchanged, I'm your <reading>guy</reading> (がえ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Each time you take a <kanji>step</kanji> up, you reach a new <kanji>floor</kanji>… a new <vocabulary>stage</vocabulary>! We're talking metaphorical stages. You're making all kinds of progress. The first stage, the second stage. The third <vocabulary>phase</vocabulary>. Man, you're blowing through all the stages and phases of Japanese learning. Keep it up!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: To get to another <kanji>floor</kanji> you have to go up one <kanji>step</kanji>, then another, and another… These are <vocabulary>stairs</vocabulary>. The word you're looking for is stairs! Do you have any 階段 in your house?
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

券 is a standalone word that means <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary>, but it's commonly used as a suffix to form words like 入場券 (admission ticket), 割引券 (discount <vocabulary>coupon</vocabulary>), or 定期券 (commuter <vocabulary>pass</vocabulary>).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Usually it's attached to things, because it tells you what kind of ticket something is.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>descend</kanji>, but this word means something closer to <vocabulary>to fall</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come down</vocabulary>.

降る is commonly used when talking about the weather, like 雨が降る (it rains) or 雪が降る (it snows). It also applies to other things falling from above, like 火山灰が降る (volcanic ash falls) or even figuratively, as in 幸運が降ってくる (good luck comes your way).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The rain is <vocabulary>to fall</vocabulary> and you're outside anyway with your mouth open so you'll get a mouth <reading>full</reading> (ふる) of rainwater! All the ponds, wells, and your yard will be full of water too!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>pleasant</kanji>? It is also <vocabulary>pleasant</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word's reading is pretty weird. We're going to think back to a couple different words to put this one together. The word for heart (心), is こころ. The word for good is よい (or いい, but for this word's sake, よい). A "good heart (feeling)" is one where your heart feels nice and warm and fuzzy (figuratively, not literally. If it's literal, go to the hospital please). That is a <vocabulary>pleasant</vocabulary> feeling. A こころよい feeling.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: It's <kanji>pleasant</kanji> but also <kanji>fast</kanji>. When getting on a train, it's nice to find a train that's both of these things. What makes it pleasant? That would be the <vocabulary>high speed</vocabulary>. What makes it fast? Also the <vocabulary>high speed</vocabulary>. Really, if you're on a train you'd rather get to your destination sooner than later, so a high speed 快速 train is the way to go.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>push</kanji>, and this verb means things like <vocabulary>to hold something down</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to grasp something</vocabulary>. This verb is pretty versatile, and you can use it if you're holding down a piece of paper, holding a cloth to a wound, or grasping a concept.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, so hopefully you can read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>push</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to push</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji, actually!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>normal</kanji> <kanji>steps</kanji> are the ones that are totally <vocabulary>usual</vocabulary>. They're the ones you <vocabulary>usually</vocabulary> do, unlike those weird not usual steps.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 押し is <kanji>push</kanji>, and a ボタン is a button, then you have yourself a <vocabulary>push button</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 押す.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>throw away</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to throw away</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji, so no need <vocabulary>to throw away</vocabulary> that bit of knowledge just yet!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned.

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: These look like <radical>fins</radical>. What's a pair of disembodied fins doing here?! Some fish must have left them here by accident. Bet they're really missing these fins right about now.
This looks like something you'd put on a kettle or a pot, right? It even has a little handle to make sure you don't burn yourself. This is some kind of <radical>lid</radical>.
Imagine a guy flexing his arm downward to show off his steroid-pumped arm. It's huge. It's so full of <radical>power</radical>. RARRRWWWRRR!!

This radical looks just like a stick figure—more specifically, a really <radical>big</radical> guy with his arms stretched out nice and big. When you see this radical, just think big, because this guy is really BIG!
This radical looks like a curtsying <radical>woman</radical>. Another way to think of it could be as two stacked Xs, since women generally have XX chromosomes. That's why this is the woman radical.
Imagine viewing this one from above — looks like a couple of streets, right? Maybe a three-way intersection at the top there? Well, that's why this is the radical for <radical>street</radical>.
This looks just like a folding <radical>stool</radical>, am I right?
This is the radical for <radical>child</radical>. Aww, see how they're wearing a cap and have their little arms stretched out? You can almost hear them saying "pick me up!" A very child-like child.
See the <radical>flag</radical> in this radical? There's a pole with a flag on the end of it, blowing in the wind. Basically, this radical looks just like a flag.
These three streaks look like the flowing locks of someone's <radical>hair</radical>. Pretty easy to see and remember that this is the hair radical, right?

This is the <radical>moon</radical> radical. See how it looks like a crescent moon with a couple of little clouds floating by? Try not to mix this up with the evening radical 夕 — you can see the whole crescent moon this time, so obviously this should be the radical for moon!

This is the radical for <radical>fire</radical>. It's got three little flames on top and even a couple logs underneath.

But if it helps you can also focus on the person radical here. See it? It's got things coming off of it... What are those thi— OH MY GOD IT'S FIRE!!! Help, help! Put the fire out! Wait, it's fine… It's just the fire radical.
This radical looks like a dude running off to the right. He's heading in a very distinct <radical>direction</radical>. Which direction was it again?

This is the <radical>father</radical> radical, since you can see a very fatherly face in it — two droopy eyes at the top, a big nose in the middle, and a mustache flaring out at the bottom. Sort of a generic older gentleman father-type face, isn't it?

Put a cross over the mouth of a container full of all the <radical>old</radical> things you no longer need. They've all served their purpose but have gotten old, so it's now time to let them rest in peace under the cross. Goodbye, old things!

This looks like a little whiteboard to keep track of your <radical>task</radical>s for the day. It's got three little legs on the bottom. And see those blank squares? They're sticky notes you can write your tasks on. Work tasks, school tasks, WaniKani reviews… So what are your tasks for today? Imagine putting them in those little squares.

This is a gun on top of a big person. The gun is big too, obviously. Why is this big guy's gun so big? Because it shoots <radical>arrow</radical>s! Bullets are pretty small, so the guns that shoot them can be any size. But you need a big gun if you want to shoot a big arrow, right? That's why this is the radical for arrow.

Have you ever used one of those triangular rulers? This looks just like one of those, because this is the <radical>measurement</radical> radical. Just think of all the angles you could measure with this thing!

This radical looks like some sort of <radical>spirit</radical>. It faces to the left with a big hood over its head, and creepy arms slanting downward at the sides. Can you picture it?

If not, just think of this as the katakana character for "ne." Ne for necromancer, bringing back spirits from the grave! OooooOOoooOoo!

The leader (ｲ) radical has a little something extra on top of him — he's got a casual cap on because it's his day off. And what does he like to do on his day off? He likes to <radical>loiter</radical>. Look at him just loitering around. What a loiterer.
You know <radical>Wolverine</radical> from the X-Men? He has three claws that come out of his hand whenever he needs to fight, not at all unlike the radical you see here.
You have 十 plus 十 (never mind that the left one is kinda curvy)... What do you get when you add these two kanji together? You get <radical>twenty</radical>.

Remember the eye radical? Imagine that's your eye now, and there's a drop of paint falling into it, making your eye color unique. Now it's what makes you you. It's what makes you your <radical>self</radical>.

You have the radicals for loiter, two, and barb. Someone who uses two barbs on you while you're loitering really wants you to <radical>GO</radical>!! GO on, stop loitering outside of my convenience store, ya dang kids!
There's a <radical>ladle</radical> scooping up two drops of liquid. See the handle and the scoop part of the ladle? Imagine ladling some water into your mouth. Mmm.

First of all, there's a cross making up the middle, which automatically makes this a religion-based radical. That cross is the frame of someone's body and the things coming off of it are wings. This is an <radical>angel</radical>.
This radical looks like the fire from the burner of a stove. That's because this is the <radical>boil</radical> radical. You need to boil a bunch of water over some flames.

This is a tree with a drooping slide shape on top. What causes the top of plants to sag? The <radical>grain</radical>s. Imagine seeing how the heads of wheat or rice droop when they're ready for harvest. It will look like this radical. Look at all that ripe grain!

This might remind you of 米, which has three stalks sprouting upward. You can tell the difference because the top of this one is slanted from the weight of the ripe grain.
This is a very fluffy <radical>sheep</radical>. See the two horns poking up and all its wool poking out to the side? It's so fluffy that you can hardly see its tiny little legs. What a cute sheep!

This radical is just like the katakana character "ma" (マ). So let's keep things simple and make the radical <radical>mama</radical>. It even looks like a mama leaning over and gently tapping her baby to help them fall asleep.

Someone has a toe in their mouth. She's a fortune teller telling your <radical>fortune</radical>. But for her to do it, she has to take one of your toes and taste it. This better be a good fortune for you to let her put your foot in her mouth.

This is the radical for <radical>cloud</radical>. See how the cloud is puffy on the bottom but has two lines up top? That's because a plane flew through it.

It was a nice cloud to hang out privately in, until that darn plane came through and ruined it. So much for your private cloud!

Think of an old-style <radical>lantern</radical>. It's in a box-shaped holder lined with rice paper and sits on four legs (you can only see two from this angle though). You can imagine people using these before electricity, right? That's why this radical is a lantern.

A leaf-shaped protrusion coming out of a shellfish. What is it? The mysterious <radical>geoduck</radical>! The geoduck is a giant clam so big that most of it grows outside its shell. If you've never seen a geoduck, look it up now. You'll never be able to unsee it.

This radical is the same as the kanji you learned earlier, but the meaning is a little different. It's not just for saying things humbly, it's for being <radical>humble</radical> in general. When you see this radical, think about being humble.

You can kinda see this as someone with their hands pressed together in front of their body, in a very humble posture. Maybe a humble Buddhist monk wearing some big robes? Imagine him all humble there, head bowed, hands pressed together.

This radical looks kind of like a <radical>temple</radical>, don't you think? With all the layers and stuff? Just picture the top part as a roof, and the drop-looking bit at the bottom as a giant temple bell, with a monk standing beside it and ringing it with a large wooden beam. You see this kinda thing every day at a temple.
This kinda looks like a head with an arm under it pointing up at itself. That's why this radical means <radical>oneself</radical>. One points to oneself when one wants to… indicate oneself…

See that cliff with the white and small bits in it? That's an <radical>original</radical> cliff — we call it that because the white and small bits are actually the bones and fossils of our planet's original inhabitants, buried in the cliffside. (And this one's got a massive sign that says "ORIGINAL," because everything's gotta be a tourist spot these days… sigh.)
What do you call a prison for drops of water? A <radical>pool</radical>! The water may not like being in there, but the rest of us sure appreciate it on a hot summer day.
The flowery paragraph isn't just regular writing. It's flowery, which makes it a <radical>poem</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means  <radical>talent</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>together</radical>. And see how it kind of looks like two people happily sitting together arm-in-arm? These two clearly enjoy doing stuff together. They're together so much they're practically joined at the hip.

Alternatively, think of this as blackjack cards held together by fins. Fish love blackjack because the hands are usually just a few cards, so even fins can hold them together.

When you're in prison, your only task is to count every <radical>angle</radical> in your cell. You count the angles of the walls and ceiling over and over again to pass the time. How many angles could there be in a room with four walls? Picture it and try to count those angles now.
See the guy sitting in the box? His head is sticking out of the top. That's a <radical>bathtub</radical> he's sitting in.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>cheap</radical>.

This is the inside radical, since it looks like a person (人) inside a… head (冂)? I guess if you think about it, every person is sort of trapped inside their own head. Imagine a second, tinier version of you sitting up inside that head of yours, like a mecha pilot. Yep, that's real you. The you inside.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>request</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: Look at the ground! You spilled some water drops, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?

This radical looks like a <radical>helicopter</radical> coming straight at you, doesn't it? You can't see the tail part because it's behind the bigger front cab of the helicopter. But you can see the front windows and the big spinning blade on top.
This looks a lot like a <radical>gun</radical> pointing to the right. You have a handle on the left, and the barrel pointing to the right. Imagine it hanging in a case on the wall in a museum.
Do you know those rice paddy hats? The ones shaped just like this radical? That's why this radical is a <radical>hat</radical>.
The three horns represent the <radical>triceratops</radical>, one of the most awesome dinosaurs ever.

There's the bottom of a shoe with spikes coming out of it. Only one kind of shoe is like this, and that's a <radical>cleat</radical>. You know, like those studded shoes athletes wear. Soccer cleats, baseball cleats, running cleats… You knew they were called cleats, right?

This is a <radical>cape</radical>, like the kind a superhero would wear. Use your imagination to picture a hero facing left, with a cape tied around their neck and hanging down their back. With that cape on, they're ready to save the world!

This radical has a figure reaching out both hands at you with some dirt on his head. This is a <radical>zombie</radical>, and he must have just recently dug himself out of the grave by the looks of it.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>festival</radical>.

This is the <radical>droopy</radical> radical because it looks like a droopy ice cream cake on a stand. Melty goodness droops over the edge of each layer, and the whole top section is drooping toward the left like it's about to give in to gravity. Imagine how melted it must be for it to be so droopy… better eat it quick.

This is the <radical>broom</radical> radical, because the top part looks like a sideways hand broom and the bottom part looks like a dustpan.

Alternatively, you can remember this one with its components: Wolverine wipes his forehead with a towel every time he picks up a broom, because sweeping gets him sweaty fast. Poor guy can fight supervillains all day, but give him a broom and he's instantly exhausted.

example.jp: 旅行の準備をしています。
example.furigana: りょこうのじゅんびをしています
example.en: I am preparing for the trip.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Riding a <radical>tsunami</radical> you see a <radical>turkey</radical> carrying a <radical>cross</radical>, but that’s pretty <kanji>standard</kanji> here. This is your dreamland. You always dream about tsunamis and the turkeys carrying crosses that ride them. This might be strange for other people, but for you it’s pretty normal.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: These wacky dreams are only <kanji>standard</kanji> fare in <reading>June</reading> (じゅん) though. You don’t have them any other time of the year, just in June. You don’t know why June is the only time you have dreams about tsunami riding turkeys, but that’s just the way it is.

compounds.meaning: to prepare, to provide, to have

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> put <radical>flowers</radical> on a <radical>cliff</radical>. That is their <radical>task</radical>. It is to <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Why do they <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers? It's all for the <reading>bee</reading>s (び).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>Viking</radical> who knows how to use a <radical>bathtub</radical> will have to <kanji>manage</kanji> all the baths for the other Vikings. Vikings aren't so great with bathing... if you can get one Viking to figure it out he has to manage the rest of them.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The poor Viking trying to <kanji>manage</kanji> all the others keeps having to confiscate <reading>a</reading>corns (えい). "You can't take baths in acorns and wood, it has to be water!" he shouts.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gate</radical> to <radical>talent</radical> is now <kanji>closed</kanji>. In fact, the gate to talent is always closed. It's not like anyone can just waltz in and get themselves some talent. You have to work for it! You have to work hard to get through that closed gate to talent!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Outside the talent gate that's always <kanji>closed</kanji>, <reading>hay</reading> (へい) is piled up to make beds for the people who are still trying to get in. Who knows how long they'll be there outside the closed gate, sleeping in the hay, but they're all working hard to become talented.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cheap</radical> <radical>tree</radical> has a <kanji>plan</kanji>. A plan to stay cheap.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The cheap tree's <kanji>plan</kanji> involves only buying <reading>an</reading>chovies (あん) and surviving on them. Good exposure to the sun and fresh water is too expensive. The tree plans to save money by eating anchovies.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>inside</radical> radical and the <kanji>inside</kanji> kanji are exactly the same, yay. But is the radical inside the kanji here, or is the kanji inside the radical? I don't know, it's inside-ception.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If you need to get <kanji>inside</kanji> something, the quickest way is to use a <reading>kni</reading>fe (ない). With a knife, you can cut something open and see what's inside it and <kanji>within</kanji> it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What does your <radical>mama</radical> tell you to do in the <radical>street</radical>? Look before you cross! You gotta do it <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, or it could be too late.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you look <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, you see a <reading>yo-</reading>yo (よ) lying in the street.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You tie a <radical>thread</radical> on your finger before jumping in the <radical>pool</radical> to remind yourself of the <kanji>promise</kanji> you made to your mother. The thread represents the promise you made to mow the lawn after you finished swimming in the pool.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you get out of the pool, you keep the <kanji>promise</kanji> you made to your mother. So you get on your <reading>yak</reading> (やく) powered mower and trim the grass. Yes, your mower is pulled by a yak. It’s very efficient.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you have a <radical>fire</radical> and a <radical>helicopter</radical> hovering beside it, there's going to be a lot of <radical>dirt</radical> and <kanji>smoke</kanji> billowing around. Mostly smoke, on account of the fire. Now it's in your eyes and mouth. It gets in your lungs and you can't breathe. Why, helicopter, why!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>smoke</kanji> is too much and you realize this is the <reading>en</reading>d (えん) for you. You're gonna die here!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What superhero is most like a <radical>triceratops</radical>? …If you said <radical>Wolverine</radical>, you're <kanji>correct</kanji>! Why is that the <kanji>right</kanji> answer? Because the triceratops has three horns, and Wolverine has three blades coming out of his hands. It's obvious, isn't it? But you knew that of course.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Because you got the answer <kanji>correct</kanji>, you win a free trip to <reading>とう</reading>きょう. Congrats!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>hat</radical> crowns the <radical>king</radical>, because <kanji>all</kanji> kings must have one.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But, as you're going through <kanji>all</kanji> the kings, it turns out not all of them have hats after all. The last one you come to is hatless. He's the king of <reading>Zen</reading> (ぜん). He has simple clothes and a shaved head, unlike all the other fancy kings standing around nearby.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Under your <radical>roof</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> there are more <radical>mouth</radical>s to feed because you let <kanji>guest</kanji>s stay with you when it's cold. Some of them aren't family, so they have to pay to stay under your roof and get food. Those are <kanji>customer</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: One of your <kanji>guest</kanji>s is a regular named <reading>Kyaku</reading> (きゃく) the <kanji>customer</kanji>. Kyaku is always staying over at one place or another, so everyone knows their name.

compounds.meaning: an honorific added to people's names, particularly in letters

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
By a <radical>tree</radical>, there's a <radical>sheep</radical> in the <radical>water</radical> with a <kanji>formal name ender</kanji>. That means everyone calls him Sheep-sama. No one calls him just "Sheep," since he's kind of a big deal. He's actually like sheep royalty. When he's not in his castle, Sheep-sama enjoys playing in the water by the trees.

This can also mean <kanji>manner</kanji>, as in your manner of doing things. I guess someone with a formal name ender has a different manner of doing things.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This sheep with the <kanji>formal name ender</kanji> only likes to play outside in the water during the <reading>summer</reading> (さま). Summer is the best season for this fancy sheep. The other seasons just can't compare.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Angle</radical> your <radical>sword</radical> correctly at this <radical>cow</radical> to <kanji>solve</kanji> its riddle. The key is to <kanji>untie</kanji> the cow with the sword without hurting it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Did I mention that you have to <kanji>solve</kanji> this whole riddle while on a <reading>kay</reading>ak (かい)? No?! Whoops.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Next to the <radical>cross</radical> we combine our <radical>power</radical> <radical>power</radical> <radical>power</radical> so that we have <kanji>cooperation</kanji>. And with our powers combined, we become stronger than we ever could have been apart, lifting the cross above our heads!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Nowhere is the power of cooperation more apparent than in <reading>きょう</reading>と. When invaders are attacking, when the townspeople want to rebel, when there is a kitty up a tree, the people combine their power from all reaches of Japan and cross into きょうと to put a stop to the madness through cooperation.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>original</radical> <radical>geoduck</radical> had a <kanji>request</kanji>. He wants there to be more geoducks in the world!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The only person that would even hear the geoduck's <kanji>request</kanji> was <reading>Gan</reading>dhi (がん). Gandhi closed his eyes, sat down, and spread the geoduck's request to the rest of the world.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's an <radical>arrow</radical> in a <radical>turkey</radical> that you can <radical>see</radical> in your <kanji>view</kanji>. The turkey seems to be viewing you too, from afar.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>view</kanji> the turkey, Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) suddenly comes into your view too. He towers over the injured turkey, leans down, and... pulls the arrow out!?

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You examine the <radical>mouth</radical> of a <radical>zombie</radical> and find a small <kanji>garden</kanji> in there. There are even benches... it looks like a <kanji>park</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You look closer at the <kanji>garden</kanji> and suddenly everything <reading>en</reading>ds (えん).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>tsunami</radical> coming and you want to be <radical>together</radical> with it by <radical>yourself</radical> (oneself) so you go to the <kanji>harbor</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you look around at the <kanji>harbor</kanji> in your last moments you suddenly see someone in the water. It's <reading>こう</reading>いち! He's sitting in an inner tube in the harbor waiting for the tsunami too.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: On a <radical>scooter</radical> running in one <radical>direction</radical> is a <radical>gun</radical>-toting <radical>child</radical>. This is a terribly dangerous situation, but to the child it is just <kanji>play</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Everything is <kanji>play</kanji> for <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう), even if it's a terrible, scary, not good situation like this one.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> that's <radical>big</radical> is a true <kanji>beauty</kanji>. Big is <kanji>beautiful</kanji>, and that's all the more true for sheep.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The big sheep's <kanji>beauty</kanji> has attracted a swarm of <reading>bee</reading>s (び). The sheep is so beautiful that the bees have mistaken it for a flower.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There <radical>go</radical> some <radical>angel</radical>s with <radical>drop</radical>s on their shoulders. Carrying drops like that requires <kanji>technique</kanji>. It’s a real <kanji>art</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Angels are so good at this because they are trained in nin<reading>jutsu</reading> (じゅつ), or the "ninja techniques." Everyone knows that ninjas are great at carrying drops on the go!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>spirit</radical> should feel <radical>humble</radical> before a <kanji>god</kanji>'s <kanji>spirit</kanji>. You never really feel humble in front of anyone else, but if you meet a god's spirit… Well, you should probably lower yourself appropriately. Gods have powerful spirits.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you meet a <kanji>god</kanji>'s <kanji>spirit</kanji>, you need to get down on your <reading>shin</reading>s (しん). Get down on your ankles? No, not low enough. Knees? No, no, get your shins flat on the ground to show how humble you really are. Luckily, you're wearing <reading>jean</reading>s (じん), so at least that will stop your poor shins getting chafed!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>temple</radical> radical and the <kanji>temple</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Brilliant.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Someone died. You ask how this person died, the person who's getting buried by the <kanji>temple</kanji>. The priest/monk says it was in a tragic <reading>terror</reading> (てら) attack.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>loiter</radical> around with a <radical>weapon</radical> because you're currently doing your <kanji>service</kanji> and <kanji>duty</kanji> to your country. You're standing guard outside, waiting just in case something will happen.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're about halfway through your <kanji>service</kanji>, when a <reading>yak</reading> (やく) walks by. It stops directly in front of you and grunts. "Excuse me, Mr. Yak, but it's my <kanji>duty</kanji> to escort you away from my country."

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>droopy</radical> <radical>building</radical> is where people droop under big sacks of <kanji>mail</kanji>, aka a <kanji>post</kanji> office.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Because it's such a physically demanding job, all the <kanji>mail</kanji> carriers in this <kanji>post</kanji> office are <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう). Only the youths can handle this kind of heavy mail-bag lifting, I guess.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your nation's <radical>flag</radical> sits on top of a <radical>cape</radical>d <radical>mouth</radical>. This is the symbol for the "<kanji>Bureau</kanji> of Secret Things." It's a special <kanji>department</kanji> of your government made to keep things hidden.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>bureau</kanji>'s best-kept secret is cloaking devices that <reading>cloak you</reading> (きょく) with the press of a button.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You put a <radical>lid</radical> on your <radical>father</radical>. But, he won't taste good alone, so you <kanji>mix</kanji> in some other ingredients. They <kanji>mingle</kanji> inside the pot with him.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: With a <kanji>mix</kanji> of your father and other ingredients <kanji>mingl</kanji>ing in your cooking pot, you lift up the lid... your father pops up. Your father is <reading>こう</reading>いち. He stares back at you with a big smile.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>sheep</radical> tries its hoof at <radical>construction</radical>, it gains <kanji>distinction</kanji>. Now that is something that really sets a sheep apart! After all, have you ever seen a sheep working in construction?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The extra <kanji>distinction</kanji> of this sheep is that its really skilled with a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). That's why it's so good at construction.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fortune</radical> <radical>boil</radical>s down to a single <kanji>point</kanji> in time. One point in time determines how the rest of your future will go.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you stare at the <kanji>point</kanji>, you watch in awe as it moves to the <reading>ten</reading> (てん) spot in a long series of numbers.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>tree</radical> must've been sent from <radical>heaven</radical>, because it has a <radical>mouth</radical> and a <radical>mustache</radical>. Like some kind of special heaven tree that talks. And why was it sent? To be a <kanji>bridge</kanji>. To be the great heavenly bridge that we all, someday, must cross.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Actually, to get across this <kanji>bridge</kanji> you have to give it some <reading>hash</reading> (はし) browns. That's what the bridge's mouth is for. Hash browns to get across the heaven bridge? Small price to pay, really.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have <radical>fins</radical> in <radical>private</radical>. But, you want the world to see them, so you take them <kanji>public</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You head out into the <kanji>public</kanji> where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of <reading>こう</reading>いちs walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Someone throws a <radical>cleat</radical> at your <radical>forehead</radical> while you sit on a <radical>stool</radical>. You must <kanji>accept</kanji> this. Then another guy cleats you in the forehead, but you remain on the stool and <kanji>receive</kanji> it without complaint. This is some kind of acceptance ritual for the most prestigious Spanish soccer club in the world. If a cleat to the forehead doesn't knock you off the stool, you'll receive an offer to join.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After they <kanji>accept</kanji> you, they give you a small <reading>ju</reading>ice (じゅ) box. It's to help you recover from the trauma of getting kicked. And you <kanji>receive</kanji> the juice with grace.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When you take your <radical>leader</radical>'s <radical>measurement</radical>s, you realize they're too short, so you <kanji>attach</kanji> things to them to make the measurements more impressive. Attach some heels to the shoes, then attach another head on top of theirs. There — perfect measurements thanks to these attachments.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You have to remember the kun'yomi reading of this kanji, and the part you need to remember is つ. So, think of how you would <kanji>attach</kanji> something to something else. What would you need? You'd need <reading>two</reading> (つ) things to put together!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You scoop some <radical>grain</radical>s into a <radical>ladle</radical> to do <kanji>science</kanji>. You're doing experiments on these grains in your science <kanji>course</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Using your <kanji>science</kanji> skills, the right temperatures and measurements, you manage to get these grains to grow into a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). This is the science <kanji>department</kanji>'s special car now!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You're all by your<radical>self</radical> and you have to check your <radical>rice paddie</radical>s — all <radical>twenty</radical> of them! Luckily, you have an incredible <kanji>nose</kanji>, so you can quickly assess the state of your twenty rice paddies with just a few sniffs.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you sniff your rice paddies, an unexpected smell wafts into your <kanji>nose</kanji>: <reading>花</reading>s (はな). Oh no — did you accidentally plant 花s instead of rice? Oh well, the 花s are putting your nose in such a state of bliss that you actually think things might be better this way.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: See that <radical>woman</radical> with the <radical>broom</radical>? That's the <kanji>lady</kanji> of the house. She's getting ready to hand that broom to you — her butler — because you missed a spot over there.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Instead of your name, the <kanji>lady</kanji> of the house just calls you "<reading>foo</reading>l" (ふ). You rarely meet her ladyship's lofty standards, so from her perspective you're just a silly nincompoop fool who can't get anything right.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You're walking at night when you discover a <radical>lantern</radical> covered entirely in <radical>hair</radical>, making it a very strange <kanji>shape</kanji>. In fact, this is a <kanji>form</kanji> you'd never expect a lantern to take.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You stare at the <kanji>shape</kanji> until you finally recognize it: <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい)! Well, it's hairy, glowing cake, but it's still shaped like a big slice of cake.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you have a <radical>mustache</radical> and you hit your <radical>forehead</radical> on the <radical>moon</radical>, you’re probably going to break a <kanji>bone</kanji>. Ok, so it doesn’t matter so much if you have a mustache, but if you’re travelling fast enough to make it to the moon, you’re definitely breaking a bone if you run into it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Outer space is cold, and if you're traveling to the moon, you're going to need a lot of <reading>coats</reading> (こつ). All of these coats will keep you warm, even if you do end up breaking your forehead <kanji>bone</kanji>.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If your <radical>fingers</radical> are strong enough, you can take an <radical>axe</radical> and <kanji>fold</kanji> it in half. But be careful not to <kanji>bend</kanji> it too far, or you might just <kanji>break</kanji> it!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, as you <kanji>fold</kanji> these axes in half you realize they come in <reading>sets</reading> (せつ), so there are twice the axes you thought there would be. To compensate, you start folding them in sets too.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you put your <radical>mouth</radical> on a <radical>tree</radical> and try to eat it, you’re probably a <kanji>distressed</kanji> and <kanji>troubled</kanji> individual (unless you’re a woodchuck). You don’t need to eat this tree, you have plenty of food at home. Get your mouth off that tree you distressed child.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You thought you were the most <kanji>distressed</kanji> and <kanji>troubled</kanji> person in this situation, but then you look up and see a very equally distressed and troubled <reading>con</reading>dor (こん). The tree you've been mouthing is its home. And now you've slobbered all over it, ruining this condor's day.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A long time ago a huge <radical>tsunami</radical> swept a <radical>triceratops</radical> up into the <radical>moon</radical> and <kanji>extinguish</kanji>ed its life.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This famous event where almost all life was <kanji>extinguish</kanji>ed is reenacted every year for the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). He's got a bit of an unhealthy obsession with extinguishing life...

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If there is a <radical>building</radical> in the <radical>direction</radical> you want to go it will <kanji>prevent</kanji> you from going any further. Like, come on kid, you think you can just walk right through a building? Don't make me laugh!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The building is <kanji>prevent</kanji>ing you from going the right direction, so you pull a <reading>bow</reading>ling (ぼう) ball out of your bag, aim, and bowl the building over. The building, and all the ones around it, go tumbling down. But now the rubble is preventing you from going further.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>request</radical> that <radical>winter</radical> <kanji>rescue</kanji> you from the warmth of the other seasons.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You get a note in the mail from winter! This is it, you're going to be rescued! You open the note and it says, "I have <kanji>rescue</kanji>d you with this <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう)." A cucumber falls out of the note.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>poem</radical> about <radical>winter</radical> that you <radical>say</radical> to <kanji>warn</kanji> people against going outside. It's cold and dangerous in winter! You <kanji>admonish</kanji> anyone and everyone you see going out there with your scary winter poem.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To make sure people listen to your <kanji>warn</kanji>ing, you threaten to take away their <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい). People will do anything for cake, so when you bring it up, they actually take your attempts to warn them about winter seriously.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you're on the <radical>roof</radical> of the <radical>festival</radical> you'll have to <kanji>guess</kanji> what's actually going on below you. You can kind of see that there are rides and maybe food? It smells like food. But you have to guess on the specifics because you're above it and not in it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To get a better <kanji>guess</kanji>, you ask <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) for help. She's that little girl you know from some earlier mnemonics, and she happens to be up on the roof with you. Picture her as you ask, "What's your guess, Satsuki?"

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>old</radical> <radical>winter</radical> is to blame for today's <kanji>circumstance</kanji>. It is the <kanji>reason</kanji> things are bad now.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: In reality, this <kanji>circumstance</kanji> was actually caused by a single <reading>子</reading> (こ), though. This kid went through town, destroying everything in their path.

kanji.kunyomi: つたえる, つたわる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> has a <radical>cloud</radical> that he uses to <kanji>transmit</kanji> all of the messages he needs to send to his people. The cloud floats above him and when he wants to tell people something he just whispers into the cloud and it transmits his message really, really loudly to all of them.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As the leader <kanji>transmit</kanji>s his latest series of messages to you and the others, you notice a pretty large <reading>den</reading>t (でん) in it. That dent is probably a clue to what this cloud is really made of.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word share one of the same meanings: <vocabulary>form</vocabulary>. It doesn't just mean form though, it means <vocabulary>tense</vocabulary> too. Like verb tense.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>mix</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to mix something</vocabulary>. 

It’s transitive, so you’re doing the mixing. With this word, the things you’ve mixed are still distinguishable from each other. Two types of fish in your aquarium, books of different genres on your shelf — that kind of thing.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Who always said not to mix your white and red socks in the laundry? That would be your <reading>Ma</reading> (ま).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>right</kanji>. What happens when you get "a right?" You get <vocabulary>a success</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have to remember the あ portion of this word to read it. What is the correct answer that will give you <vocabulary>a success</vocabulary>? It is the first answer, <reading>A</reading> (あ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know this is a verb because it ends with an う sound. The kanji for this word is <kanji>right</kanji> or <kanji>success</kanji>, so what's the verb form of that? Turns out it's a ton of things. But it's mostly for when things go right. As in <vocabulary>to be right</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be on target</vocabulary>. 

当たる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Your answer is right, or your shot is on target. See? No direct object.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the あ portion.

When your guess turns out <vocabulary>to be right</vocabulary>, you can't help but shout, "<reading>Ah</reading> (あ)!" That "Ah" is your victory cry.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This has a little hiragana attached to it but nothing that suggests it's a verb or an adjective. That means you can assume this word has the same meaning as its parent kanji.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You wanted to remember <vocabulary>everything</vocabulary> about your trip, so you bought every <reading>souve</reading>nir (すべ) available in the entire shop to ensure you had all the mementos possible.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. As luck would have it, this word actually covers most of the meanings of the English word <vocabulary>point</vocabulary>, too! So it can mean things like <vocabulary>score</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>viewpoint</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>decimal point</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the reading for the kanji that makes it.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>attach</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to attach something</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is actually the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this one just fine.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

What <vocabulary>shape</vocabulary> do you <reading>cut a chee</reading>se (かたち) into? Stars, triangles, little cubes, hearts! Anything but the boring slices other people do. You're like a mozzarella Michelangelo, the way you cut a cheese into those beautifully sculpted <vocabulary>form</vocabulary>s.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 交ぜる means <vocabulary>to mix</vocabulary> and that the kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji> as well. So, this probably has something to do with mixing things. This word means <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>. This is when something is mixed but it's not mixed by you. It's just being mixed. Think of it this way - the じ in 交じる is Jesus, who just uses Jesus magic to mix something. So, you're not mixing it. It's just when something is <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as with 交ぜる. So long as you know the ま portion of that word's reading, you'll be able to read this word as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word is a little tricky — at first, the combination of <kanji>mix</kanji> and <kanji>number in a series</kanji> doesn't seem to add up to <vocabulary>police box</vocabulary>, but there's a catch. This word is actually an abbreviated combo of two other words: The 交 comes from 交替 (in rotation) and the 番 comes from 立番 (standing watch).

A <vocabulary>police box</vocabulary> is basically a tiny community police station staffed by one or two officers. It's something that is not common in many Western countries, but it is pretty much all over Japan.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji <kanji>all</kanji>. So, it's like you add an 'ly' to it. But, that doesn't work too well (allly? c'mon). So, instead think of this word as <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>entirely</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>truly</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

The person who <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary> doesn't understand this vocab word is <reading>Matt</reading> (まった). Be sure to take note of the small っ, too.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The kanji and the vocab are exactly the same, even the reading. This one uses the on'yomi probably because it's often attached to other words (specifying a bureau, for example), so that's why it follows jukugo conventions despite being all alone.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji 当 means <kanji>right</kanji> or <kanji>success</kanji>. So since this is a verb, you're doing right and success (which doesn't make much sense). Instead, you're guessing something and getting it right. So, this word means <vocabulary>to guess</vocabulary> something. Hopefully you don't have to guess too hard when it comes to the meaning of this word as well.

It also carries an implied contrast with 外 (outside), so it's often used to talk about yourself or your group, like うちの犬 (our dog) or うちの会社 (the company I work for). In this case, it's almost always written in hiragana as うち — which is why we used it like that in these examples (but hey, now you know where that うち is coming from!).

It's your <vocabulary>snot</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>boogers</vocabulary>. Eww, stop eating them!

You remember this because the door keeps shutting on your hand, <reading>marr</reading>ing (まる) it over and over again. Ouch.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 閉める.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: If someone seems <vocabulary>to be distressed</vocabulary> maybe someone they know is in a <reading>coma</reading> (こま). Not too many things are more distressing and troubling than that.

vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You sort of did learn this reading with the vocabulary word 煙, but this one is just different enough where we thought we should make a mnemonic for this one: 

All this <vocabulary>smoki</vocabulary>ness is from a terrible <reading>chem</reading>ical (けむ) spill that happened nearby. It was acid, so it burned everything up real good, causing the air to get pretty smoky.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Another verb version of the kanji 閉! This is a special one that can be either transitive or intransitive, so 閉じる means <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary>.

閉じる is for returning things that have expanded open back to their closed state. It's used for books, umbrellas, web browsers, and even eyes and mouths. There are some overlaps with 閉める (you can 閉じる or 閉める a gate, for example) but 閉める is mostly used for things like doors, windows, and curtains.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is different from 閉める or 閉まる. Instead, 閉じる is read とじる.

Why? Because <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> that's expanded or spread open, you always use your <reading>toe</reading> (と)! It's easy enough with books, but umbrellas are a real challenge… But you, you can do it! You have the toe-tal control and can close anything expanded to the way it was before.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You're doing a <kanji>prevent</kanji>ion. When you prevent something, what are you really doing? You're trying <vocabulary>to defend against</vocabulary> something from happening. That's why this verb is a little weird and means <vocabulary>to defend</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to protect against</vocabulary>. It can also be <vocabulary>to prevent</vocabulary>, too, but just make sure you're thinking of it more like you're defending something with your prevention.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You want <vocabulary>to defend against</vocabulary> the enemy? You should probably put out that <reading>fuse</reading> (ふせ) attached to that giant bomb first then.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>public</kanji>ly <kanji>manage</kanji>d is something that is <vocabulary>public</vocabulary> aka <vocabulary>government run</vocabulary>. Compare this to 私営 which is private / privately run.

Depending on the context, this can also be <vocabulary>information</vocabulary> and even <vocabulary>invitation</vocabulary>. These are all things that guide you in some way, after all.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading here is actually the same as 見る. This is easy to remember because the meanings are so similar too, not to mention it has a 見 right inside the kanji itself!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>guest</kanji>s who are <kanji>view</kanji>ing are the <vocabulary>audience</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>spectators</vocabulary>. That's all that viewers who are guests at a location do, right? Makes total sense.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have <vocabulary>to provide</vocabulary> your friends with their own <reading>sauna</reading> (そな) because they don't want to use your shower. This requires you to go out and buy a sauna for your house (very expensive) just so you can provide your needy friends with what they want (a sauna). Feel angry you have to provide this.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: When you follow standard procedure to provide what's needed, you make the perfect preparation! Both 準備 and 用意 mean "preparation," but the nuances are different. 準備 is about preparing in advance for an event or situation, often involving planning or setup. 用意 is about making sure specific items or resources are ready and available. For example, as part of the 準備 for a party, you might 用意 food and drinks for the guests. You could use 準備 for the food and drinks too — it would just emphasize that they're part of the overall event setup.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>mix</kanji>, but there's a <kanji>distinction</kanji> as to where you mix at this <kanji>point</kanji>. Where is this point? It can be found when two streets cross, at an <vocabulary>intersection</vocabulary>, also known as a <vocabulary>crossing</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>distinction</kanji>, and the verb version here means… a million things. Let's just focus on a few common meanings. Things with distinction tend to stick out from the others. They tend <vocabulary>to shine</vocabulary>, you know? And if you imagine shining a beam of light on something, that light tends <vocabulary>to project</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to extend outward</vocabulary>. It sticks out, shines on something, then makes that thing more distinct too. 

That's why you can say 光が差す (light shines), かげが差す (a shadow is cast), 指差す (to point at), or even カサを差す (to open and raise an umbrella). Basically, 差す usually has to do with causing something <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary>, either by shining or projecting outward.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading of the kanji is actually the same as the reading for this word, making things easy (both on'yomi and kun'yomi are さ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When you want to use your <kanji>finger</kanji> to explain the <kanji>distinction</kanji> between more than one thing, you need <vocabulary>to point at</vocabulary> it. Otherwise the person you're talking to won't be able to tell which one you're talking about.

In general, 指差す specifically means using one’s index finger to physically point at something or someone.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You learned 様 is a "formal name ender," but it can also mean <kanji>manner</kanji>. When you attach this to another noun with の and add に on the end to make it an adverb, you can describe something that's being done <vocabulary>similarly to</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>in the same way as</vocabulary> something else. In other words, something about it is just <vocabulary>like</vocabulary> that other thing — almost <vocabulary>as if</vocabulary> they were one and the same!
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Even though this word isn't a compound, 様 actually uses the on'yomi here. Since you didn't learn the on'yomi with the kanji, here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Many foods are made <vocabulary>similarly to</vocabulary> <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう): kefir, skyr, lassi… The list goes on. What's that? Those are just subcategories of yogurt, you say? No, no, no. They're made <vocabulary>in the same way as</vocabulary> yogurt and they taste a lot <vocabulary>like</vocabulary> yogurt, but they're not yogurt. Yogurt stands alone.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Full</kanji> <kanji>point</kanji>s are when you get a <vocabulary>perfect score</vocabulary>.

満点 can also be used to describe a state of being at the pinnacle of a certain quality or standard, such as サービス満点 (excellent service) or 栄養満点 (highly nutritious).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 準備 is <kanji>preparation</kanji>. This is the verb version, so it means <vocabulary>to prepare</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get ready for</vocabulary> something.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 準備.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
At the <kanji>present time</kanji> you're providing a <kanji>service</kanji>, so you're <vocabulary>actively working</vocabulary>. 現役 means you have a certain role (such as school teacher or a high school student, etc.) and you're still <vocabulary>active</vocabulary> in that role, as opposed to being retired or having graduated.

This word is also often used to describe students who are taking or have passed a university entrance exam while they were still high school students.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You learned the reading for 現 , but 役 uses a less common reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

You're <vocabulary>actively working</vocabulary> at the <reading>駅</reading> (えき) and you plan to remain <vocabulary>active</vocabulary> there forever! You sure do love that 駅, it's like you're inseparable.

When thinking about the <vocabulary>circumstance</vocabulary> of your current situation and the <vocabulary>reason</vocabulary> you're there (which is studying kanji and vocab). Whose fault is it? It's WaniKani's fault! But, your brain has been beaten to a mush from all the studying, so when you say "it's your fault" it comes out as "it's <reading>yue</reading> fault!" Go ahead and say it out loud that way.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 故 means reason. Basically, whatever comes before 故に in a statement is going to be the reason for something that comes after. So 故に works like <vocabulary>therefore</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>consequently</vocabulary>. It can also be translated as "because" or other similar conjunctions depending on the context.

Also keep in mind that 故に is mainly used in formal contexts, like in academic writing or politicians' speeches — just like "therefore" in English.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
By knowing the word 故 you'll know the reading for this word too! Here's a mnemonic in case you need a reminder, though:

You're using WaniKani, <vocabulary>therefore</vocabulary> you're studying kanji and vocab. Whose fault is it? It's WaniKani's fault! But, your brain has been beaten to a mush from all the studying, so when you say "it's your fault" it comes out as "it's <reading>yue</reading> fault!" Go ahead and say it out loud that way.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: You want <vocabulary>to play</vocabulary> with everyone, but every once in a while someone doesn't want to play with you. You know what? That's okay. If someone doesn't want to play with you, they're the <reading>a**hole</reading> (あそ), not you.
