This word is generally used in the names of gardens, like エデンの園 and 桜の園. It's also used in phrases like 学びの園, which means "school" and carries the connotation of being a haven for learning.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Which <vocabulary>garden</vocabulary> is the Garden of Eden? <reading>その</reading> garden! That garden right next to you is the Garden of Eden!

It can also use the on'yomi, though, which you've already learned. When it takes the on'yomi and is used as a standalone word, it usually refers to some kind of institution, like a 幼稚園.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>rescue</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to rescue</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to save</vocabulary>.

救う is a relatively formal word for saving someone from a dangerous or difficult situation, like 命を救う (save someone's life) or 心を救う (save someone emotionally). It's usually reserved for particularly significant or meaningful contexts, like heroes saving the world or people being saved from deep suffering or extreme hardship.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

When disaster strikes, the first place you should go <vocabulary>to rescue</vocabulary> people is a <reading>schoo</reading>l (すく) . You need <vocabulary>to save</vocabulary> all those innocent, adorable schoolchildren! Can you imagine how mad everyone would be if you skipped over a school and went to rescue people at a law firm or something? No, a school is definitely the place you've got to rescue first.

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: Close your eyes and imagine you're a kid again. Now open them and... look! It's a <radical>slide</radical>! Imagine little you sliding down this slide over and over, having a great time. Imagination + emotion makes for good memorization!

This radical is shaped like a <radical>barb</radical>. Kind of like the barb you'd see on a barbed fishing hook. Imagine that thing getting stuck in your arm or something. Not exactly pleasant. Say out loud, "Oh dang, I got a barb stuck in me!" Alright, relax, it's only a little barb.

This radical looks like a <radical>narwhal</radical>. See the tail at the bottom, and the majestic narwhal horn poking out at the top? It also looks like the katakana character ナ (na), so you can remember it that way too. Na-na-na-narwhal! Just be careful not to confuse this with the treasure radical (メ). The sideways line for that one is at more of a downward angle, like an "X." But the sideways line for narwhal is horizontal (ナ).

This looks like someone in a standing position with legs planted firmly on the ground, spreading their arms out in a T-pose to maintain balance. So that makes this the radical for <radical>stand</radical>.

You have two lines with legs below them. And what is that bit above the legs? Well, it's where you came from — your <radical>origin</radical>. Yep, between two legs is where you originated, no matter how you look at it.

This one looks like a flag, but don't be fooled — it's got a line over the top of it, kind of like a door frame. That makes this a little <radical>door</radical>. Specifically a swinging door, with the vertical line on the left being its door hinge. Kind of a weird door, it's true, but you can see it, right?

This is a few plates drying on a rack. They're stacked together in a line. Imagine reaching out and grabbing one of those plates for yourself. And you only need one, so let's call this radical <radical>plate</radical>.

For better or worse, this looks enough like the poop emoji (💩) to make this the <radical>poop</radical> radical. Try to remember it for its distinct outline. If it helps you can also note the private radical on the bottom of this one, since you should probably be in private when you poop…

Doesn't this look like a top-down view of the frame of a <radical>car</radical>? There are the axles at the top and bottom, and the body in the middle between them. That's why this is the car radical.

A rice paddy and some dirt — dirt roads, in fact, because this is a <radical>village</radical>. Small villages like this are mostly rice paddies and dirt (roads), you know? You could even think of this as a bird's-eye view of a village.

Kind of a strange <radical>tent</radical>, I'll admit, but one that will protect you from things trying to get in (that's why it has all the spikes). It's the best you can do, considering you're in a cloth tent.
Flying to the sun with wings is <radical>easy</radical>! Or so Icarus thinks. Someone should probably tell him…

A <radical>clown</radical> face, with the funny hat at the top, the silly eyes in the middle, and the big laughing mouth at the bottom. This thing is pretty cute, unlike a lot of clowns…

You could also see this as the stand radical on top of the mouth radical, since standing on their mouth is the kind of weird trick a clown would do.

This radical has a bean (the square in the middle) between the ground and some roots. That bean is going to turn into a plant someday. What will that plant produce? Great big <radical>beans</radical>, like the ones from Jack and the Beanstalk.

This radical means <radical>orders</radical>, because it looks like Napoleon with his big bicorne hat, giving orders. You move, or his orders move you.

See how his body looks like the stamp radical (卩)? If it helps, you can think of Napoleon's written orders as bearing his stamp of approval. All official orders need the stamp of that guy under the big hat, you know?

This is a ceremony radical with a slide radical. Why would a ceremony need a slide? For <radical>drunkard</radical>s, of course! People love to drink at ceremonies, and when they've had too much, those drunkards like to go down slides. If your ceremony has a slide, the drunkards will be happy.

Imagine a <radical>root</radical> vegetable, like a turnip or something. See the twisted bulb at the top, with long, stringy root tendrils dangling under it? That's why this is the root radical.

Alternatively, focus on the components: sun and kick. When the sun is out, you're outside kicking things around. But be careful — kick a root, and you might trip over it!

This looks like the shellfish radical, but a little different. It's the mighty <radical>crab</radical>! See the eyes and raised pincers at the top, the segmented belly in the middle, and the legs bunched up at the bottom? It takes some imagination, but this spiky shellfish definitely looks like a crab.
This radical looks like an <radical>umbrella</radical>, specifically just the handle part. A good old curvy umbrella handle, so you can hang that umbrella on your arm when it stops raining.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>anti</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: The stool (又) is in the cliff (厂). If someone has a stool deep inside a cliff, they are most likely pretty <kanji>anti</kanji> society, hiding away like that.
Behind that tree the sun is rising in the <radical>east</radical>. The sun always rises in the east, so if you head that way, past the tree, you'll be going east too.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>past</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>part</radical>.

This is the <radical>gambler</radical> radical. Imagine the 十 on top as a ten-gallon cowboy hat, sitting on the head of a man holding a card in each hand, with tall stacks of casino chips rising from the table in front of him. He's your stereotypical high-stakes gambler.

You could also remember this with the components: a gambler holding a cross while playing blackjack, standing on his two legs expectantly, praying to win because he's just gambled those legs on the next card.
This looks like a <radical>mask</radical>, right? Kind of a scary, non-human mask, what with the horns on top and everything, but definitely a mask.
Can you see the flipped $ sign? That's the <radical>dollar</radical> radical. It was drawn by a kid, so naturally, it's a little backwards, but we won't be the ones to correct the artistic vision!

The sun is coming up out of the ground, making this radical <radical>dawn</radical>. Of course, don't confuse this with dusk! You can do that by thinking that the sun is an optimistic and bright thing, so it tends to come up, not go down. (Also, Japan is the Land of the Rising Sun. I mean come on!)
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>control</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>announce</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>farming</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>substitute</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>specialty</radical>.
This is the <radical>clothes</radical> radical, it looks a little like clothes hanging on a clothes hanger, right? Now that these clothes are hung up, you've gotta get to the rest of that pile…
This is the <radical>call</radical> radical. Do you see how it looks like an old-timey phone with the handset on top? "Nothing better than a phone for making a call," as my dad used to say.

Your flowers become your servants. You plant them, you water them, you bring them up, then you cut them down and put them in your <radical>storehouse</radical>. They do what you want because they become YOUR servants, not the other way around. That's why you can tell them to sit in the storehouse where they wait until you come to eat them.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>sell</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: A samurai has come bearing foreheads and legs that he's trying to <kanji>sell</kanji>. He thought it was a waste to leave all his slain enemies on the battlefield, so he gathered up their foreheads and legs to sell on the black market for some extra cash. Hey, no judging! A samurai's gotta sell what a samurai's gotta sell, okay?
This is a <radical>stick</radical>, sticking straight up. It even looks like a stick.

This looks like a stick-figure foot on the left kicking at something, which makes it the radical for <radical>kick</radical>. See the shin and foot swinging up for the kick? You can think of that part on the right as the edge of a ball that's about to be kicked.

This is the radical for <radical>canine</radical>, because it looks like a police dog — aka a K-9 — marching around on patrol. You can see its proud little head on the top right, its front legs below crossing as it walks, and a police vest labeled "K-9" strapped around its body. Evil-doers beware — this canine's gonna sniff you out and bring you to justice.

Alternately, you could see the F-shape on the left as a cheerful canine on its hind legs dancing with a drunkard, arm in arm as they sway along together. What a happy canine, dancing like that with a drunk person.
This kinda looks like a spine with some rib bones, don't you think? That's why this is the radical for <radical>rib cage</radical>.

example.jp: 重要な会議があります。
example.furigana: じゅうようなかいぎがあります。
example.en: I have an important meeting.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>helicopter</radical> is piloted by a <radical>woman</radical>, it stirs an insatiable <kanji>need</kanji> in her. She doesn't know what it is. But she needs it. And that's why she's flying around looking for it!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Finally she knows what she <kanji>need</kanji>s! It's <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう)! Delicious, creamy yogurt!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you know the radical meaning <radical>orders</radical> you know the kanji meaning <kanji>orders</kanji> as well!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>orders</kanji> are to get a <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun.

example.jp: ビールを冷蔵庫に入れてください。
example.furigana: ビールをれいぞうこにいれてください。
example.en: Please put the beer in the refrigerator.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>storehouse</radical> radical and the <kanji>storehouse</kanji> kanji meanings are the same. If you know the radical, you know the kanji!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>storehouse</kanji>. Inside is where you keep all your <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Ice</radical> from the <radical>east</radical> is <kanji>frozen</kanji>. Well, of course, all ice is frozen, but ice from the east is like, really super frozen.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Japan is a country in the east, and this ice was <kanji>frozen</kanji> in <reading>とう</reading>きょう. とうきょう is really good at freezing frozen things, so it makes sense that this frozen ice came from there.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>canopy</radical> is over your <radical>car</radical> because your car is in <kanji>storage</kanji> in a large <kanji>storehouse</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your car is in this <kanji>storage</kanji> <kanji>warehouse</kanji>, just sitting there. A <reading>子</reading> (こ) notices this, and decides to take your car on a joyride. You won't notice, right? You never drive it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>call</radical> radical and the <kanji>call</kanji> kanji are the same. This kanji can also mean <kanji>eat</kanji>, because why would you call someone if not to ask them to eat with you?!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You are <kanji>call</kanji>ed to come <kanji>eat</kanji> by the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). He's been really impressed with you lately and he wants to chat over drinks, he says on the phone.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> of a <radical>tree</radical> <radical>leader</radical> is all about trying to <kanji>preserve</kanji> the trees. In fact, she <kanji>guarantee</kanji>s that she will preserve the trees if it's the last thing she does.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: She chains herself to a tree to <kanji>preserve</kanji> them. But, unfortunately, the lumberjacks just take a giant back <reading>hoe</reading> (ほ) and tear this tree leader and the tree she's attached to in half.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>narwhal</radical> <radical>stick</radical>s a <radical>child</radical> with its horn then you have to admit that it <kanji>exist</kanji>s. We know some of you have been doubting narwhals and whether they're real. Well now your kid is a kabob, so do you believe they exist now? I <kanji>suppose</kanji> you do.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Oh, and the child we had to narwhal stab to prove they <kanji>exist</kanji> - that's your <reading>son</reading> (そん). Maybe you should have listened and kept your son out of the Narwhal Danger <reading>Zone</reading> (ぞん) after we warned you about it.

example.jp: 必ず来週までに連絡してください。
example.furigana: かならずらいしゅうまでにれんらくしてください。
example.en: Please be sure to contact me by next week.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your heart has a slide running through it because you want to be certain that the blood is flowing in and out of it smoothly. Given how important this is, you want to be absolutely certain.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To be <kanji>certain</kanji> that the heart-slide is working, the doctor who put it there <reading>hits</reading> (ひつ) you in the chest a few times as a test.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Dollar</radical>s and <radical>shellfish</radical> are used to pay <kanji>expense</kanji>s and <kanji>cost</kanji>s. Shellfish used to be used as currency, so they're like the coins that go with dollars.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What is the biggest <kanji>expense</kanji> and <kanji>cost</kanji>? It's the <reading>hea</reading>t (ひ) bill.

example.jp: 賞味期限を確認してください。
example.furigana: しょうみきげんをかくにんしてください。
example.en: Please check the best-before date.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A "<radical>crab</radical> <radical>moon</radical>" is a specific <kanji>period of time</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When the crab moon <kanji>period of time</kanji> is upon us, we must take a special <reading>key</reading> (き) and lock everything in such a way that crabs cannot get in.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>building</radical>'s <radical>root</radical>s will <kanji>limit</kanji> the things under and around it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The person who hates these <kanji>limit</kanji>s more than anyone else is <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). He wants to be able to tunnel under buildings, sneak in, smooch ladies, and sneak back out. But all the building root limits make that impossible!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you want <radical>control</radical> over the <radical>clothes</radical> you wear, you'll have to <kanji>manufacture</kanji> them yourself. You'll never truly control your own wardrobe as long as you're letting big apparel companies manufacture it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Encouraged by your success in clothing manufacturing, you also start to <kanji>manufacture</kanji> <reading>sa</reading>bers (せい). Sabers are another thing you're very picky about — handle shape, blade curvature, etc. — so you want to control how they're manufactured too.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: "A <radical>scooter</radical>!" you <radical>announce</radical>. You are announcing this because you decided this is what you would <kanji>create</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But, a scooter has been <kanji>create</kanji>d before. What is different about yours? The scooter you will create is specifically designed to keep <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう) busy.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>Viking</radical> opens his <radical>mouth</radical>, and below it, a <radical>shellfish</radical> sits. Grab that shellfish and throw it into his mouth to win a <kanji>prize</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>prize</kanji> you're working so hard to win is lunch with the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). This is a pretty huge prize, considering all you're doing is knocking something over.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Tsunami</radical>s in the <radical>past</radical> changed the <kanji>method</kanji>s and <kanji>law</kanji>s of today.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: These <kanji>method</kanji>s and <kanji>law</kanji>s affected your own <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう) the most.

kanji.kunyomi: あたたか(い)、あたたまる、ぬく、ぬるい
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>tsunami</radical> which washes a <radical>plate</radical> out into the <radical>sun</radical>. Because it's in the sun, it becomes  <kanji>warm</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The plate starts to get so <kanji>warm</kanji> that you could fry an <reading>on</reading>ion (おん) on it. Who doesn’t love fried onions? That plate sure is warm enough, so start cookin’ ‘em!

example.jp: 自動販売機でジュースを買った。
example.furigana: じどうはんばいきでジュースをかった。
example.en: I bought juice at the vending machine.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A sudden aversion to <radical>shellfish</radical> makes you <radical>anti</radical>-shellfish, so you <kanji>sell</kanji> off every shellfish in sight.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're going to <kanji>sell</kanji> all of our shellfish to <reading>Han</reading> (はん) Solo. He isn't anti-shellfish like you, and he knows how to turn a profit too!

example.jp: 飛行機で東京に行きます。
example.furigana: ひこうきでとうきょうにいきます。
example.en: I go to Tokyo by plane.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Next to a <radical>tree</radical>, you spot <radical>poop</radical>, not once but twice. Only a <radical>drunkard</radical> would be the type of <radical>person</radical> to not use the nearby <kanji>machine</kanji> toilet. There's a perfectly good outhouse with a machine toilet right there, but this drunkard is so drunk that he decides to poop under the tree instead. And not only does he poop once, he poops twice.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Oh, I see — the door to the outhouse with the <kanji>machine</kanji> toilet is locked, and the drunkard doesn't have the <reading>key</reading> (き). If he had a machine like a jackhammer, or a circular saw, or some other heavy duty machine, he might be able to get in without a key, but since he has none of those or a key, he's reduced to pooping under the tree instead.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>dirt</radical> <radical>mask</radical> is a mask which, when put on, will greatly <kanji>increase</kanji> the amount of dirt.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Use the dirt mask to <kanji>increase</kanji> the dirt around you. The <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう) are trying to escape, so you just keep increasing the dirt on top of them so they can't get out.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Direct a <radical>tsunami</radical> into a <radical>canine</radical>'s <radical>mouth</radical> to <kanji>decrease</kanji> the amount of water that strikes the surrounding area.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you and your canine <kanji>decrease</kanji> the tsunami's power, <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん) comes out to thank you. That tsunami was on track to wash away Genji's house, which would have forced him to majorly decrease his frivolous playboy activities.

example.jp: 水の量を減らしてください。
example.furigana: みずのりょうをへらしてください。
example.en: Please reduce the amount of water.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When <radical>dawn</radical> reaches this <radical>village</radical> it increases in <kanji>quantity</kanji>. That's right. Every morning the <kanji>amount</kanji> of people or animals living here goes up by at least one.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Today's dawn has brought with it an increase in the <kanji>quantity</kanji> of <reading>row</reading>(りょう) boats! Aww, aren't they cute? Look at all of the new row boats lined up together. They all have their own sets of oars too.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Add a <radical>drop</radical> of something magical to <radical>water</radical> and suddenly it turns into big block of <kanji>ice</kanji>, just like that.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you think of <kanji>ice</kanji>, I want you to think of someone frozen with ice. Do you know anyone named <reading>Corey</reading> (こおり)? Anyone famous named Corey, perhaps Corey Feldman? Imagine this Corey person frozen solid with ice.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>scooter</radical> is <radical>anti</radical> scoot. It doesn't want to run. So you have to <kanji>return</kanji> it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>return</kanji> to the store and wait in line to return the scooter but the person working returns doesn't want you to return it. He stares you dead in the eyes, waves his hand, and turns you into a <reading>hen</reading> (へん)!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If there's a <radical>tsunami</radical> it's <radical>easy</radical> to get <kanji>hot water</kanji>. Just stick your hand out the window as the tsunami goes by and poof! That water's HOT.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As the <kanji>hot water</kanji> comes, you just lift up the bottom of the <reading>yu</reading>rt (ゆ) you live in, and it comes flowing in. All of the cups, pots, and barrels you laid on your floor are now full of hot water.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> with <radical>talent</radical> can become <kanji>lumber</kanji>. Not all trees can do this. Only the talented ones are able to turn themselves into lumber or <kanji>material</kanji>, to be used for a million different things.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Trees can be turned into all kinds of things, but this one wants to use its <kanji>lumber</kanji> and <kanji>material</kanji> to build a <reading>xy</reading>lophone (ざい). It's the most difficult instrument to create, so it suits the talent level of this tree!

example.jp: 卵焼きを作ります。
example.furigana: たまごやきをつくります。
example.en: I make a Japanese omelet.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Two <radical>pool</radical>s, both altered and not quite like a pool you’ve seen before are put together and flipped around – this is an <kanji>egg</kanji>. One pool is the egg white, the other pool is the egg yolk. They’re different, but similar.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You remember <reading>Tamago</reading>tchi (たまご), right? Well, Tamagotchi is an <kanji>egg</kanji>, and the toy looks like an egg, so it’s pretty easy to remember that tamago means egg.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Giving <radical>cleat</radical>s to a <radical>child</radical> carrying an <radical>umbrella</radical> is the best way to gather <kanji>milk</kanji>. You don't have any containers, so the child has to hold milk in the upside-down umbrella. The cleats are so the child can run back and forth to transport the milk around.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But where is this child exactly? He’s in <reading>New</reading> (にゅう) York City. What’s he doing in New York City you ask? Well, he's milking a cow. Why is there a cow to be milked in New York City? Good question. It’s the end of the world and New York City is the last remaining civilization. This is how people live now. <kanji>Milk</kanji> is important.

example.jp: 小麦粉を買ってください。
example.furigana: こむぎこをかってください。
example.en: Please buy wheat flour.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you grind <radical>rice</radical>, every <radical>part</radical> of it, eventually it will become a fine <kanji>powder</kanji>. You can then use this rice powder as a part to create some other dish. Some kind of cake, perhaps.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Actually, grinding the rice down to a <kanji>powder</kanji> is super <reading>fun</reading> (ふん). It’s so fun you don’t want to stop! AH HAHAHAHA! RICE POWDER! SO FUN!

compounds.meaning: tabi (traditional Japanese socks worn with a kimono)

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <radical>substitute</radical> <radical>clothes</radical> in a <kanji>sack</kanji>. The clothes in the sack are just substitute clothes, so they only come out in emergencies.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You need your substitute clothes so you take out your substitute clothes <kanji>sack</kanji>. You open it up to grab your substitute clothes, only to find out that there is a ton of salmon roe inside your sack. Oh man, you forgot all about putting that in there. You yell: <reading>F**K ROE</reading> (ふくろ) because that roe destroyed all your clothes and made it nasty.

example.jp: 牛乳と卵を混ぜます。
example.furigana: ぎゅうにゅうとたまごをまぜます。
example.en: Mix milk and eggs.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A raging <radical>tsunami</radical> rises next to the calm <radical>sun</radical>. When you try to <radical>compare</radical> these two things, it's clear that they cannot <kanji>mix</kanji>. If a tsunami is coming, it will likely get in the way of the sun.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Just before the tsunami crashes over you, a <reading>con</reading>dor (こん) swoops out of the sky and grabs you up. This condor must be a <kanji>mix</kanji> — a normal condor is not strong enough to pick up a human. The condor must be mixed with something else. Like a pterodactyl.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
In a dangerous <radical>fire</radical>, a <radical>gambler</radical> will always try to <kanji>bake</kanji> something before fleeing to safety. It could be his own house on fire, and the gambler would still use the free heat source to get some baking done. Maybe he's gambling that those baked goods will offset the cost of a new home…

This kanji also means <kanji>burn</kanji>, because that's what happens when you expose something to a lot of heat.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: He used to <kanji>bake</kanji> for the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や). Baseball cakes, bat baguettes, that kind of thing. A career-ending kitchen injury forced him to retire. That's when he developed a gambling problem. But he still likes to bake whenever the Yankees are on TV.

kanji.kunyomi: おもて、あらわす、あらわれる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If your <radical>rib cage</radical> is suddenly <radical>kick</radical>ed you'll probably want to <kanji>express</kanji> something. Anger or surprise, I'm guessing. At any rate a lot will get expressed on the <kanji>surface</kanji> of your face.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The only thing you can think to <kanji>express</kanji> is "<reading>Heyo</reading>" (ひょう)! Kind of a cross between "hey" and "yo." Like "heyo, stop it!" It doesn't really match the moment, but it's how you expressed yourself.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>lid</radical> on your <radical>village</radical>, so you <radical>kick</radical> it over on its <kanji>backside</kanji> to see what's on its <kanji>underside</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: It turns out your village's own <kanji>backside</kanji> is covered in <reading>ura</reading>nium (うら). Eureka! You're all gonna be rich!

example.jp: アメリカに留学しています。
example.furigana: あめりかにりゅうがくしています。
example.en: I am studying abroad in America.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A group of <radical>private</radical> <radical>sword</radical> guys are in your <radical>rice paddy</radical>. You must <kanji>detain</kanji> them at once! Private sword guys are people who work for private companies and use their swords on people. They're basically paid assassins. And you're going to detain them!
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
You're running out of steam and you're afraid you might not be able to <kanji>detain</kanji> all of these guys when <reading>Ryu</reading> (りゅう) from Street Fighter appears. He hates swords, and will only use fists because it's the honorable way to fight, so he starts helping you detain them!

He's also found a <reading>loo</reading>phole (る) in the system and you don't have to be super gentle with these guys either. So detain them as forcefully as you want. It is your rice paddy they're in, after all.

example.jp: ルールを守りましょう。
example.furigana: るーるをまもりましょう。
example.en: Let's follow the rules.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>roof</radical> needs <radical>measurement</radical>s done every year to make sure it will <kanji>protect</kanji> you properly.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If the measurements are off, and your roof doesn't <kanji>protect</kanji> you, then you get to <reading>sue</reading> (す)! If you're still alive, that is.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: After a <radical>tsunami</radical> hit your <radical>farming</radical> land, you're gonna see a lot of <kanji>dense</kanji> silt left behind. This <kanji>thick</kanji> layer really enriches the soil, and your crops will come out tasting extra thick and dense in flavor.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Know who’s likely responsible for this <kanji>dense</kanji>, <kanji>thick</kanji> layer of silt? <reading>No</reading>stradamus (のう). He’s the one who urged you to buy this farmland in the first place, likely because he predicted the tsunami would bring this thick layer of silt.

kanji.kunyomi: うすい、うすめる、うすまる、うすれる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>flowers</radical> are being worked upon by a <radical>tsunami</radical> with a <radical>drop</radical> <radical>specialty</radical>: this tsunami can <kanji>dilute</kanji> flowers with just one tsunami-powered drop of itself. That’s its specialty.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You watch the flowers become <kanji>dilute</kanji>d with just one drop, and realize that this is a nature <reading>hack</reading> (はく). You’ve never seen anything like this before, so you think the tsunami found out how to hack nature and that’s how it got so good at diluting things. By hacking nature.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>clown</radical> <radical>building</radical> is over in that <kanji>part</kanji> of town. We keep the clown part as separate as we can from the rest of the normal people. In fact, the entire clown education <kanji>department</kanji> and their clown <kanji>club</kanji>s have to stay in their part, they can't come in ours.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You see, that <kanji>part</kanji> of town is full of <reading>boo</reading>ze (ぶ). Clowns need a lot of booze to keep their charade going, so we just let them have it. But they aren't allowed in our part anymore, because they all stink of nasty clown booze.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Give <radical>rice</radical> to a <radical>woman</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> so she can <kanji>count</kanji> it. The woman will count each individual grain of rice, then tell you the <kanji>amount</kanji> or <kanji>number</kanji> of grains.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The rice this woman has to <kanji>count</kanji> is for your <reading>sou</reading>p (すう). It's important to ration! You may not be getting many grains — few enough to count on two hands, probably — but at least you can enjoy them in a nice, hot bowl of soup.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>cow</radical> tribe is too important to deal with small <kanji>matter</kanji>s and trivial <kanji>affair</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: All of his <kanji>affair</kanji>s are taken care of by <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai, who he hired as his underling.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Under the <radical>ground</radical>, a <radical>head</radical> covered in <radical>dirt</radical> emerges... <kanji>again</kanji>! It's not the first time you've seen this buried head, nor is it the last. This dirt-covered head hides beneath the ground wherever you go, and keeps popping up to scare you again and again.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The dirt-covered head asks for help <kanji>again</kanji> and again, but you've only got a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). So you start digging with it, scraping the dirt away, until you see this head has the body of a <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい)!

example.jp: インターネットに接続してください。
example.furigana: インターネットにせつぞくしてください。
example.en: Please connect to the internet.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> touch as you <radical>stand</radical> with a <radical>woman</radical> and <kanji>adjoin</kanji> yourselves. You are united, you are one.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: All the women <kanji>adjoin</kanji> in <reading>sets</reading> (せつ). Sets of two, of course. One woman with another woman, standing in unison.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have to gather <radical>thread</radical> to <radical>sell</radical> if you want to <kanji>continue</kanji> living. You want to make a living, don't you? Make sure you continue to sell that thread every single day!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You have to <kanji>continue</kanji> to sell that thread because a Boso<reading>zoku</reading> (ぞく) bike gang is forcing you to do it. You see? If you want to continue to live, you have to appease this Bosozoku gang. You better keep selling!

He takes one <radical>barb</radical>, and connects the end of it to the top of another <radical>barb</radical>. When he does this, he knows his work is finally <kanji>finish</kanji>ed.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: How does the fish lure maker test his newly <kanji>finish</kanji>ed lure out? The one he just finished? He gets in a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and rows out into the sea.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>tent</radical> of <radical>beans</radical>. You try to <kanji>climb</kanji> it.

You hopefully know the word 返す, which means "to return" (as in, you're doing the direct action of returning something). This word, on the other hand, is the version where something just returns (and you're not doing the action of returning it). Use the る to help you to remember this. る the Kangaroo is returned to you. You don't do any of the returning, it just happens or someone else does it. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be returned</vocabulary>.

Note this word is often combined with くる (to come), which reinforces the aspect that something is coming back to you.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 返す, so as long as you know that you'll be able to apply it here to learn the reading of this word as well.

It's all about you doing something to another object to make it hot, like putting it in the microwave.

焼く means to apply heat to something to change it in a physical way. It can refer to lightly toasting something, charring it, or even burning it to ashes depending on the context. It's commonly used in cooking contexts to describe baking, grilling, or roasting food. But it can also be used with pottery, film photography, and even sun-tanning.
