vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You've already learned one verb for this kanji: 薄まる (to be diluted). Well, this is its transitive sibling, so it means <vocabulary>to dilute</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to water down</vocabulary> something. Here, you're the one actively thinning something down.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 薄い, so if you know that you'll be able to read this too.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. So, put that knowledge in a <vocabulary>sack</vocabulary> and move on to the next item.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>call</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to call</vocabulary>, as in calling someone over.

召す is an honorific verb, so it's used to talk about the actions of social higher-ups. 召す suggests the image of a superior who summons someone or something to themselves, hence the main meaning to call. But it can also be a polite way to say <vocabulary>to take</vocabulary>, like when they take a meal or a drink, and <vocabulary>to wear</vocabulary> when talking about their clothes.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If a noble decides <vocabulary>to call</vocabulary> you over, don’t look them in the <reading>目</reading> (め). That's super rude! To show respect when you're called, turn away your 目.

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: What does this radical look like? Hmm, nothing much. What about if you turn it upside down? Now does it look like a 7 with a line through it? Close enough to help you to remember that this radical is <radical>seven</radical>, right? Just remember, when you see this radical, flip it over and see what number it looks like. If you can do that, you can remember the meaning!

Watch out! This isn't the person radical, it's something else. What's the difference? The right side is longer than the left. This radical also has that extra part sticking out at the top. See it? It kind of looks like a person lowering their head to go inside a tent or something. That's why this radical is <radical>enter</radical>.
This radical already looks like a pair of <radical>legs</radical>. There's even feet on these legs. That's how you know these are legs and not fins (or something else).
This radical is <radical>treasure</radical> because "X marks the spot," as they say. Doesn't it look like the X on a pirate treasure map? You want to go find that treasure now, right?!

You see two fins around a barb, but when you look closer, you realize those fins are actually two tiny fish. Think how small these fins (and fish) would have to be to look so much smaller than an already small barb. Talk about small fry… Yeah, that's why this is the radical for <radical>small</radical>.

There's a stick and a giant toe stuck in the ground. Imagine walking along and seeing these things in your path. What would you do? Most likely come to a complete <radical>stop</radical>. You know, because of the toe. I guess a normal stop sign wasn't good enough, so they also put up this big toe to really get people to stop.

There's a cross branching off of this stool. Since it's branching out, we'll just call this the <radical>branch</radical> radical. I guess the tree this stool was made of is coming back to life in the form of a branch.

This is the <radical>ear</radical> radical, since it looks like an ear. As much as a radical can, anyway. Those two middle lines are the ridges that guide the sound into your ear, and the lines that stick out to the right are where the ear attaches to your head.

If you think about it, ears are just eyes that see sound. Whoa, dude… That explains the eye (目) and ear (耳) radical resemblance. Just remember this one is "ear" because ears stick out, just like the lines sticking out of the side of this radical.

This looks like something hooked around the corner of a mouth — it's a <radical>lip ring</radical>! Use your imagination, because it's either a giant lip ring or a very small mouth. It's angular because kanji prefer straight lines, but try to picture it as the kind of studded, angular lip ring your trendy friend wore in high school.

This radical looks like a <radical>yakuza</radical>. See him facing left, with that threatening jawline and big pompadour hairstyle? Maybe imagine a couple scars on his face too. You know, real yakuza-like.

You could also remember this because it's the evening radical under the ground radical, and people who do stuff underground in the evening (or night) are definitely yakuza.

This looks like the west radical with a little something extra under it… And if you ask for "a little something extra" in the Wild West, you're going to get a big ol' decanter of bourbon, moonshine, or some other kind of very strong <radical>alcohol</radical> — which happens to be exactly what this radical looks like! That extra line at the bottom is just the little bit of alcohol still left in the bottle.

Remember the stairs (乃) radical? This is a lot like that, but it has another stroke to motorize it. The extra bit makes the stairs move by themselves — that's why this is an <radical>escalator</radical>!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>few</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher, just in case: You have a small slide. The thing about small slides is that <kanji>few</kanji> people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down. That's why this means "few"!

Remember the sprout from the dirt radical? This looks like that, but wait a minute… there's some extra growth now! This thing is so full of <radical>life</radical>! It's even got a big, slide-shaped leaf growing on the top left. That's why it's the life radical.

There's a lid on a lion. And you're stuck under the lid with the lion, which means you will surely meet your <radical>death</radical>. Or if you don't want to die, think of the poor lion. If you leave a lion under a lid for too long, death will come for it too. Either way, somebody's gonna die today.
This looks like a bunch of books on a shelf. It's a <radical>bookshelf</radical>!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>reason</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>guest</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>beforehand</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: What does your mama tell you to do in the street? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand, or it could be too late.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>tooth</radical>.

This radical is made up of horns and older brother. Why horns? They're part of your older brother's new <radical>guard</radical> uniform. He's a guard now, of a bank or a museum. And the horns are actually part of his guard hat, which of course makes him a more intimidating guard.
There's something made of leather with some dirt on the bottom of it. It's a <radical>boot</radical>!

It's the drunkard from before, but this time she's leaning on some kind of horizontal surface. Knowing her, it's probably the counter of a <radical>bar</radical>. Hopefully she's not causing too much trouble for the bar staff with her drunken antics.

Oh no, you let the pope's hat get snatched by a lion! You get it back, but it's all crooked, so you've got to make it <radical>straight</radical> again. The pope needs a straight, dignified hat, so you'd better straighten that thing out.

example.jp: 砂で遊ぶのは楽しいです。
example.furigana: すなであそぶのはたのしいです。
example.en: Playing with sand is fun.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you grind a <radical>stone</radical> down to more than just a <radical>few</radical> pieces, it will become <kanji>sand</kanji>. Stones that get broken up enough will become sand, and you pick up a few grains in your hand.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After breaking up your stone into <kanji>sand</kanji>, you fetch your special sand <reading>sa</reading>w (さ). A few bits are still too chunky, so you'll have to use a sand saw now.

example.jp: 料理に塩を少し入れてください。
example.furigana: りょうりにしおをすこしいれてください。
example.en: Please put a little salt in the dish.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: In the <radical>dirt</radical>, there's a <radical>gun</radical>. Its <radical>mouth</radical> points toward a <radical>plate</radical>. What's on the plate? Why, it's <kanji>salt</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you see the <kanji>salt</kanji>, you think to yourself, "<reading>She owe</reading>s (しお) me big time, so I'm going to go ahead and snatch her salt!" Who is she, you ask? She's the lady who owns the salt. And the gun in the dirt, of course.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>tsunami</radical> is the <radical>reason</radical> we have so much <kanji>oil</kanji> now. The tsunami moved a bunch of earth out of the way, so now it’s really easy to dig for oil. Thanks tsunami!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Now that <kanji>oil</kanji> is so abundant, everyone lives in <reading>yu</reading>rts (ゆ). They're light and mobile, so people can just move from oil well to oil well, collecting oil.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you tie a <radical>thread</radical> around <radical>Wolverine</radical> and dip him in <radical>water</radical>, he'll turn <kanji>green</kanji>, like the Hulk. Some kind of weird chemical reaction. But I… I wouldn't try it if I were you. You wouldn't like him when he's green.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As the flailing Wolverine begins to turn even more <kanji>green</kanji>, he calls out, "HELP <reading>ME DORY</reading> (みどり)!" Me, Dory? No, not you. He's calling out to that fish from Finding Nemo, another Disney IP. "Help me Dory, I'm green!" Then Dory leaps out of the water to bite through the thread and save Wolverine… THE END. Fade to green.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You use <radical>thread</radical> in your <radical>construction</radical> project to hold everything together. The color of the thread is a <kanji>deep red</kanji>, and it gives everything a <kanji>crimson</kanji> look.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're done, and the whole building is a <kanji>deep red</kanji> <kanji>crimson</kanji> color (it takes a lot of thread to hold a whole building in place). It's time to show the client, Emperor <reading>こう</reading>いち, the finished product.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You use a <radical>bookshelf</radical> as a <kanji>book counter</kanji>. Duh. What, are you gonna count them one by one? Okay, well maybe, but you should count them while they're nice and organized on the shelves. Otherwise counting is going to be a huge pain.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You use this <kanji>book counter</kanji> method to count all the books <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) has in her house. Remember her? She's got, like, a ton of books, but she's just a little girl so she needs some help. That's where your book counter know-how comes in handy.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical>'s <radical>mouth</radical> has grown <radical>old</radical> from saying so many things. This is what makes them different from everyone else, they speak truly like an <kanji>individual</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As an <kanji>individual</kanji>, they must teach all the <reading>子</reading>s (こ) their way. Their individual way.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> that's been sliced up in <radical>winter</radical> can be used as a <kanji>flat object counter</kanji>. Since it's winter, all the leaves have fallen off the tree, so it's easy to cut into slats. These slats can be used as counters for flat objects.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you count each <kanji>counter for flat objects</kanji>, a bunch of <reading>mi</reading>ce (まい) show up and start climbing all over you. This won't do, so you take two slats and start smashing and flattening all the mice. Now that the mice are flat too, you can also use them as a counter for flat objects. Good job, mice.

example.jp: 新しい広告を見ました。
example.furigana: あたらしいこうこくをみました。
example.en: I saw a new advertisement.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You see a <radical>slide</radical> covered in <radical>dirt</radical> and use your <radical>mouth</radical> to clean it off. Then, you <kanji>announce</kanji> to everyone that the slide is clean and they can use it safely again.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you <kanji>announce</kanji> the slide is clean, you take a big swig of <reading>Coke</reading> (こく). The dirty slide left a nasty taste in your mouth, but the Coke is helping to wash it away.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Cut <radical>grain</radical>s with a <radical>knife</radical> to make them smaller and you'll make a great <kanji>profit</kanji>. By cutting them, now you can get three grains worth of money for what was once a single grain.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To make an even better <kanji>profit</kanji>, you decide to cut up <reading>ree</reading>ds (り) too. You stuff the grains in the reeds and sell that as "self-cooking" sets.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>roof</radical> falls on you right between your <radical>rib cage</radical> and your <radical>mouth</radical>, slicing through you like a <radical>knife</radical> and managing to completely <kanji>divide</kanji> your body in two.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Who caused this roof to fall on you and <kanji>divide</kanji> your body in two? <reading>Wari</reading>o (わり) and his <reading>wa</reading>lrus (わ) sidekick. Wario's always been a bad guy, but since teaming up with his walrus buddy, he's gotten into some really twisted stuff… like using roofs to divide people in half, guillotine-style.

example.jp: 去年の倍のお客さんが来た。
example.furigana: きょねんのばいのおきゃくさんがきた。
example.en: Twice as many customers came as last year.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
A <radical>leader</radical> who hires his own personal <radical>clown</radical> will likely <kanji>double</kanji> his entertainment. Clowns are funny and make people laugh, so the leader decided to hire one. Since that time, the leader's amount of mirth has doubled. 

This also means <kanji>times</kanji>, which makes sense when you think about the kind of math you'll need to double something. What is A * 2? It's A doubled, first of all, but you're using multiplication. You're "timesing" something.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When the clown stops being funny, it's time to say <reading>bye</reading> (ばい). At first, the clown <kanji>double</kanji>d the leader's entertainment, but now the clown is just annoying. It's time to say bye-bye.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A great <radical>leader</radical> can look <radical>straight</radical> at something and know its <kanji>value</kanji>. That social media site? 44 billion dollars. That job position? 50k a year. A four-day work week? Um… sorry, no, there's no value there. See? Leaders can see straight to the heart of matters to grasp something's true value.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: One thing your leader knows has great <kanji>value</kanji> is <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). Say goodbye to your days of casually snacking on cheesy treats from the conbini, because your leader's decided the value of cheese is going up 1000%!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stand</radical>ing <radical>mustache</radical> with <radical>legs</radical> is able to sell <kanji>merchandise</kanji>. Most mustaches can’t stand because they don’t have legs. This mustache, however, does. It also has a keen business sense, which is why it’s selling merchandise.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The mustache is selling his <kanji>merchandise</kanji> so well that even the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) notices. He leans down really close to the standing mustache man's merchandise and stays very still. Then he snaps his fingers and his servants come rushing out to buy it all!

compounds.meaning: the main branch of a store

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>branch</radical> radical and the <kanji>branch</kanji> kanji are the same! This kanji also means <kanji>support</kanji>. To remember it, think about a tree with lots of branches. The branches support each other and the trunk of the tree. If you were to climb the tree, the branches would be able to support your weight too!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're happily sitting on this <kanji>branch</kanji>, letting it <kanji>support</kanji> all this weight, when a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) starts to climb the tree. A very, very big sheep. Uh oh... no no, sheep. If you get on this branch it won't be able to support all this weight!!!

example.jp: 代金を現金で払います。
example.furigana: だいきんをげんきんではらいます。
example.en: I will pay the price in cash.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> are <radical>private</radical>, no one can see them unless they <kanji>pay</kanji>! And you decide if what they pay is enough to get a peek.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If someone tries to look without paying, that's <reading>hara</reading>ssment (はら)! Nobody gets to see something of yours without proper payment, but more importantly, your consent!

example.jp: 米国へ留学に行きます。
example.furigana: べいこくへりゅうがくにいきます。
example.en: I am going to study in the United States.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>rice</radical> radical and <kanji>rice</kanji> kanji are the same in looks and meaning. This kanji can also mean <kanji>America</kanji>, maybe because America is covered in rice or fields or something?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: A ton of <kanji>rice</kanji> is grown in <kanji>America</kanji>. And yet you never see rice in American cuisine. So where's all that unused rice going? Actually, it all gets dumped into a big <reading>bay</reading> (べい). They have too much rice and no place to store it, so they've started using bays to store it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There are pieces of <radical>thread</radical> on each <radical>escalator</radical> showing you what <kanji>level</kanji> they go to in your school. Each escalator takes you to a different <kanji>grade</kanji>, so make sure you follow the right thread or you'll end up in a class that's either way above or way below your level.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You want to see what the highest <kanji>level</kanji> is, so you go up the wrong escalator. At the top you find a giant <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Yakuza</radical> <radical>bars</radical> barely exist. The <kanji>remainder</kanji> of them aren't even in Japan.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>remainder</kanji> of the yakuza bars aren't in Japan. Strangely, they are all in <reading>Zan</reading>zibar (ざん).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There is a <radical>lantern</radical> on top of a <radical>knife</radical> in the <radical>dirt</radical>. You walk up to take the knife and lantern when you realize it's just a <kanji>model</kanji>. It all looked real from far away, but now that you're up close you can see none of it is real.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You touch the <kanji>model</kanji> and see that it's made of <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい)! Someone really into lanterns and knives must have been given this model cake as a birthday present! Though they left it out here so they probably didn't like it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Some of your <radical>grain</radical> has just been taken by a <radical>guard</radical>. This is the <kanji>tax</kanji> you pay for living in this town. Back in the day, grain was used like currency, so it makes sense that guards went around collecting grain tax.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You have to pay this <kanji>tax</kanji>, because if you don't the guard will cut you down with his special German saber, a <reading>zei</reading>ber (ぜい). "Don't you hear vat I zei? Pay ze tax or I vill zlei you vis my zeiber!" he shouts.

compounds.meaning: transfer money to a person's account

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you get on your <radical>scooter</radical> and <radical>enter</radical> somewhere, you’re going <kanji>into</kanji> that place.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Once you’ve gone <kanji>into</kanji> this place, what do you see? Your <reading>子</reading> (こ)!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> only uses the <radical>helicopter</radical> with the highest <kanji>value</kanji>. They choose to fly in only the very best, most valuable helicopter. That's why it's worth way more than the others. Actually, any helicopter they use goes up in value. That's the amazing effect of a good leader.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To further increase the helicopter's <kanji>value</kanji>, the leader tied it to a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Wow, now it has the value of a helicopter and a car combined! For a total value of… Well, imagine for yourself what value the car adds.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tree</radical> wants to <radical>kiss</radical> you, it's a sign of your <kanji>status</kanji>. Only someone of high status would be worthy enough to receive the gnarly but gentle kiss of a tree. Trees don't kiss just anyone, you know.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The best way to convince a tree of your <kanji>status</kanji> is to say "cock-a-doodle-doo" at it, like a <reading>cock</reading> (かく), i.e. a male chicken. Trees really place a lot of status on the ability to sound like a cock crowing.

example.jp: 鈴木と申します。
example.furigana: すずきともうします。
example.en: My name is Suzuki (humble).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>cross</radical> inside your <radical>mouth</radical>, so the things you say are very pious. Everything you say, you <kanji>say humbly</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you're saying all these humble things, you're also <reading>mow</reading>ing (もう) your neighbor's lawn. Your neighbors love you so much, because you're so humble, and you mow their lawn for them.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> to <radical>oneself</radical> (yourself), you decide to <kanji>write down</kanji>. Whether this is in the form of a journal, diary, or blog, you feel the need to <kanji>record</kanji> these important thoughts in some way.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You need to protect what you <kanji>write down</kanji> and <kanji>record</kanji> for yourself with a <reading>key</reading> (き). These are your special thoughts and feelings, you don't want anyone else to see! Lock them away with a key!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>yakuza</radical> shows you his <radical>knife</radical>. He says, "This is an <kanji>example</kanji> of a knife."
kanji.reading_mnemonic: "This is an <kanji>example</kanji>," the leader of the yakuza tells you. "Next time, I'll show you an example of a <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun."

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You get <radical>tooth</radical> <radical>orders</radical>. You get these tooth orders various times in your life, depending on your <kanji>age</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Gaining and losing teeth aren't the only things dependent on <kanji>age</kanji>. There is also an age in which you get your first <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have to <radical>stop</radical> keeping <radical>canine</radical>s which are <radical>small</radical> once you reach a certain number of <kanji>years old</kanji>. You'll be hitting that age limit this <kanji>year</kanji>, which means your <kanji>time</kanji> with your small canine will end and you'll have to grow up and get a bigger one.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Remember the vocab word 〜才 which also meant "<kanji>years old</kanji>"? Well, this has the same reading: さい.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone has a <radical>soul</radical> in their <radical>life</radical>, and that soul shapes their <kanji>gender</kanji>. It's not just about body parts — it's about what's inside. In the end, it's one's <kanji> nature</kanji> that truly matters.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Once you've decided what your <kanji>gender</kanji> is, someone comes to your house and lays a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) on your shoulders. "This is now your <kanji>nature</kanji>," they say, lifting the saber. It's official! It's in all the newspapers, there's a parade, and everyone pats you on the back. Thanks, gender saber!

kanji.kunyomi: つれる, つらなる, つらねる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>scooter</radical> and your <radical>car</radical> is what you always <kanji>take along</kanji> with you. Make sure they're <kanji>connect</kanji>ed well so you don't lose them!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>take along</kanji> your scooter and your car. Anything else, you can do a <reading>ren</reading>tal (れん) for!

kanji.kunyomi: からむ, からまる, まつわる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you put a <radical>thread</radical> in the middle of a <radical>kiss</radical>, you’re going to <kanji>entangle</kanji> it. Things can get pretty messy in a kiss, so adding a thread to the mix will definitely entangle it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This isn't going well, so you pull out the weird kiss thread and <kanji>entangle</kanji> it around a <reading>rack</reading> (らく). Good thing that rack was there! Much better to have it entangled around a rack when you're trying to kiss someone.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The American <radical>flag</radical> is the <radical>reason</radical> you need to <kanji>deliver</kanji> this package. The flag is inside the package, and you need to deliver it to the president. He lost his old flag, so now it’s up to you to deliver this new one to him. What more of a reason do you need?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To <kanji>deliver</kanji> this flag is something you just have <reading>to do</reading> (とど). Need to do. Want to do. There is no one else to do it. This is something only you are equipped to do.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You need to go up on the <radical>roof</radical> and use it like a <radical>slide</radical> <radical>seven</radical> times to make this your <kanji>house</kanji>. A house isn't a <kanji>home</kanji> until you've slid down its roof exactly seven times, you know.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When you slide down the roof of your <kanji>house</kanji>, you end up with a <reading>tack</reading> (たく) in your butt cheek. All the roof shingles on your new <kanji>home</kanji> are attached with tacks, so it's honestly a miracle that you only got one tack stuck in you.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You don't want to keep all the <radical>alcohol</radical> to yourself (<radical>oneself</radical>), so you <kanji>distribute</kanji> it to all of your friends. Heck, not just your friends, to everyone you can find!
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
As you <kanji>distribute</kanji> the alcohol you say a <reading>hai</reading>ku (はい):

Here you go my friends
Alcohol for everyone
Never drink alone

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There is a <radical>treasure</radical> on top of a <radical>narwhal</radical> who wears a <radical>towel</radical> that will grant your greatest <kanji>wish</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: In order to open the treasure and get your <kanji>wish</kanji>, you need the <reading>key</reading> (き). The narwhal knows where it's hidden, so you'll have to convince it to tell you where the key is.

kanji.kunyomi: のぞむ, のぞましい
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Causing <radical>death</radical> at every turn, the <radical>moon</radical> <radical>king</radical> sits inside his moon, getting ready to cause death on anything in his sights. Sounds a lot like the Death Star from a certain movie. One of which is "Star Wars: A New <kanji>Hope</kanji>."
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The name A New <kanji>Hope</kanji>, as we all know, comes from the ending where the moon king's son sends a <reading>bow</reading>ling (ぼう) ball into that little opening and knocks it out of the sky.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You offer <radical>flowers</radical> to your <radical>leader</radical> and compliment them on their <radical>lip ring</radical>. You think that by doing this they might carry your <kanji>luggage</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Unconvinced by your flattery, the leader refuses to carry your <kanji>luggage</kanji>, so you get on your <reading>knee</reading>s (に) and beg them to carry it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You count with your <radical>fingers</radical> in <radical>prison</radical> all of the <radical>mouth</radical>s and <radical>legs</radical> you've acquired. Soon you'll be able to make a <radical>big</radical> <kanji>exchange</kanji> with all of these body parts to get something awesome.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You learned this type of <kanji>exchange</kanji> from the mighty Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん). You read a book or watched a show about him once and you're pretty positive that Genghis Khan would exchange the body parts of his enemies all over the continents of Asia and Europe for nicer stuff.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have a <radical>guest</radical> over, you give them a <radical>geoduck</radical> because it's worth a huge <kanji>amount</kanji>. You're nothing if not a hospitable host.

This kanji, weirdly, can also mean <kanji>picture frame</kanji> or <kanji>forehead</kanji>. Why? Who knows. Just imagine going to a museum and seeing a geoduck in a picture frame, and scratching your forehead in confusion because it's supposedly worth a vast amount of money. Modern art, am I right?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The geoduck you gift to your guest is worth such a lavish <kanji>amount</kanji> that it makes them <reading>gawk</reading> (がく). Everyone gawks when they see a geoduck, really — first at how weird it looks, and then at the amount it's worth.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>narwhal</radical> sticks a <radical>stick</radical> into the <radical>dirt</radical> to see what might <kanji>exist</kanji> underneath it. Narwhals live in the sea, you see. So they're convinced nothing can exist anywhere else.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The narwhal can't find anything but it can't stop thinking about what could <kanji>exist</kanji> outside of its world. It pulls out a <reading>xy</reading>lophone (ざい) and starts tapping the keys with its horn. It plays a sad song about the meaning of life and whether existence is worth it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's an <radical>ear</radical> just sitting on a <radical>stool</radical>. Nobody's watching, so, you <kanji>take</kanji> it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're the kind of person who likes <vocabulary>to take</vocabulary> things. "What things?" you ask. Little <reading>toe</reading>s (と). Because that isn't creepy.

kanji.kunyomi: あずける, あずかる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Beforehand</radical>, to buy a <radical>geoduck</radical>, you have to go to the bank to <kanji>deposit</kanji> enough money. If you don't deposit your money you won't have enough in your account to buy one! They're expensive, after all.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You go to the bank to make the <kanji>deposit</kanji>, and there is a kid standing in your way playing with a <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ). You try to squeeze past and he hits you in the face with the yo-yo. Now you can't even see, let alone make the deposit.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>clothes</radical> radical and the <kanji>clothes</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Surprising!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: An <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) sees a pile of your <kanji>clothes</kanji> and lays an <reading>e</reading>gg (え) in them. The eagle’s egg needs a soft warm place to incubate, and your pile of clothes is the perfect place.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You try to be <radical>private</radical>, but because of your <radical>big</radical> <radical>hair</radical> you end up having to <kanji>participate</kanji> in everything. Can you imagine people asking for volunteers or something, and you trying to look inconspicuous with your big hair? Of course they're going to notice you and make you participate.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You know who has big hair and loves to <kanji>participate</kanji> in everything? <reading>San</reading>ta-san (さん)! Well, his hair is more big on the bottom (it's a beard) than whatever you have on your head, but hair is hair. And he participates in present-giving in every house in the world! See? Big hair = participation!

kanji.kunyomi: たち, たつ, はるか
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You ride your scooter through the dirt while carrying a sheep because you're determined to attain something. Greatness? Glory? Everlasting fame? Maybe you'll attain a plural combination of all those things. After all, you are the best sheep-carrying off-road scooterist the world has ever seen.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you <kanji>attain</kanji> that <kanji>plural</kanji> combination of glory, greatness, and fame, you get a <reading>tattoo</reading> (たつ) to celebrate: "world's greatest," in gothic lettering, above a picture of you and your sheep on your scooter.

kanji.kunyomi: つとめる, つとまる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Boot</radical>s give you the <radical>power</radical> to <kanji>work</kanji>! That's why so many professions require you to have work boots.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You need boots to give you the power to <kanji>work</kanji> for the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. Really, all work is for the King, since everything is for him. But even he wears boots. And they give him the power to uh... king over things.

compounds.meaning: a time zone, a time slot

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There's a <radical>mountain</radical> coming out of the <radical>ground</radical> that you want to climb, but your <radical>forehead</radical> needs a <radical>towel</radical> for all your sweat. You don't have a towel, so you take off your <kanji>belt</kanji> and tie it around your forehead.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>belt</kanji> isn't absorbent enough, so you wrap it in your <reading>tie</reading> (たい) and then tie the whole thing around your forehead again.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>say humbly</kanji>, and this is just the verb form, <vocabulary>to say humbly</vocabulary>. You can also call this <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary> — just remember that it's humble!

This is a very humble way to say "to say," so it's used in especially formal situations, and only to talk about yourself or your associates. Because of its formality, it's almost always in the ます form, which is 申します.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this kanji is the kun'yomi reading, but that's the reading you learned with the kanji. High Fives.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 

Note that this word refers to the grains of rice more than something that's a meal. If you're eating rice at a meal you'd call it ごはん. This is like when you're talking about the rice in the fields or rice grains or something like that.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

"Everyone, we have rice! <reading>Come</reading> (こめ) and get it!"

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>take</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to take something</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already know this kun'yomi reading, so you should be able to read this word.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 米 means "rice," but remember how it can mean "America" too? Well, <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>America</kanji> is exactly what it sounds like: <vocabulary>all America</vocabulary>. Just keep in mind that we're not talking about America as a continent here. This word specifically means <vocabulary>the entire USA</vocabulary> — no more, no less.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>support</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to support</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You need <vocabulary>to support</vocabulary> someone. In order to support them, you grab two saws. One saw and another saw. It's a <reading>saw saw</reading> (ささ) combination good enough to do all the supporting you need - and maybe cut some supports too.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>support</kanji> <kanji>bureau</kanji> is the group that supports a business. It is the <vocabulary>branch office</vocabulary>. 

If it helps, this word has the same meaning as <vocabulary>支店</vocabulary> which you will also be learning in this level.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 受ける means "to receive something." Combine it with 取る (to take something), and 受け取る… still means <vocabulary>to receive something</vocabulary>.

However, while 受ける generally implies passive reception, 受け取る carries a stronger connotation of actively taking possession of something. It is used when receiving a package or gift, or even when interpreting someone's words as having a specific meaning, such as an insult or compliment.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: If you know how to read 受ける and 取る, you should be good to go.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>distribute</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to distribute</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You’re going <vocabulary>to distribute</vocabulary> flyers about your favorite country: <reading>Cuba</reading> (くば). You’re the biggest Cubaboo there has ever been, so you’ll gladly stand out in the street distributing flyers about Cuba all day long… right?

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If you want to <kanji>transmit</kanji> the story of someone's life, you have to <kanji>write down</kanji> all of it in a <vocabulary>biography</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know the kanji means <kanji>profit</kanji>. When you make it into a verb, though, it means <vocabulary>to work well</vocabulary>. If you think about it, when something works well it makes you a profit.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: What works so well? Your special <reading>key</reading> (き) that can unlock anyone and anything's potential. Imagine putting it into a key slot in someone's back. Someone who's a good for nothing can't-do-anything is now an effective member of society! Go around using your key on other non-effective things and show them that anything is possible!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Throw this onto a number and you have yourself the number of <vocabulary>times</vocabulary> something has increased. For example, ３倍 means something increased "three fold."
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Omit the 〜 when writing out the answer, though. That just represents that there should be something before the kanji in this word when being used.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. Something comes off. Something is removed. No direct object here. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to come off</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be removed</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 取る.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This has almost the same meaning as the kanji it comes from. Instead of just simply being "example," though, it's <vocabulary>for example</vocabulary>. It can also sometimes mean <vocabulary>supposing that</vocabulary> when talking about hypothetical scenarios. So, supposing that I start a sentence with this, I can be all like "例えば, I am using 例えば in a sentence."
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Using all kinds of "<vocabulary>for examples</vocabulary>" like this, you were <reading>taught</reading> (たと) many things throughout your life. For example, you were taught about...

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>participate</kanji>, so you'd think this word would mean "to participate" but it's a little more complex than that. Think of it as "to participate" but where you have <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go</vocabulary> in order to do it. This is the humble way to say those things, so you're going to these places with your tail between your legs, just happy you can participate more than anything. By extension, this is also a humble way to say <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>, often used if you're visiting something sacred like a shrine or a tomb. 

Historically, this word arose as a humble way to indicate visiting a person of higher social status. In a weird twist, this word has come to also mean <vocabulary>to be defeated</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be at a loss</vocabulary>. Think of it as what can happen when you're trying to participate while in an inferior position to someone or something.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You get <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> to participate! "It's <reading>my</reading> (まい) lucky day!" you exclaim.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Both your <kanji>hope</kanji>s and <kanji>wish</kanji>es are held within this vocab word. So, what is the meaning of this word? It is both <vocabulary>hope</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>wish</vocabulary>. Either will work.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

性 is a somewhat formal word to talk about <vocabulary>gender</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>sex</vocabulary>, including sexual desire or activity. It's also a common suffix to describe the <vocabulary>nature</vocabulary> of something. 安全性 refers to how safe something is by nature, for example, and ウィルス性 describes something virus-caused, like viral pneumonia.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 性 can also mean <kanji>nature</kanji>? Well, the <kanji>status</kanji> of your nature is your <vocabulary>personality</vocabulary>. What kind of personality do you have? Cheerful? Kind? Maybe you should take one of those online personality tests to find out.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>hope</kanji> is really a <vocabulary>wish</vocabulary> that you have inside of you (though it can still be a <vocabulary>hope</vocabulary> too).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: What's your one big <vocabulary>wish</vocabulary>? It's to have a different <reading>nose</reading> (のぞ). Alternatively, you could think "<reading>nose on me</reading>" for のぞみ.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If you have a <kanji>hope</kanji> and you turn it into a verb, you'd think it would be "to hope." But what is really behind a hope? It's a desire or wish, right? That's why this word means <vocabulary>to wish</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to desire</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Your one wish that you have is to have a bigger <reading>nose</reading> (のぞ). Feel your nose, it's too small. You wish it was two or three inches longer. Of course, if it helps to imagine you want a smaller nose or a nose at all, that's fine too. Just make sure you wish you have something nose-related.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This has the same meaning as the kanji. The little り thrown on there is just a little <vocabulary>remainder</vocabulary> sticking off the end of the kanji. No need to pay attention to that.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're waiting inside. The <vocabulary>remainder</vocabulary> of your forces are out there, fighting. You don't know who will survive... or if they even will. You have a secret <reading>knock</reading> (のこ), though, that you use to find out if it's one of the remaining forces outside or the enemy, broken through. You hear a knock. What is it? Is it your men or theirs? Imagine it out, focusing on the knock conversation that happens between you and the remainder.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>remainder</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is "to remainder." Let's make that sound better: <vocabulary>to remain behind</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You decide <vocabulary>to remain behind</vocabulary>. Everyone else leaves, and you think you're alone. Then, someone <reading>knock</reading>s (のこ) on the door. Your heart jumps in your throat. They knock again.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hope</kanji> you <kanji>request</kanji> is your <vocabulary>desire</vocabulary>. Just imagine yourself hoping and requesting some higher power for something you really want. What is this? It's your <vocabulary>desire</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wish</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pay</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to pay</vocabulary>.

This word also means <vocabulary>to brush off</vocabulary>, like when you brush dirt or dust off of something.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The hiragana ends with an う sound, so you know this is a verb. To <kanji>support</kanji> <kanji>pay</kanji> is another way to say <vocabulary>to pay</vocabulary>.

支払う is a common word used when paying for something, such as a bill, fee, or purchase. It can be used in both casual and formal contexts, but it feels a bit more complete and proper than 払う. For example, in casual conversation you'd be more likely to say 私が払うよ (I'll pay), but you could use 支払う too — it would just sound slightly more polite.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is just the on'yomi reading of 支 added on to 払う. You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be okay here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>bone</kanji> <kanji>status</kanji> is your <vocabulary>bone structure</vocabulary>. It's the way all the bones in your <vocabulary>skeleton</vocabulary> are arranged and put together!

骨格 is a relatively formal word that refers to the skeletal structure or underlying frame of something. It can literally describe a person's physical build, or it can be used figuratively to talk about the basic <vocabulary>framework</vocabulary> of a plan, argument, or piece of writing.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just note that こつ changes to こっ.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Your job is to <kanji>take</kanji> <kanji>material</kanji>s from a bunch of different people because you're <vocabulary>covering an event</vocabulary>. This <vocabulary>data collection</vocabulary> needs to be thorough, so you try to take all the materials you can from as many people as you can find.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned the on'yomi of 取 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're <vocabulary>covering an event</vocabulary> featuring all kinds of <reading>chu</reading>tes (しゅ). They have the whole range, from laundry chutes and garbage chutes, to evacuation chutes and so much more. You'll be doing some <vocabulary>data collection</vocabulary> and interviews about all these chutes, and you can't wait!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 希望 is a "wish." When you "do a wish," that means <vocabulary>to wish</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to request</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hope</vocabulary>.

This is a formal way to say that you wish for something, so you might use it at work to request an opportunity to work abroad, or let them know politely that you're resigning.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 希望. It's also the on'yomi jukugo reading as well, if that helps any.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>pay</kanji> that <kanji>support</kanji>s you is made in <vocabulary>payment</vocabulary>s. Whether you make payments to keep your house or your car, or you get payments from your boss, they keep you going.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the on'yomi reading of 支 and the kun'yomi reading of 払. You've learned them both, so you know this too!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>remainder</kanji>, but you can't really "to remainder." What is something that's similar that would make sense? How about <vocabulary>to leave behind</vocabulary>. This is when you're actually doing the leaving behind too. For example, you eat some food and you leave behind your rice because you're a bad child. You can remember this because of す. Every time you leave some food behind your mom would <reading>sue</reading> you, because she was a terrible mom. Imagine this.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word can come from level 14 item 残る. Associate the two in your mind and you'll be able to read both.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, no extra salt needed.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You've learned the word 塩, meaning salt. Add コショウ, which means pepper, and you get <vocabulary>salt and pepper</vocabulary>. You haven't learned the word for pepper yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: If salt wanted to start a cooking podcast, who would be a better <reading>co-show</reading> (コショウ) host than pepper? Imagine the most classic pair of seasonings getting into a studio to co-show host a podcast. Now that's a spicy combo.

Just a side note: The コショウ part can also be written in different ways, such as in kanji, all hiragana, or as コショー, especially on product packaging.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: 塩 uses the same reading you learned with the vocabulary, and if you remember your katakana too, you should be able to read this.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well, so this is <vocabulary>flat object counter</vocabulary>.

This counter can be used with various "flat" things, such as <vocabulary>clothing items</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>sheets</vocabulary>, paper, stamps, dishes, and more. Notice how they're all kind of flat shaped?
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You'll see this attached to other words to make them <kanji>plural</kanji>. That's why it's called a <vocabulary>pluralizing suffix</vocabulary> (or a <vocabulary>plural suffix</vocabulary> for short).

〜達 is stuck onto the end of nouns (usually people or animals) to make them plural. It can also be used with a person's name, like マリア達. In that case, it refers to Maria and the group of people she's with (rather than a bunch of Maria clones or something).

Note that you'll often just see this word written in hiragana as 〜たち.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:

If you want to pluralize something, <reading>touch</reading> (たち) it to something else. One friend touches another friend, well now they're friends. Plural friends! All thanks to the good ol' pluralizing suffix touch!

Oh, and don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached in front of this word.

価格 refers to something's market value, or to product pricing in a broader sense. It's sort of a formal word, so you might see it on fliers or in business and economic discussions about pricing strategies, for example.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

Generally, あたい refers to a numerical value in math, while ね is a formal word for "price."

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>divide</kanji> the <kanji>duty</kanji> up amongst various people. Each person will have their own <vocabulary>role</vocabulary> in completing this duty.

It can also mean <vocabulary>to break</vocabulary>, as in ワイングラスが割れる (the wine glass breaks). After all, when an object breaks, it’s divided into parts, right?

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. In modern Japanese, 衣 is more often used to describe the clothes your food is wearing, e.g., the coating on tempura or the breading on deep-fried foods.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:

Other people say clothes are simply the <reading>key</reading> to not being <reading>nu</reading>de (きぬ). What do you think?

Both ころも and きぬ mean "clothes," but these usages are old-fashioned. Also note that the more modern meaning of "coating" or "breading" uses only the ころも reading!

vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 届く and you can use that to deliver the memory to your brain.

値段 refers to the price attached to something you can buy, like in stores or markets. For example, you could use 値段 to ask how much something costs at a shop or when talking about the price of a particular meal.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading for 値 plus the on'yomi reading for 段. Combine them together to get the reading here. You've learned both of these readings already, so just remember 値 is ね because you <reading>neigh</reading> (ね) when you see a good <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:

取り替える generally means <vocabulary>to swap out</vocabulary> something with a new or different item of the same kind, like replacing an old gas meter with a new one, or exchanging books with your friend after you've both read your own.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 取る and 替える put together into one. If you know those words you'll be able to read and understand this one as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Write down</kanji> a <kanji>record</kanji> of the events so we have a <vocabulary>record</vocabulary>, please. Don't want people to forget about this momentous occasion, when King Felix got his perfect game.

記録 refers to the act of putting something on record or to the record itself. Just like English "record," it can also refer to the best performance or most remarkable event of its kind that's been officially measured and noted, like the record for fastest baseball pitch.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to entrust</vocabulary>. 

You use 預ける when you leave something in someone else's care for a while, expecting to get it back. For example, you can use 預ける when you deposit money in a bank, leave your coat in a cloakroom, or even when you park your bicycle in a parking area. You can also use it when you leave your child with grandparents or leave your dog at a pet hotel.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

In terms of places where you want <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> your money, the last place on your list should be <reading>a zoo</reading> (あず). I mean seriously, you know the animals are just gonna munch up all your dolla bills.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are the same, except that this isn't just any type of <kanji>belt</kanji>. It's an <vocabulary>obi</vocabulary>, a wide cloth <vocabulary>belt</vocabulary> worn with traditional clothes like kimono and yukata.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word ends with the hiragana う, which tells you it's a verb. The kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to get into</vocabulary>.

This word generally attaches to the stem of another verb, and adds a nuance of moving something towards the center of something, or going deep into something. You’ll be seeing lots of examples of words with 込む on the end, so you’ll gradually get a feel for the nuance it adds!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Lucky for you, the reading you learned with the kanji is the one you use here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji>, and this word is for when someone is depositing something (or someone) with you, because they want you <vocabulary>to look after</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to take care of</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to hold on to</vocabulary> it.

Remember that 預ける is used when you leave something with someone else to take care of temporarily. 預かる, on the other hand, is used when you're the one receiving something to look after. You can remember this because you're great at taking care of cargo (かる). You're always looking after everyone's cargo, but you're happy to hold on to it for them.

Also note that even though 預かる ends with かる and kind of looks intransitive, it's actually an exception! It'll pretty much always have a direct object to specify what you're looking after.

You need someone <vocabulary>to look after</vocabulary> your kids for the day. Hey, I have an idea! Leave them with the monkeys at <reading>a zoo</reading> (あず)! Monkeys love kids, and kids love monkeys. Now you can zoom off in your <reading>car</reading>s (か) for the day!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is <kanji>work</kanji> which means this verb has something to do with working. It's not straight up "to work," instead it's "<vocabulary>to work for</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>to be employed at</vocabulary>."

I must <kanji>say humbly</kanji> that I want to get <kanji>into</kanji> this position, so I'm planning <vocabulary>to apply</vocabulary> for it and <vocabulary>to submit an application</vocabulary>.

申し込む isn't just about applying, though. It's about officially communicating desires, whether you want <vocabulary>to propose</vocabulary> marriage, challenge someone to a game of tennis, or even offer a donation to a good cause.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the word 申す and the kanji 込, stuck together... humbly.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>. This verb is transitive, meaning you are doing the action. If you “do something into something” you are putting it into that thing. So this means <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to load something</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Lucky for you, the reading you learned with the kanji is the one you use here. In case you need a hand with the okurigana, here’s a mnemonic for you:

You always try <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary> your emotions into the <reading>mail</reading> (める) you send. You don't just load your mail with words, but also with emotions, to make it truly heartfelt mail.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: I am going to <kanji>descend</kanji> my <kanji>participat</kanji>ion in this conflict. I am going to descend all my weapons to the ground. I am going to <vocabulary>surrender</vocabulary>.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You’re doing a 飛ぶ and 込む at the same time, or you <kanji>jump</kanji> <kanji>into</kanji>, meaning you're <vocabulary>diving in</vocabulary>. Picture yourself standing somewhere up high, and then jumping to dive into a deep body of water.

Alternatively, this can also refer to doing something, or joining or going somewhere without an appointment, announcement, or prior registration, which is where the <vocabulary>dropping by</vocabulary> meaning comes in. For some use cases of this, check out our common word combinations and context sentences below!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: As long as you remember that we're combining the kun'yomi readings of the verbs and then turning them into a noun, you should know how to read this.
