vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If you let someone <kanji>cut off</kanji> your <kanji>oil</kanji> supply, it's probably because of your <vocabulary>inattentiveness</vocabulary>. You <vocabulary>let your guard down</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 勤める is "to be employed at," then the noun version of this is <vocabulary>work</vocabulary>. I mean, I really hope you're doing work at the place that employed you... if not you'll probably be fired.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 勤める.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>exchange</kanji>, so this verb is <vocabulary>to exchange</vocabulary>. If you exchange one thing for another thing, you are going <vocabulary>to exchange</vocabulary> it, after all. This word refers to exchanging one thing for something different.

Wondering about the difference between 替える and 換える? 替える means swapping one thing for another of the same kind, whereas 換える means exchanging or trading one thing for something different, often of similar value. So, you use 替える when switching out light bulbs, but opt for 換える when trading jewelry for cash.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: I don't like this car. I would like <vocabulary>to exchange</vocabulary> it for another <reading>ca</reading>r (か).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: If you walk around on the beach, you'll get <vocabulary>sand</vocabulary> in your shoes <reading>sooner</reading> (すな) or later.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 降参 is "surrender" so the verb version would be <vocabulary>to surrender</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading is the same as 降参 as well, of course.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
If 払う is "to pay" or "to brush off," then the noun version is <vocabulary>payment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>brushing off</vocabulary>.

Usually 払い is tacked on the end of another word, like in カード払い (payment by credit card).

When it indicates a kind of brushing off or brushing away, it appears in words like 足払い (sweeping an opponent's legs in judo) or, more figuratively, せき払い (clearing one's throat).
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading comes from 払う, so know that and it will pay forward your knowledge to this one.

Note that when 払い is added to the end of a compound, it becomes ばらい.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>take</kanji> and <kanji>return</kanji> something to yourself is <vocabulary>to take back</vocabulary> something. Give it back!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 取る and 戻す. Combine them to get this.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 払い is a "payment" and 戻す is "to return." If you return a payment, you are going <vocabulary>to repay</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to refund</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to reimburse</vocabulary> someone for their payment.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 払い and 戻す.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same, so this also means <vocabulary>deep red</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>crimson</vocabulary>. Additionally, it can also mean <vocabulary>rouge</vocabulary>, usually in reference to the cosmetic.

紅 is also a bit of an old-fashioned and somewhat literary word, so keep that in mind!
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This is where things get a little complicated. You already learned べに as a reading with 口紅. 紅 can also be read べに just by itself, and in that case, it means <vocabulary>rouge</vocabulary>. However, there’s a different reading that’s used for <vocabulary>deep red</vocabulary>, which we’d like to focus on here, so here’s a mnemonic to help you remember it:

There's so much <vocabulary>deep red</vocabulary> blood everywhere, there's no way of helping this person bleeding out. One might say, <reading>cure ない</reading> (くれない).  Just remember: when there's deep red everywhere, cure ない.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You're a <kanji>resident</kanji> and you <kanji>exist</kanji> in the place you're residing in. That means you have <vocabulary>residence</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is put on the end of numbers to show how old someone is.

You already learned 〜才 (years old), and 〜歳 means the exact same thing. No trick questions here. The difference is that 歳 is a pretty complicated kanji, so 才 is the simplified, more casual option for easier readability. Basically, 才 is the jeans-and-t-shirt version, while 歳 shows up in a suit and tie when things get official.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>sand</kanji> makes a lot of <kanji>profit</kanji>, it swells up and becomes <vocabulary>gravel</vocabulary>. They're like the fat cats of the beach.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
You learned the reading for 利 with the kanji, but the reading for 砂 is irregular, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're walking through that big fat <vocabulary>gravel</vocabulary>, when a pile of it starts moving, and something suddenly leaps out at you. It's a... <reading>ja</reading>guar (じゃ)! Run!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

価 refers to the monetary value or the price of goods in a transaction. Although it's somewhat old-fashioned and less common these days, you may still see it used in advanced phrases like 価をつける (to set a price) or 一文の価もない (not even worth a penny).

Note that あたい can also refer to a numerical value in mathematics, such as the value a variable or function takes, but it's more commonly written with the kanji 値 in this use.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: Okay, this is a great <vocabulary>value</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>. Wait, what is? <reading>A tie</reading> (あたい). Get a tie, and it will make you more professional which will help you to get a better job. Great value, right there, just for a tie.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>public</kanji> <kanji>announcement</kanji> is a <vocabulary>public notice</vocabulary>.

公告 looks and sounds a lot like 広告, but the meanings are different. You might remember 広告 is for advertisements, but 公告 here is for the kind of official statements that companies or governments put out for the public, especially shareholders, creditors, or other stakeholders.

You can remember 公告 is a public notice because the kanji for "public" is 公, and it's not covered by a canopy like the other one. It's uncovered, all out in the open for everyone to see — public!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
It's kind of like you're saying <kanji>say</kanji> <kanji>say</kanji>, and it’s used in classical Japanese to get someone’s attention, so this is <vocabulary>excuse me</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary>.

You would generally encounter 申し申し in dialogues set in older times, unlike its modern, shortened version もしもし, which is used for telephone greetings (and almost always written in kana).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the reading you learned with the kanji. You should know it already.

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: One line plus another line equals <radical>two</radical> lines. This radical represents the number two. Pretty simple, right? Can you guess what three looks like? I bet you can...

This is the top half of a moon peeking out as it begins to rise. When does that happen? In the <radical>evening</radical>! Don't confuse this with the moon radical 月. 夕 is for the evening, when the moon's still low enough to be partly covered (by a mountain, for example).

This looks like a clothesline pole you would <radical>dry</radical> clothes on. It's got two very straight horizontal poles, for maximum drying efficiency. If you were gonna dry your clothes, you'd dry them on this thing.

Don't confuse this with 千 (thousand), where the top line curves down. 千 would be impossible to dry clothes on, because they'd slide right off!
See the mouth and long, fang-like teeth of this <radical>alligator</radical>, which is facing to the right? You wouldn't want to get your hand stuck in there, that's for sure.

This looks like the middle radical on top of a sideways leaf. What can you often find sitting on the middle of a leaf? An <radical>insect</radical>. Insects looove sitting right in the middle of leaves. That's why this is the insect radical.
This is a very oddly shaped <radical>key</radical>, but it's a key nonetheless.
This <radical>box</radical> is open. There could be any number of things inside, but for now all you need to know is the meaning of this radical, which is box.

Under a cliff, you spot a cross, slightly tilted. The cross is there to mark a famous <radical>clan</radical> that once ruled the lands below the cliff. It's a pretty unique cross, so whenever you see it there under the cliff, you'll know it honors the clan who lived there.

You take your head and pack clay dirt around it to just above your mouth. You need the <radical>circumference</radical> of your head for your helmet maker, and sending them a clay dirt mold of your head will just do the trick. That way they'll know your head's exact circumference!

This is the <radical>tongue</radical> radical. See that sturdy slide holding a thousand people above a mouth? An open mouth can't support that much weight, but a strong tongue can — it's the muscle of the mouth, after all.

Alternatively, you can think of this as something sticking out of a mouth with thousands of tiny taste buds on it. It's your tongue!

This is the <radical>spicy</radical> radical. See how it's wide at the top, with a little stem sticking up, and narrow at the bottom? Just like a chili pepper. It's so spicy it can't even handle its own heat!

This is the canopy radical with ice running down the back. If you hang out in a cold canopy like this you'll definitely get <radical>sick</radical>. Imagine being sick and alone inside a cold canopy. Brrrr, oh no... ACHOO!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>older brother</radical>.

In case you need a refresher, here's the mnemonic again: Who's someone who's just a mouth with legs? That's your know-it-all older brother, who won't shut up about anything.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>skin</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You go down a slide made of branches and your skin scrapes right off — ouch! Lucky for you, it was just your old outer layer of skin, and now you've got a fresh shiny layer. Yay for exfoliation! You're not sure what to do with this big, floppy layer of old skin, though…

This the radical for <radical>simple</radical>. Why? Because it looks like a simple little stick figure drawing! Just a big head on top with a few hairs, and a stick figure body. What could be more simple?

Legs appear between two lumps of dirt. This is the earth's version of a <radical>womb</radical>. Imagine a tiny baby growing under the ground and then sprouting out, legs first, into the world. Imagine being inside this dirt womb. It's warm and damp. You feel safe.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>circle</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: What's something with <radical>nine</radical> sides? Just add a <radical>drop</radical> and you'll have something that's almost a <kanji>circle</kanji>.

This is the radical for <radical>now</radical>. It's a bit tough to see, but it kind of looks like a fancy clock. The 𠆢 is the top part hanging over the clock. The ラ shows a triangular clock face with a little cuckoo on top, peeking out to tell you this means now — right now!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>valley</radical>.

A samurai opens his mouth to wish you <radical>good luck</radical>. Samurai are usually considered strong, silent types, but before any big battle they open their mouths to say one thing to each other: "good luck!"

You shoot your gun at the sun in winter, making it implode and turn into a <radical>black hole</radical>. Great, now it's permanent winter and the black hole is sucking everything on Earth into it — including your gun and some unlucky skier who's having the ride of their life around the edge of the black hole.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>director</radical>.

There's something standing up on this head that's old. It's a <radical>mohawk</radical>. What other hairstyle stands straight up? Mohawks are also kind of old-school, as far as hairstyles go, which is why this mohawk stands straight up off an old guy's head.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>peace</radical>.

Who's that guy wearing Korean clothes? That is a man from <radical>Korea</radical>, and this is the Korea radical—go figure! He's wearing a samo hat on his head to complete the rest of his hanbok outfit.

Alternatively, you can remember this one using the radical components:
There are five mouths eating cow at a Korean BBQ. Korea is famous for their delicious BBQ, and you need a lot of people to eat all that beef. At least five people. (Get it? Five people!) That's why this radical is Korea.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>peoples</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>interval</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>machine</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: You have a <radical>private</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> that's a <kanji>machine</kanji>. But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.
This radical looks just like a top hat. That's why it's <radical>top hat</radical>!
On the ground there are a bunch of <radical>spikes</radical> coming out. You wouldn't want to step on those, now would you?

This is the <radical>Chinese</radical> radical. Why? Because it looks like a traditional Chinese pagoda! One of those towers with a bunch of tiered roofs, you know? Sure, lots of Asian countries have pagodas, but let's be honest — the Chinese probably came up with them first.
This ice is in the shape of a stick. It's an <radical>icicle</radical>! You can even see two little ice chunks breaking off of it on the left side.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What do you get if you lend a <radical>spirit</radical> your <radical>umbrella</radical>? <kanji>Thanks</kanji>, of course! Especially if that spirit is Totoro, the spirit of the forest.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: So what did you receive as <kanji>thanks</kanji>? You open it up, and there's a <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun inside!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Being a <radical>leader</radical> or <radical>director</radical> in a company means you have to <kanji>inquire</kanji> about lots of things. Have you started this yet? Have you finished that yet? Did you get that thing I sent you? Where's my coffee? Basically if you're a leader or director, your main job is to inquire about these very important things.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Turns out the leader and director of your company is Chairman Kaga from the TV show Iron Chef. Every time he tries to <kanji>inquire</kanji> about weird stuff, you have to say <reading>Ooh, Kaga</reading> (うかが) disapprovingly. "What are you doing for dinner tonight?" he inquires. Ooh, Kaga! "What's the best way to soften an eggplant?" he inquires. Ooh, Kaga!

compounds.meaning: to be late, to fall behind

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Next to the <radical>scooter</radical>, there's a <radical>flag</radical> warning you that there are <radical>sheep</radical> around here, so you should go <kanji>slow</kanji>. That means you might be <kanji>late</kanji>, but at least the sheep will be okay!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You follow the flag, but the sheep refuse to <kanji>slow</kanji> down so you have to get creative. You place <reading>chee</reading>se (ち) every ten feet or so, that way the sheep slow down to bend down on their scooters and take a bite.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: That <radical>slide</radical> is your <radical>husband</radical>'s only <kanji>fault</kanji>. He loves that slide, more than you, and it's the only thing you don't like about him.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You try to come up with another <kanji>fault</kanji> of his so you can complain, when you see a tiny <reading>shih tzu</reading> (しつ) trotting by. Oh no! Before you can call out, your husband has fallen off the slide and crushed the poor thing. You hear a sharp yelp and then nothing.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>tsunami</radical> going down your <radical>dry</radical> face is just <kanji>sweat</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>sweat</kanji> isn't just on your face, it's also dripping down your <reading>ass</reading> (あせ).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You live in the <radical>now</radical>, so your <radical>heart</radical> controls your <kanji>thought</kanji> process. You don't have time to think with your brain — all your thoughts come straight from the heart.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What has your heart been giving a lot of <kanji>thought</kanji> to lately? <reading>Nen</reading>doroids (ねん). Nendoroids are those plastic anime figurines with the really big heads. You've gotten addicted to collecting them and now they occupy your thoughts 24/7.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> goes through a little <radical>door</radical>, and plops down a <radical>big</radical> drop on your face. This tsunami is your tears inside your eye area. The door is your tear duct. The big drop is the <kanji>teardrop</kanji> coming down your eye.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>teardrop</kanji>s are like little waves. What are they? They're <reading>波だ</reading> (なみだ).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Bamboo</radical> <radical>heaven</radical> is a place for <kanji>laugh</kanji>ing. Bamboo is a very jolly plant, and they love to laugh. Even after death in bamboo heaven, the bamboo continue to laugh joyfully. Bamboo heaven is truly a place of laughter.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: There’s actually a war a goin’ on up in that there bamboo heaven, y’know? Ye might not have heard of it with all that there <kanji>laugh</kanji>in’ a goin’ on, but there definitely be a <reading>war a</reading> (わら) goin’ on up in bamboo heaven, y’hear? The bamboo are scared so that’s why they be laughin’ so much. They nervous.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>say</radical> something about the <radical>circumference</radical> of this area. You've looked around this whole area, making a big circle around it, because you are trying to <kanji>investigate</kanji> something that happened here. You also say this thing in a really quiet <kanji>tone</kanji> of voice, because you don't want the person or thing you're investigating to know you're on to them.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: "I came here to <kanji>investigate</kanji> this place, and I did indeed find out who the criminal is... it's none other than Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう)!"

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tree</radical> is growing out of a <radical>top hat</radical> you need to <kanji>inspect</kanji> it to find out why and how this happened. You should probably <kanji>investigate</kanji> the area too. I mean, how could a tree grow out of a top hat anyway? Seems suspicious.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>inspect</kanji> the tree, you pick up a <reading>saw</reading>(さ) and start cutting it. You need to investigate how the tree and the top hat are connected, and a saw is the only way to do it properly.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>grain</radical>, from one <radical>evening</radical> to the next <radical>evening</radical>, experiences a <kanji>shift</kanji>. After two evenings, the grain has shifted from one location to another.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>shift</kanji> is caused by the <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) that wants to eat the grains. Every other evening, the eagle swoops down, shifts the grains (eating a few) and then flies off.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>Chinese</radical> <radical>turkey</radical> is <kanji>difficult</kanji> to find because they are so rare. Chinese turkeys are the rarest variety of turkey, so naturally, finding one is exceedingly difficult.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Do you know the actual reason Chinese turkey are so <kanji>difficult</kanji> to find? It’s because they’re all made out of <reading>Naan</reading> (なん). Of course they’re elusive when they blend in so well with all the other Naan!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You line up stalks of <radical>bamboo</radical> with an equal <radical>interval</radical> between each one. This pattern creates a sense of <kanji>simplicity</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: That kind of <kanji>simplicity</kanji> is what Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) always demanded. Everything he decided was based on simplicity.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>simple</radical> radical and the <kanji>simple</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: One of the most <kanji>simple</kanji> things in the world is getting a <reading>tan</reading> (たん). All you have to do is stand outside long enough. It doesn't matter what skin type you have or what the weather is like. Eventually, if you stand out there long enough, you'll get a tan.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>canine</radical> puts its <radical>mouth</radical> on your <radical>heart</radical>, it's a pretty unforgettable <kanji>feeling</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Overall, though, it's a good <kanji>feeling</kanji> — so good that you feel like Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん)! With this canine lovingly slobbering on your heart, you feel like you could go out and conquer the world!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Only a <radical>tree</radical> with <radical>eye</radical>s and a <radical>heart</radical> has the ability to <kanji>imagine</kanji> and to <kanji>contemplate</kanji>. For a tree to imagine and contemplate things, it needs eyes to see and a heart to feel.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If a <radical>tree</radical> can <kanji>imagine</kanji>, it likely has a <reading>soul</reading> (そう). Its soul is what makes it possible for the tree to <kanji>contemplate</kanji> things, you see?

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Pointing a <radical>thread</radical> to the <radical>east</radical> is what you <kanji>practice</kanji> every day. You're incredibly passionate about eastward thread-pointing, so you make sure to practice every day.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You do all of this <kanji>practice</kanji> to try and afford all of your <reading>ren</reading>tals (れん). One day, all of this practice will pay for all of your rentals.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Let the <radical>sun</radical> shine into your <radical>ear</radical> while sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> and make sure <kanji>most</kanji> of it gets in your head. You want to fill your brain with the most sun anyone ever has.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Most</kanji> of this is for your <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい). You're testing out a new way to power it, but if you can't get most of the sun into your ear, it won't be enough to power most of the cyborg's robo-parts.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>scooter</radical> with a <radical>mohawk</radical>, now that's the most <kanji>suitable</kanji> hairstyle you could ever think of for a scooter!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You want this <kanji>suitable</kanji> hairstyle for your scooter too, and luckily you're a <reading>techie</reading> (てき), so it's easy for you to install one.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You want to get a <radical>scooter</radical>, so you have one self (<radical>oneself</radical>) and another self working <radical>together</radical> to <kanji>choose</kanji>. The two tiny yous sit on each of your shoulders, like angel and devil, and argue about which scooter you should choose.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Suddenly your selfs both gasp and <kanji>choose</kanji> a scooter in front of you that looks like a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん). The scooter is designed like a human on the top, the bars are its arms, and the bottom with the seat and the wheels are all horse. This centaur scooter is what you choose to ride.

compounds.meaning: to make a mistake, to get wrong

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You take your <radical>scooter</radical> to <radical>Korea</radical> and everything is <kanji>different</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What's also <kanji>different</kanji> is that there's a weird tiger bouncing on its tail alongside you yelling that its name is <reading>Tigger</reading> (ちが). You didn't know Tigger was living in Korea these days. That's definitely different.

kanji.meaning: straight line; direct; fix, be repaired
kanji.kunyomi: ただしい なおす なおる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
This kanji is the same as the radical — <kanji>straight</kanji> as straight can be.

It can also mean <kanji>direct</kanji>, because when you go straight to a place, you're going there directly. Depending on the context it can even mean <kanji>fix</kanji>, since fixing something means straightening out all the messed up crooked bits.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Put food <kanji>straight</kanji> into your esophagus without chewing and you will <reading>choke</reading> (ちょく). You want to get straight to the most important part of eating — the digesting part — but if you don't follow all the intermediate steps, you'll end up choking.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>loiter</radical> around a <radical>black hole</radical>, waiting for it to finish destroying stuff so you can switch it to <kanji>restore</kanji> mode. You were told all black holes finish eventually, and when they do you can press a button to restore everything back to the way it was.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When there's nothing else for the black hole to eat, you hit the <kanji>restore</kanji> button.... but nothing happens. "Oh, <reading>f**k</reading> (ふく) you!" you scream, as you realize you were lied to.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <radical>tongue</radical> becomes too <radical>spicy</radical> for you to bear, it’s time to <kanji>quit</kanji> the jalapeño eating contest. You’ve been eating them for three hours now and the spiciness from the peppers is really burning your tongue. Throw in the towel, it’s time to quit the contest.

This kanji has another meaning too:

Eating isn't the only thing that makes your <radical>tongue</radical> <radical>spicy</radical>, so do certain <kanji>word</kanji>s. Say your favorite words out loud right now. Feel them on your tongue. Words are the spicy food of language!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Oh, you're probably wondering who won that spicy food contest after you <kanji>quit</kanji> and became obsessed with <kanji>word</kanji>s instead. It was <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ). Who did you expect? He was great with words AND never quitting when things got spicy.

kanji.meaning: a homework; an inn, a hotel
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>roof</radical> under which the <radical>leader</radical> can house one <radical>hundred</radical> of his people is at the local <kanji>lodge</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>lodge</kanji> <reading>shook</reading> (しゅく) as the hundred people came tumbling in through the door. It shook, but it didn't fall over. The roof stayed firmly in place, and everyone got to sleep under it okay.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Once the <radical>sun</radical> comes out, you can use this <radical>key</radical> to unlock it and take you to any <kanji>previous</kanji> day, even just <kanji>yesterday</kanji>! The sun is in charge of the day changes, so if you use a key to unlock it, you can control the flow of time and return to yesterday, or a previous day in the past. Behold the power of the sun.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Time traveling to a <kanji>previous</kanji> time, like <kanji>yesterday</kanji>, can be rough on the body. As such, you wear a small <reading>sack</reading> (さく) to hold your valuables while you're ripped through the sands of time. The sack keeps your important stuff from getting lost. The sack holds your key to the sun as well.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
<radical>Wolverine</radical> is going down a <radical>slide</radical> and from your <radical>mouth</radical> you scream, "Hey, <kanji>buddy</kanji>! Watch it with that slide, it's really fast and you might hurt yourself, buddy!" 

You're a really good buddy to Wolverine. He also happens to be the local <kanji>ruler</kanji> of these lands. You make it a habit to befriend the local strongmen, just in case… No wonder you're so buddy-buddy with all the rulers around here.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The biggest perk of having Wolverine as your <kanji>buddy</kanji> is that he teaches you <reading>kun</reading>g fu (くん). Wolverine wants you, his good buddy, to know how to defend yourself. That's why he uses his martial arts knowledge to train you in kung fu every day after he gets done playing on the slide.

kanji.meaning: splendid, nice; after all; tie, connect

compounds.meaning: to tie, to connect, to conclude

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You use a <radical>thread</radical> for <radical>good luck</radical> by <kanji>bind</kanji>ing two fingers together. You <kanji>tie</kanji> them nice and tight.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you <kanji>bind</kanji> your fingers, the good luck starts pouring in. Literally. Suddenly <reading>ketsu</reading>p (けつ) starts pouring down from the heavens.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You meet a <radical>woman</radical> from another <radical>clan</radical> under the rising <radical>sun</radical> to prepare for <kanji>marriage</kanji>. Your clan and her clan are standing together as the two of you watch the sun rise together.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: For the <kanji>marriage</kanji> to be official, you need to wait for a <reading>con</reading>dor (こん) to appear. If it doesn't show up before the sun goes down again, the marriage was a failure. You have to try again tomorrow with a different woman.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>spirit</radical> blesses your <radical>older brother</radical> it's time to <kanji>celebrate</kanji>! This isn't something that happens every day to everyone's older brother. Yours is very good and very lucky. So celebrate with him!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, the two of you <kanji>celebrate</kanji>d too much, and you went a little crazy. The spirit grabbed your brother and <reading>shook</reading> (しゅく) him. Shook him so hard his head popped off.

kanji.meaning: a piece of music; a curve; bend

compounds.meaning: to bend, to turn a corner

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: There are <radical>mouth</radical>s, <radical>twenty</radical> of them, singing beautiful <kanji>music</kanji> together. The music seems to <kanji>bend</kanji> toward you through the air.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The twenty mouths make so much <kanji>music</kanji> that they literally <reading>cloak you</reading> (きょく) with it. They cloak you with the music.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If there’s a <radical>drop</radical> on your <radical>head</radical> and the <radical>rice</radical> is <radical>big</radical>, you know you’re in the <kanji>interior</kanji>. And by interior, I mean you’re actually inside someone. The rice is big because you’ve shrunk to a tiny size and are inside someone’s stomach. The drop on your head is actually digestive fluid.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: While you’re in the <kanji>interior</kanji> of this guy, you hear him break out in song. He starts singing “<reading>Ok</reading>lahoma” (おく) at the top of his lungs. The big pieces of rice slosh around as he sings and dances. “OOOOk-lahoma, where the wind comes sweepin' down the plain!”

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: From the <radical>roof</radical>, an <radical>icicle</radical> falls and hits <radical>Wolverine</radical> in the <radical>forehead</radical>, and he has to go over to the <radical>stool</radical> to <kanji>lie down</kanji>. And eventually he goes to <kanji>sleep</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: While wolverine <kanji>sleep</kanji>s, he makes a horrible <reading>neigh</reading>ing (ね) sound. It's like there's a giant horse in his mouth screaming to get out! NEIGH NEIGH!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When your <radical>sick</radical> <radical>mama</radical> tries to do a <radical>task</radical> she's filled with <kanji>pain</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your mama's <kanji>pain</kanji> is <reading>too</reading> (つう) much for her to handle, so now you have to do all of her tasks too.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>womb</radical> spins in a <radical>circle</radical> and starts to <radical>boil</radical> with <kanji>heat</kanji>. Uh oh, I think you have a <kanji>fever</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>heat</kanji> from your <kanji>fever</kanji> is making your insides and your head and your entire body spin and boil, until your doctor throws some <reading>nets</reading> (ねつ) around you. You were flailing around and they couldn't get you to stop, so they had to catch you in a series of nets.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>insect</radical> radical and <kanji>insect</kanji> are the same in looks as well as and meaning.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: It's an <kanji>insect</kanji>! Get it! You squish it with your foot - what sound does it make? A <reading>mush</reading> (むし) sound.

kanji.meaning: dentistry; teeth; a dentist; a decayed tooth
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Stop</radical>! That <radical>box</radical> of <radical>rice</radical> is actually full of <kanji>teeth</kanji>! I know it says "rice" on the cover, but I promise you those are all teeth and if you bite into them you'll break a <kanji>tooth</kanji> of your own.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Why do I have a rice box full of <kanji>teeth</kanji>? <reading>Hah</reading> (は)! Wouldn't you like to know. Hah! I definitely have an answer that isn't weird or creepy…

kanji.meaning: politics, government; heal, cure; a treatment
kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
After a <radical>tsunami</radical>, use this <radical>machine</radical> to <kanji>cure</kanji> the people and the country from the damage. <kanji>Heal</kanji>ing machines are all over Japan just in case a tsunami does way more damage than they can handle. 

Oh, and whoever cures and heals the most people will be able to <kanji>rule</kanji> over them once everything starts going back to normal. So keep that in mind, kay?
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
Alternative ways to <kanji>cure</kanji> yourself after a tsunami are either praying to <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ) or eating your weight in <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). I'm not sure if I have enough cheese for all the people that got hit though... Hmm, do you have cheese?

Before you make your decision, remember that whoever cures you will be able to <kanji>reign</kanji> over you and your people. So do you want to be led by Jesus or by some cheese? The choice is yours.

kanji.kunyomi: けがれる よごれる きたない
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> hit not one, but <radical>TWO</radical> <radical>prison</radical>s, making them extremely <kanji>dirty</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What's the most <kanji>dirty</kanji> are the prisons' <reading>o</reading>bi (お) collections. You can hear the prisoners crying, "Oh, not the obi. Our obi are all dirty, oh no!"

kanji.meaning: line up, set up; the alignment of your teeth

compounds.meaning: to line up, to stand in a line
to line up, to set up

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You stick <radical>horns</radical> in the <radical>ground</radical> using them as <radical>spikes</radical> and you <kanji>line up</kanji> the horns in a straight line. Horns are pretty much the same thing as spikes once you stick them in the ground, and you line these ones up precisely for optimal protection.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>line up</kanji> these horns and stick them into the ground, you notice a bull munching on <reading>hay</reading> (へい) nearby. It's staring at the horns you're lining up. Somehow it feels like it's munching that hay angrily. You gulp, looking at its horn as it grabs another mouthful of hay, and you feel pretty guilty.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of <radical>alligators</radical>... she's no ordinary leader, that's for sure. She's not a politician, she's not a queen... She's one of the <kanji>Other</kanji> Ones, a group of strange, eccentric people who become leaders of animals.
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco":

Then there's the <kanji>other</kanji>s of the others. These are the <reading>ta</reading>co (た) worshipers. They're really strange.

kanji.meaning: height; single, unmarried; social status; sashimi
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When your <radical>self</radical> goes down a <radical>slide</radical> and hits a <radical>barb</radical>, it's a painful reminder that you have a <kanji>body</kanji>. Sometimes people think their self is just some kind of floating, disembodied consciousness, but getting a barb stuck in <kanji>oneself</kanji> while going down a slide will quickly remind one of one's bodily existence.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What part of your <kanji>body</kanji> did the barb get stuck in? Your <reading>shin</reading> (しん). That pointy little barb dug deep into your shin and made you painfully aware of the fact that <kanji>oneself</kanji> and one's body are inextricable.

kanji.meaning: sake; cooking sake; alcohol; a liquor store
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> is an <radical>alcohol</radical>ic beverage containing a lot of <kanji>alcohol</kanji>. It’s 3 different kinds of rums, pineapple juice, and grenadine. It’ll hit you like a tsunami though. This alcoholic drink has a kick to it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As you lie on this beach, the <kanji>alcohol</kanji> keeps coming down a <reading>chu</reading>te (しゅ), straight into your mouth. You can feel the sand in your toes and the alcohol sliding down your throat from this special tsunami chute.

compounds.meaning: to breathe, to inhale, to smoke

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>mouth</radical> is like an <radical>escalator</radical> you use to <kanji>suck</kanji> and <kanji>inhale</kanji> things into your body.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Use this mouth ability to <kanji>suck</kanji> <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう) into your mouth. Cucumbers are shaped like cylinders so you can suck them into your mouth like this. Just as nature intended.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: In the <radical>valley</radical> you feel a <radical>lack</radical> of <kanji>want</kanji>. You want for nothing in this valley. It is the valley of plenty.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Once you get to the valley, you <kanji>want</kanji> some protein. Egg <reading>yolk</reading> (よく) falls from the sky! It’s a miracle! You wanted protein, and egg yolk was presented. It falls right into your open mouth.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Closing each <radical>eye</radical> is something that the <radical>peoples</radical> do before they <kanji>sleep</kanji>. The peoples can’t sleep with both eyes open and they can’t sleep with just one eye open either. Peoples have to close each eye before they can sleep.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The reason you want to <kanji>sleep</kanji> is because all the other peoples were <reading>mean</reading> (みん) to you. They were so mean that the only way you could get over it was to close your eyes and sleep. You just want to sleep.

compounds.meaning: to get tired, to be exhausted

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: I have <radical>sick</radical> in my <radical>skin</radical>. Just look at it, it doesn't look too good. Whenever I have sickness in my skin, I know that I'm probably <kanji>tired</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Why so <kanji>tired</kanji>? Your body is <reading>hea</reading>ted (ひ) up from exercising way too much. You should let that heat cool down so your skin starts looking better.

kanji.meaning: a breath; a son; be short of breath
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Imagining one’s <radical>self</radical> without a <radical>heart</radical> can make it hard to draw <kanji>breath</kanji>. Without a heart, you’d have no blood pumping and you would start to die. This would make it increasingly harder to draw breath and get oxygen to stay alive.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You know how when people are unconscious and their <kanji>breath</kanji> slows or comes to a stop, they use smelling salts to revive them? Well a smelly <reading>sock</reading> (そく) can work just as well. Socks get really stinky and their stench is powerful enough to revive someone who isn’t drawing breath.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> that wants <radical>peace</radical> can <kanji>call</kanji> for it. If you don’t have a mouth, you can’t call for peace. So use your mouth and call for peace when you can. Peace is great.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: But before you <kanji>call</kanji> for peace, you must first placate the masses. To do so, you astound them with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ) skills. Once they are so entranced by how talented you are with a yo-yo, you easily convince them to make peace.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The meaning of this word is the same as the kanji, except it has an お before it, which just makes the thing you're saying elevate the other person more. Basically, it's more polite and awesome.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You need to go for a drive to the public gardens, but you aren't going to get your normal car, you're going to get your <kanji>other</kanji> car. Your <reading>hoe car</reading> (ほか)! It's a car made entirely out of garden hoes. You can drive it and hoe with it at the same time! Your other car can't do that.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This word is actually more general than the English words <vocabulary>insect</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>bug</vocabulary>, though. It covers things like worms and spiders, too, so in that sense it's more like <vocabulary>creepy-crawly</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading, which is also the reading you learned when you learned this kanji!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: その means "that" or "the", and その plus <kanji>other</kanji> means things like <vocabulary>the others</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>other</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>other than that</vocabulary>, depending on the context.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This has two readings, but luckily you learned one of them when you learned the kanji, and the other one when you learned the word 他. The two readings are usually interchangeable, too.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This almost shares the meaning with the kanji. It's essentially the same thing, though when it's alone it refers to a specific <vocabulary>piece of music</vocabulary> (aka a <vocabulary>tune</vocabulary>).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji as well, so you should be able to read it.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji portion means <kanji>fault</kanji>, so you would think the verb version is "to fault." It's a little different, though. Think of it this way, if you "fault" something, you're messing up. What's a great way to mess up? By losing something. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to lose</vocabulary>. 

Pretend like you are supposed to hold on to someone's wedding ring. You make the biggest fault of all. You lose it. Ouch.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

So how did you lose the wedding ring anyway? Well... it was eaten by a cow. The <reading>牛 now</reading> (うし + なう) has to have it surgically removed. What a mess!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When you do something that's your <kanji>fault</kanji> and then you say "<kanji>thanks</kanji>" after you do it, that's super-duper <vocabulary>rude</vocabulary>, wouldn't you say? Imagine doing something like this and then thinking to yourself after... wow, I was really rude.

This is also often used to mean <vocabulary>excuse me</vocabulary>, typically followed by ですが or します. Occasionally, it’s also used just on its own, usually when the speaker holds a higher or equal status to the person being spoken to. This particular usage is more prevalent among older generations and is commonly associated with masculine speech.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Add this to the end of someone's name, it's like saying ______<kanji>buddy</kanji>. It's generally used as a name ender (like さん) for boys and young men. Don't use this on people who are higher ranked than you (socially or literally). As in, you wouldn't use it on your boss. Use it on your younger male subordinates as well as boys who aren't adults yet.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (on'yomi), probably because it usually is attached to other words (aka names, like こういち君) making it act more like jukugo words do.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>All</kanji> of someone's <kanji>body</kanji> is their <vocabulary>whole body</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>entire body</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Okay, so the kanji itself means <kanji>buddy</kanji> and so does the word, but it also means <vocabulary>you</vocabulary> as well. This is one of the several ways to say "you" in Japanese, and this one is kind of an "affectionate" you. Maybe you'd say it with someone you're close to. Maybe you'd say it with a girlfriend or boyfriend. You wouldn't want to use it with your boss or teacher, though. Make sure to keep that in mind. It's kind of like saying "hey buddy" or "hey you," after all.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Who's your <vocabulary>buddy</vocabulary>? It's <reading>Kimmy</reading> (きみ)! If you know a Kimmy, imagine her. If you don't, find a famous Kimmy or make up a Kimmy to imagine. You ask... is it you?? Wait, you're my buddy?

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a verb because it ends with an う sound. What does the kanji mean? It's <kanji>music</kanji> and <kanji>bend</kanji>. In the case of this word, we're going with the "bend" version. The verb of that is <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary>. This is when you're doing the bending. You can remember this because げ kind of looks like the <reading>ge</reading>cko you're bending. That gecko looked good before you bent him in half.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: How were you able <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary> this gecko? Solo effort? No way! It actually took both you and your <reading>ma</reading>ma (ま) to make it happen! Just imagine you and your mighty mama, tag-teaming to bend a gecko in half!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the vocab word are the same, so this means <vocabulary>body</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>oneself</vocabulary>. It also refers to <vocabulary>animal flesh</vocabulary> sometimes, meaning the non-bone edible parts of animals, including seafood. It's the "mi" in sashimi!

Wondering about the difference between 体 and 身? Basically, 体 is for the physical human (or animal) body as a whole, and is often used in relation to its condition or appearance. 身 can refer to a physical human body too, but unlike 体, it's also used to refer to the self as an individual and, by extension, to one's social standing or circumstances.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

Who does this <vocabulary>body</vocabulary> belong to? To <reading>me</reading> (み)!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means both music and bend. For this word, we're looking at "bend." So the verb 曲がる is to be bent. It's intransitive, so don't give it a direct object. Use it to say something gets bent or bends: a knee is bent, the road bends — that sort of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading with 曲げる, so you should be good to go!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the noun version of the kanji 酒 - it has an お there to be nice. This word can mean both <vocabulary>alcohol</vocabulary> (like the parent kanji) or <vocabulary>sake</vocabulary> (the main kind of Japanese alcohol, at least back in the kanji days).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi, which isn't what you learned with the kanji. But, it should be pretty easy. You know what Japanese alcohol is called already, right? It's <reading>さけ</reading>, simple as that. So long as you've heard of sake you should be A-Okay with this reading.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>bend</kanji> in a <kanji>line</kanji> is merely a <vocabulary>curve</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji, so it has the same meaning, basically. You can say this is <vocabulary>the most</vocabulary> or just <vocabulary>most</vocabulary>. You can also use it as <vocabulary>extremely</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this is a reading you didn't learn with the kanji (the kun'yomi reading). To learn it, let's look at a mnemonic. 

Think of <vocabulary>the most</vocabulary> ridiculous <reading>motto</reading> (もっと) you've ever heard. Now imagine a motto that's even more ridiculous. Here are some actual totally real mottos that are the most ridiculous: "What Can Brown Do for You?" "It's Not for Women" "If It Doesn't Get All Over the Place, It Doesn't Belong in Your Face" and of course, "Why Not Enjoy the Go?"

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>straight</kanji> <kanji>line</kanji> is a <vocabulary>straight line</vocabulary>. You know, the shortest distance between two points and all that.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>investigate</kanji> so the vocab verb version means <vocabulary>to investigate</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You are hired <vocabulary>to investigate</vocabulary> someone's wife. It is said that <reading>she love</reading>s (しら) another man... but you need to investigate her to find out if that's true, for her husband of course.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You receive <kanji>profit</kanji> at every <kanji>breath</kanji>. What kind of profit is this? It's <vocabulary>interest</vocabulary>. As time goes by and as you take more breaths you gain more bank interest.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You smell someone's <reading>icky</reading> (いき) <vocabulary>breath</vocabulary>. It's gross. Your skin crawls and your eyes roll back in your head from the icky, icky smell. You might die.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

想定 usually refers to assumptions made in advance about certain conditions or situations. It’s often used when talking about preparing for or anticipating future events, especially ones where planning might be required, like natural disasters.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: Guess what? Even though this would use the vocab kun'yomi reading, usually, the readings for both on'yomi and kun'yomi on this kanji are the same, meaning you can read this word no matter what. Feeling better now?

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

This is for something <vocabulary>hot to the touch</vocabulary>, not for the weather (that'd be 暑い). Think boiling water or someone's forehead when they have a fever — those are 熱い. Figuratively, it can also mean <vocabulary>passionate</vocabulary>. Burning passion, right?

疲れ is a more casual version of 疲労, so people commonly choose 疲れ over 疲労 in everyday conversation.

疲れる refers to a physical or mental kind of tiredness, like you just worked out or studied a ton, but isn't used to describe sleepiness.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: For example, you're bound <vocabulary>to get tired</vocabulary> if you try to lift <reading>two ca</reading>rs (つか), right? So think about that as you learn this word's reading.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>"choose"</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to choose</vocabulary>.

You have the opportunity <vocabulary>to choose</vocabulary>. You choose, and a bright sign lights up reading "<reading>error</reading>" (えら).

meanings: Thank You For Your Hard Work

You say this to people when they've done good work — at the end of a workday or after a hard practice, for example. I guess the idea is that if they're tired, they've done some good work. Tell your coworkers お疲れ様でした when they leave for the day, or just use お疲れ in more casual situations with friends!

感じ is a casual word that talks about a general feeling, <vocabulary>impression</vocabulary>, or vibe you get from something. You'll hear it everywhere — いい感じ (nice vibe), そんな感じ (something like that), or どんな感じ? (what's it like?).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: If you can read 感じる, you should be able to read this too. It uses the same reading — just without る.

That's why this can mean <vocabulary>regrettable</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>disappointing</vocabulary> too.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

The <kanji>feeling</kanji>s you <kanji>contemplate</kanji> about a subject are your <vocabulary>impressions</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>thoughts</vocabulary> on it.

感想 is all about what you think or feel after experiencing something, like after reading a book, watching a movie, or going to an event.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.reading_mnemonic:

vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. You can laugh freely, now!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>quit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to quit</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "Hey, you going <vocabulary>to quit</vocabulary>?" "<reading>Yah</reading> (や) man, I'm going to quit."

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>perfect</kanji> way to <kanji>tie</kanji> up a research paper is with a <vocabulary>conclusion</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>cure</kanji>, so this verb means <vocabulary>to cure</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to heal</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to ease</vocabulary> something. 

This verb is for when someone actively cures something. (The illness doesn't just get better on its own.) How can you remember that? Because when you try to cure someone and you mess up, they can <reading>sue</reading> (す). Basically, to cure someone is to risk getting sued.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses a kun'yomi reading you didn't learn with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic:

I need you <vocabulary>to cure</vocabulary> him, and I need you to cure him right <reading>now</reading> (なお). NOW NOW NOW!

This also shares a reading with 直す, a similar word that you already learned means "to fix." Fixing and curing are basically the same, right? Call me crazy, but there might just be an etymological connection there that can help you remember this reading.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 笑う is "to laugh." This is a noun version of that, though it's not "a laugh," (that's 笑い). Add お to that and you have the thing that makes you laugh. It's <vocabulary>comedy</vocabulary>. It's the <vocabulary>joke</vocabulary> that's elevated with お because it made you laugh SOOOOO much. Haha!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same 笑う or 笑い. It's also the same as what you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji 治 means <kanji>cure</kanji>, but this verb just refers to the more passive process of getting better: it means <vocabulary>to get better</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get well</vocabulary>, or simply <vocabulary>to heal</vocabulary>. 

治る isn't about someone actively curing something, it's just about something getting better — like 自然に治る (to heal naturally) or 薬で治る (to get better with medicine). How to remember this? If you want to get better, tell your illness it's being <reading>ru</reading>de (る). As soon as you call it out for being rude, it'll heal. That's just science.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This uses the same reading you learned with the related word 治す, but here's a mnemonic just in case:

When you're sick, your mom calls every day to say, "You have <vocabulary>to get better</vocabulary>, <reading>now</reading> (なお)! Do it — get better NOW!" Bullying you into healing is a total Mom-move, and somehow it works. There, you're all better now.

meanings: To Be Back In Working Order
vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 直す means "to fix," where someone actively does the fixing. Well, 直る puts the focus on the thing getting fixed, so it means <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary>.

In other words, don't use it to say "I fixed it," but do use it to say "It's fixed!" or "It's back to normal!" To remember this, imagine a British person excitedly shouting, "My loo (る) was broken, but now it's fixed!”
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with 直す, but here's a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Something needs <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> <reading>now</reading> (なお)! Seriously, it's urgent! You need this thing <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary> right now!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 笑う is "to laugh." This is the noun version, because the う in 笑う turns to い (so don't confuse this as an adjective). What is the noun version of "to laugh"? It's <vocabulary>a laugh</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 笑う, so just make sure you know that so you can know this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When you're in a <kanji>bind</kanji>, visiting the <kanji>bureau</kanji> may be your only option <vocabulary>in the end</vocabulary>. You were really hoping to avoid it, but it looks like you'll need to go <vocabulary>after all</vocabulary>.

結局 is used to talk about the final result after everything is said and done. It often carries the nuance that, despite the various factors leading up to something, things didn't go as expected or the outcome wasn't ideal, like 結局行かなかった (<vocabulary>ultimately</vocabulary>, I didn't end up going).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note the けつ gets changed to けっ as つs in this situation often do.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You're <kanji>distressed</kanji> and it's <kanji>difficult</kanji>. This is quite the <vocabulary>hardship</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>difficulty</vocabulary> you're feeling.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>difficult</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: It's awfully difficult to load a cow into your <reading>Moo-zooka</reading> (むずか). Click. Boom!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>difficult</kanji> <kanji>injustice</kanji> to take from someone is a <vocabulary>criticism</vocabulary>. Ugh, what a pain to be criticized! So difficult, and besides, it's an injustice, because I'm perfect!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bind</kanji> or <kanji>tie</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to tie</vocabulary>. Tying is also a great way <vocabulary>to connect</vocabulary> things, so this verb sometimes means that too.

At its core, 結ぶ is about bringing things together and creating a connection. It can be physical, like tying a string, but it's also commonly used in abstract ways, like forming relationships or establishing contracts.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You decide <vocabulary>to tie</vocabulary> a ribbon on a <reading>moose</reading> (むす). Why? You're going to give it as a present to someone you want <vocabulary>to connect</vocabulary> with. Nothing says "let's be friends" like a moose with a big, fancy ribbon tied to it. Now if only this moose would stand still so you could tie a proper knot…

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>suck</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to suck</vocabulary>, but it's usually used to talk about what you do to cigarettes, so a better translation I think is <vocabulary>to smoke</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You smoke too much, and that gives you cancer. You decide to <reading>sue</reading> (す) the cigarette makers.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sleep</kanji> or <kanji>lie down</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sleep</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lie down</vocabulary>—just like what you do when you decide <vocabulary>to go to bed</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. So, you can go ahead and lie down for a moment before moving on to the next item.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 結ぶ means "to tie" and 付く means "to be attached"? Well, tie them together so that they're attached, and you get to be connected. The words are connected, and that's what they mean too. Very meta. 結び付く generally describes a natural connection forming between things, like 名前と顔が結び付く (a name connects with a face). Note that this is often written 結びつく, without the kanji 付.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of 結ぶ and 付く, so as long as you know how to read those, you should be okay here!

vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Of course, it will be really helpful to know the word 非難 to start.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>call</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to call</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to call out</vocabulary>. As in "HEY, YOU!"
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, so you should be good here. Just imagine yourself  calling out to someone: "<reading>YO</reading> (よ)! You!"

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>celebrate</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to celebrate</vocabulary>. When you burn this word, you should 祝う!

All your friends and family have come to celebrate your birthday, but you had no idea. Still confused and processing the situation, you keep saying, "Eee... what?" The surprise was a complete success!

vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Not different at all.

The kanji itself means <kanji>different</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be different</vocabulary>... and of course, to be different is also <vocabulary>to be wrong</vocabulary> in Japan. Don't be different!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. It's not different at all.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 呼ぶ is "to call" then this is something similar. This is when you are called by someone (and you're not doing the calling). This word is <vocabulary>to be called</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is shared with 呼ぶ, so remember that and you'll be able to read this too.

This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>celebrate</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>celebration</vocabulary>! 

お祝い is also used to mean a <vocabulary>congratulatory gift</vocabulary> itself.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 直 can also mean "direct?" Well, if you <kanji>direct</kanji>ly <kanji>adjoin</kanji> two things, their connection will become <vocabulary>direct</vocabulary> too. Nothing will stand between them!

That said, 直接 isn't limited to physical contact. In fact, it's more often used when someone does something without going through a middle step or person, whether it's in communication, action, or connection. For example, if you say 直接聞いた (I heard it directly), it means you got the info straight from the source.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

痛い is commonly used to say that some part of the body hurts or feels sore.

So now it's <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary> to eat.
