vocab.reading_mnemonic: You're so <vocabulary>sleepy</vocabulary> you can't even remember your own <reading>name</reading> (ねむ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The things that <kanji>line up</kanji> are <vocabulary>ordinary</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>average</vocabulary> things. Because the majority of things (or people) fall into the average category, you could say most of them line up side by side with each other.

This might be why 並 is often used in restaurants to refer to standard (or average) portion sizes. And in sushi restaurants, 並 can refer to a standard set, as opposed to a more luxurious or premium one.

Note that when describing something as 並 outside of a restaurant or commercial context, it could have a slightly judgmental tone. Most people wouldn't love it if you called their work (or them) ordinary and average, you know?
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember:

One day, out of the blue, you realize you're very <vocabulary>ordinary</vocabulary>. The thought thought crashes into you like a big <reading>波</reading> (なみ). "Oh my gosh… I'm totally <vocabulary>average</vocabulary>!" you exclaim as 波 after 波 of disappointment and self-loathing washes over you.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>line up</kanji>, so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to line up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be lined up</vocabulary>. 

並ぶ is intransitive, so it describes things being in a line, rather than things you're putting in a line yourself. You can remember this because you always say <reading>boo</reading> (ぶ) when you arrive at a store or a restaurant and see that there are already a bunch of people lined up outside.

Figuratively, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be on par</vocabulary> in terms of ability or status. Just imagine two people lined up side-by-side in a race, neither one able to overtake the other.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You expect all the deer <vocabulary>to line up</vocabulary> when you visit <reading>Nara</reading> (なら). You are the official Nara deer inspector, and the deer need to line up so you can inspect them whenever you come to town. (If you don't know about Nara and its deer, you should look them up — they're pretty famous.)

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Things that are <kanji>frozen</kanji> have been <kanji>tie</kanji>d up in <vocabulary>freezing</vocabulary> ice. They <vocabulary>get frozen</vocabulary> that way. 

凍結 is a relatively formal word that is used for the physical freezing of infrastructure, such as roads and water pipes. It can also refer to the freezing of systems or accounts, like the suspension of social media or bank accounts.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how <ja>痛い</ja> is "painful"? This is the verb version of that, so it means <vocabulary>to ache</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to hurt</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be in pain</vocabulary>.

痛む is an intransitive verb that suggests an ongoing sensation of pain or aching. It's a little more descriptive than 痛い, so you might see it used in writing or to describe a more persistent or recurring condition. It's also often used figuratively, especially in expressions like 心が痛む (my heart aches).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading, which you learned already!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>shift</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to shift</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: All that dubstep (<reading>うつ</reading>うつうつうつうつ) playing downstairs is causing all of your glassware <vocabulary>to shift</vocabulary> off the shelf and onto the floor. Damn that dubstep. うつうつうつうつうつ♪

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 痛い is "painful." This is the noun version, it is <vocabulary>a pain</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pain</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 痛い. No pain here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 眠い is "sleepy." The verb version of this is to sleep, or to fall asleep. yawn While 寝る can mean lying down or going to bed (not just sleeping), 眠る only refers to falling asleep or being in a state of sleep.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 眠い.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You already learned 並ぶ, which means "to line up" or "to stand in line." This is the transitive version — you're actively putting stuff in a line, so this means <vocabulary>to line something up</vocabulary>.

To remember the difference, just think about <reading>bear</reading>s (べる) and how you always have to line them up yourself. Bears are so stubborn and disagreeable, they can never line up on their own.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading of the kanji is same as for 並ぶ, so if you know that you can figure out the reading for this one as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have the <kanji>feeling</kanji> of <kanji>pleasant</kanji>ness, you are experiencing <vocabulary>pleasure</vocabulary>.

While 快感 can describe the thrill of achieving something satisfying, it's often associated with <vocabulary>pleasurable feeling</vocabulary>s from taboo or unusual experiences. For example, it might refer to the pleasure of teasing someone, indulging in a bad habit like picking earwax, or feeling sensual delight.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is both <kanji>pleasant</kanji> and <kanji>suitable</kanji> is still really <vocabulary>pleasant</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>pain</kanji>, and this verb is transitive, so it means to inflict pain. In other words, it's <vocabulary>to injure something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hurt someone</vocabulary>.

This verb focuses on the pain involved in an injury, so it can only be used for things that feel pain, like people and body parts.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the word 痛い.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>shift</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be shifted</vocabulary>. You know that this is the one where something is shifted (and you're not doing the shifting), because it's really <reading>ru</reading>de (る) to be shifted, and you don't like it when people do it to you (because it happens quite a lot, strangely).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 移す, so use that to remember this!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>bind</kanji> this <kanji>marriage</kanji> up with a <vocabulary>marriage</vocabulary>. No better way to make a marriage happen than a marriage, right?
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Everything is <kanji>suitable</kanji> and <kanji>right</kanji>. Therefore it is <vocabulary>appropriate</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>proper</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>suitable</vocabulary>. Strangely enough, this also means <vocabulary>irresponsible</vocabulary>. Maybe it's because when everything is suitable and right for you, you're taking too much and not leaving enough for everyone else, making you irresponsible?
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 結婚 means "marriage," so the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to marry</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get married</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: You've already learned 結婚, so you should be okay here. As with that word, watch out for 結's けつ reading changing to けっ.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>want</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>wanted</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What do you want? A <reading>hoe</reading> (ほ), like a garden hoe, you sicko.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dirty</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to get dirty</vocabulary>. You know you're not doing the dirtying, because it's <reading>rare</reading> (れる) for you to get anything dirty, though things do get dirty on their own.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Things seem <vocabulary>to get dirty</vocabulary> easily around here, which is why <reading>you go</reading> (よご) to great lengths to keep things clean.

Note that the reading よごれる is generally used for getting physically dirty, whereas けがれる is more figurative, so more like “to be defiled”.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>dirty</kanji> <kanji>point</kanji> is a little point of dirtiness on something. This is a <vocabulary>stain</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>smudge</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 結婚 is <kanji>marriage</kanji>, then a marriage <kanji>ceremony</kanji> is a <vocabulary>marriage ceremony</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wedding</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Simplicity</kanji> is <kanji>simple</kanji>, making this <vocabulary>simple</vocabulary> as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 汚れる is "to get dirty." This is when you make something dirty, aka "<vocabulary>to make dirty</vocabulary>." You know that this is the version where you make things dirty yourself because when you make someone dirty with all that poop you're flinging, they <reading>sue</reading> (す) you immediately. This happens a lot.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
The reading comes from 汚れる, so if you know that you can read this.

Note that the reading よごす  is generally used for making things physically dirty, whereas けがす means making someone or something impure in a figurative way.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>teardrop</kanji>s are also known as your <vocabulary>tears</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

Your <kanji>teardrop</kanji>s are like little waves. What are they? They're <reading>波だ</reading> (なみだ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
If someone tells you to get <kanji>straight</kanji> to doing something, you ought to do it <vocabulary>right away</vocabulary>. Go on, chop-chop!

直ちに means to do something <vocabulary>immediately</vocabulary>, and it has a nuance of urgency — for example, a tsunami warning asking people to immediately evacuate their homes or your doctor telling you to contact them at once if you experience a certain symptom. However, it can also mean <vocabulary>directly</vocabulary>, like 失敗は直ちに死に繋がる (failure will lead directly to death).
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses a rare reading for 直 that you haven't seen before, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

Every time your boss asks you to do something <vocabulary>right away</vocabulary>, you do it and then yell "<reading>ta-da</reading> (ただ)!!" Imagine how annoying of an employee you must be, yelling "ta-da!" every time you finish a task. You get things done immediately, though, so no one can fire you — even if they probably want to.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If something or someone is <kanji>slow</kanji>, and they "do slow" they are going <vocabulary>to be late</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: What is slow and probably going to be late all the time? A big <reading>oak</reading> (おく). Oaks have trouble moving, and are slow, and therefore are always late, too.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Tooth</kanji> <kanji>science</kanji> gives you the science of <vocabulary>dentistry</vocabulary>, simple as that!

Note that when used by itself, this word solely refers to the scientific field of dentistry. You'll often see it used in combination with other medical words, so have a look at the common word combinations if you wanna know more!
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 歯 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You know who benefits from great <vocabulary>dentistry</vocabulary>? <reading>Shee</reading>p (し)! Have you seen one smile? Their wool makes a great, endless source of <vocabulary>dental</vocabulary> floss. That's their secret. Just think of the sheep and their perfect teeth and you'll never forget this reading!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adjective form of 汚, which is <kanji>dirty</kanji>. This word is the adjective <vocabulary>dirty</vocabulary>, but you can also use it to say things like <vocabulary>filthy</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>foul</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>unclean</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is different from the other kun'yomi readings you've learned so far with this word. It is きたない. Think of it like you're saying "<reading>来た、な</reading>", as in "it came, huh?" What came? A really dirty looking monster, and it's coming for you.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>slow</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>slow</vocabulary> (or, if you're slow, you're probably <vocabulary>late</vocabulary>, too).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: How <vocabulary>slow</vocabulary> are you? You are <reading>oh so</reading> slow (おそ).

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is in the <kanji>interior</kanji> of something else is inside of it, deep, and <vocabulary>far back</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>in the back</vocabulary>. Just imagine something interior to something else, it's probably in the back.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>interior</kanji> person (the honorific さん shows it's a person) is the person who stands in the interior of the house and doesn't leave, making that person your <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary>. Ouch. Sexist kanji strikes again.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from what you learned in the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>interior</kanji> <kanji>formal name ender</kanji> (person) is the person who's waiting internal, out of the picture (remember, kanji was made forever ago and is pretty sexist). This person is <vocabulary>your wife</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>inquire</kanji>, and the verb version means the same — <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary>. Depending on the context it can also mean <vocabulary>to hear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>. 

伺う is a humble verb, so you can use with people of higher status to show your respect for them. For example, if you ask your professor a question or hear something from them, you can say 教授に伺う. If you visit them, you can say 教授のところに伺う. And in customer service, you'll often hear お伺いします, which is the polite way for a staff member to say they're ready to listen and assist.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: Excuse me, I'd like <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary> about Chairman Kaga. <reading>Ooh! Kaga</reading> (うかが). How exciting! You're asking questions about Chairman Kaga, the ruler over the Iron Chef kingdom.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 伺う is "to inquire" or "to visit" then the noun version would be a polite way to say <vocabulary>inquiry</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>enquiry</vocabulary>. In other words, a <vocabulary>question</vocabulary>. It can also mean a <vocabulary>visit</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 伺う.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
An excess of <kanji>feeling</kanji> produces <kanji>teardrop</kanji>s. These are <vocabulary>tears of emotion</vocabulary>, but not the bad kind. You're just <vocabulary>being moved to tears</vocabulary>.

感涙 is an advanced word mainly used in writing. It refers to the kind of tears you might shed when you're profoundly touched with positive emotion, like when you're truly grateful for something or moved by a powerful speech.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 涙 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your excessive <vocabulary>tears of emotion</vocabulary> have <reading>rui</reading>ned (るい) your life. Your friends didn't like being cried at for the smallest compliment or favor, so now they don't even return your calls. No one else you know is <vocabulary>being moved to tears</vocabulary> on a daily basis like this. It's ruining your life!

radicals.meaning_mnemonic: This radical already looks like a <radical>river</radical>. See how the lines represent the flow of the river? There's even a slight bend in this river. So when you see this radical, you should think "river."

This looks like a stool with a lid on it, but it's actually a desk for <radical>writing</radical>. Do you see it? You can even see the pen sticking up in the middle. Think of all the beautiful writing that's been produced here. Letters, novels, essays — any kind of writing you can think of.

This looks like a regular arrow, but it's not. Let's call it the "not arrow." It can not move forward, because it's been stopped by some kind of line above it. Every arrow wants to fly, but this one is not going anywhere. Look at it, being all negated like that. Well, that's just what this radical does. It nots things.
The towel is getting soaked with drops of liquid. That's because it's <radical>rain</radical>ing. Get your towels and other clothes inside before they get soaked through from this rain!

If you find a rib cage on the moon, it'll probably be <radical>blue</radical>. Why? 'Cause it would have to come from one of the moon's inhabitants (the Moon People), and they're all blue — you know, due to the frigid temperatures and lack of oxygen and stuff.

This is the <radical>stamp</radical> radical — the inking kind, not the postage kind. Why? Because it looks like a stamp stick! The top parts are thicker on one side so you can get a good grip. It even looks like the letter P — which just happens to be the last letter in "stamp"!

What's mama doing? It looks like she's dodging a <radical>spear</radical>. Do you see the spear rushing past her as she leaps backwards to avoid it? Phew, that was a close call! Not today, spear. Not today.
This looks like a <radical>boat</radical> coming toward you in the water. See the sail billowing on top and the reflection on the water? Yep, that's a boat. The boatiest boat that ever boated.

There is a stool sticking out of the dirt. You walk up and realize it has writing on it. It's actually a <radical>tombstone</radical>. You can sit on it and remember the people who are below the dirt now.
If you kick a cliff twice you'll start a <radical>landslide</radical>! Oh no!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>sound</radical>. You can even see someone standing at a kind of square table here. It's a DJ at the turntables! Imagine them spinning records and scratching out all kinds of cool sounds.

You could also remember this with the kanji mnemonic we gave you. Here's the gist of it: If you stand on the sun, you'll hear a very loud sizzling sound.

There's a rice paddy on top of a tree… Figuratively, because trees don't bear rice, they bear <radical>fruit</radical>! Use your imagination, and those four little boxes on top of the tree kind of look like big, ripe fruits — just waiting to be picked.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>attach</radical>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>happiness</radical>. Don't get it confused with the spicy radical 辛, they're very similar!

You want to compose some writing (文), but you also want to look at the moon (月). Well, why not make both activities <radical>simultaneous</radical>? If you write while simultaneously looking at the moon, you'll probably come up with a cool romantic poem or something.

This is the <radical>football</radical> radical. Do you see the little footballer with their massive helmet just in the process of kicking the ball away? 100% determination, with zero idea of what's going on. Team Kanji, let's gooo!

Your leader (ｲ) has become a bent spoon (匕). Well, that's quite a <radical>change</radical>. Why would your leader transform like this? Maybe they're leading a movement of people transforming into spoons, like in protest or something. And why not? If you want to change the world, start by changing yourself. Into a spoon.

This radical is a <radical>greenhouse</radical>. There are windows in the middle, flowers protruding along the top, and plants bursting up through the trellis below. The plants have officially taken over!

Alternatively, you can remember this one using the radical components:
Flowers need the sun to get big. To help them grow as big as possible, we put them in the greenhouse.

The horns on the king give him an ego. Which in turn gives him a sense of <reading>righteousness</reading>. He shouldn't act all righteous like that, but I suppose it's what kings do. If you had horns and a big ego, you'd probably think you were the epitome of righteousness too.

There's a lid on top of something you're trying to keep private. It's your <radical>trash</radical>. You wouldn't want people going through your private trash, which is why we put lids on our trash cans. It's also illegal to look through someone's trash, so make sure you never do that.

This is the <radical>spring</radical> radical, because it looks like a new plant shoot has pushed its way up through layers of dirt, snow, and ice to announce the coming of spring. Spring is the season (and the radical) full of new, growing life!

There is a hat covering the moon and it's holding a knife. Wait, that's no moon. It's a space station! It's the <radical>Death Star</radical>! It's pretending to be a moon under that hat. And it's armed! Don't let the Death Star stab your planet to death.

What's under the lid on your cook pot? Legs and fins. <radical>Again</radical>. All you know how to cook is legs (of chicken) and fins, so you cook them again and again and again. You'll be having them for dinner tonight, and again tomorrow, and again the next day. Legs and fins, again and again and again, for the rest of your days.

Alternatively, you can also think of this as a laundry hanger with a pair of pants and two little socks flapping like fins. Because laundry is something you have to do again and again… whether you like it or not!

example.jp: 明日、県内はたいていのところで晴れますが、北部では雲が広がり、雨が降るところもあるでしょう。
example.furigana: あした、けんないはたいていのところで はれますが、ほくぶではくもがひろがり、あめが ふる ところもあるでしょう。
example.en: Tomorrow, it will be sunny in most of the prefecture, but in the northern region clouds will spread and there may be some rain.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You want to share <radical>happiness</radical> with people so you <radical>stamp</radical> <radical>stool</radical>s with the <kanji>news</kanji>. Now when people want a <kanji>report</kanji> of all the happy things going on, they can just look down before they sit.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You research and <kanji>report</kanji> the <kanji>news</kanji> from <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう). Only after, once all of the news is stamped onto the stools, do you leave your home.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is out, the sky is <radical>blue</radical>, things have begun to <kanji>clear up</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When it starts to <kanji>clear up</kanji>, you exclaim, "<reading>Hah</reading> (は)! Told you so!" You had a feeling it would clear up, but no one believed you, so now you have to yell "Hah!" and rub your correctness in everyone's face.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>rain</radical> <radical>cloud</radical> is still a <kanji>cloud</kanji>! It's probably going to rain on you soon though, so I hope you have a jacket or an umbrella.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You lie down and try to figure out what the <kanji>cloud</kanji>s are shaped like. The first cloud is shaped... like a <reading>coo</reading>l <reading>mo</reading>m (くも). She's wearing high pants, and holding a kid on each hip, but she's also listening to the latest music and using slang. Huh. You look to the next cloud and see... wait, another cool mom?

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You attempt to expel wind out of your <radical>mouth</radical> but <radical>lack</radical> the breath to <kanji>blow</kanji> out any. You’re using your mouth and trying to blow out some air, but you are failing to do so.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You silly <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ), the reason you couldn’t <kanji>blow</kanji> any air out of your mouth is because your hand was over it. You can’t blow air out that way. You silly fool, you.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You're in the <radical>sun</radical> playing <radical>football</radical> and you get very <kanji>warm</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: It's <kanji>warm</kanji> like this because it's <reading>dawn</reading> (だん). That's when the sun comes up.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When <radical>rain</radical> falls on <radical>Wolverine</radical>, it turns to <kanji>snow</kanji>. He's so emotionally distant and cold that the rain freezes into snow as soon as it gets near him.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You're concerned for Wolverine's mental health. Him being so emotionally cold that he turns rain to <kanji>snow</kanji> means <reading>you kee</reading>p (ゆき) asking if he's okay. But that only makes him want to be more distant.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> causes a <radical>landslide</radical> that causes an <kanji>earthquake</kanji>!!! The earth doesn't just slide, it <kanji>shake</kanji>s and <kanji>quake</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>earthquake</kanji> shakes you so violently that you fall over, banging your <reading>shin</reading> (しん) on the coffee table. The edge of the coffee table is very sharp, so it cuts into your shin pretty badly.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What part of a <radical>tsunami</radical> do you feel with your <radical>skin</radical>? The <kanji>wave</kanji>s. Tsunamis are accompanied by all kinds of terrifying sights and sounds, but what you feel on your skin are the powerful waves.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: When each <kanji>wave</kanji> hits your body, you shout, "<reading>Hah</reading> (は)!" It's not like it's on purpose. When the wave crashes into you, the wind gets knocked right out of you, making you say "Hah!"

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>ground</radical>! You spilled some <radical>water</radical> <radical>drop</radical>s, so I <kanji>request</kanji> that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Oh, one more thing. I <kanji>request</kanji> that you wipe up the water with this <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>greenhouse</radical> is the newest <radical>power</radical> of the city you decided to <kanji>recruit</kanji>. You’re trying to recruit all the buildings in town and the greenhouse was the next on your list. It adds just a little bit of power to the town, but it's important nonetheless.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: After you <kanji>recruit</kanji> the greenhouse, you recruit <reading>Bo</reading>bo (ぼ) the clown to guard it for you. Bobo the clown has a terrifying amount of power so he’ll make an excellent guard for the greenhouse.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Reaching your <radical>ear</radical> is the <radical>sound</radical> of a <radical>drunkard</radical> who can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. You hear him before you see him because he’s behind some trash cans. Being a drunkard, he’s like, super wasted and just kind of rambling to himself, making strange sounds. No wonder he can’t find employment.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Since this guy is such a pathetic drunkard, it comes as no <reading>shock</reading> (しょく) that he can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. If he did find employment, I would be filled with both shock and awe.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: If you put a <radical>roof</radical> over a <radical>valley</radical> it will change its <kanji>form</kanji>. Its <kanji>appearance</kanji> will alter completely!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Its new <kanji>appearance</kanji> looks familiar to you, like it's a big <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう) cup! A valley with a roof on it looks exactly like a yogurt cup. Huh!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You can make your <radical>fingers</radical> <radical>branch</radical> out. It's your special <kanji>skill</kanji>, a very advanced <kanji>technique</kanji>. Your fingers branch out into smaller fingers and you can hold things really well. You can type super-duper fast. And you can win any tickle fight. These are skills you have thanks to your branching fingers.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, these <kanji>skill</kanji>s are too much for the normal skill-less people to handle, so they pull out the <reading>gui</reading>llotine (ぎ). I guess they're going to chop off your skillful fingers because they're kinda scary.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>boat</radical> will have at least one <radical>weapon</radical>, <kanji>generally</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Generally</kanji> a boat with a weapon will be owned by <reading>Han</reading> (はん) Solo.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You use a special <radical>spear</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> to give yourself the <radical>power</radical> to do all of your <kanji>task</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>task</kanji> is to spear this cow. "<reading>Moo</reading> (む)!" it yells at you and runs away. You need to make dinner though... that's your task, so you better catch up to that cow and put an end to its mooing.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: I always <radical>say</radical> the <radical>fruit</radical> <kanji>section</kanji> at the grocery should be at the front of the store. It’s the perfect place for the fruit section, I say.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: To get to the fruit <kanji>section</kanji>, you have to go to the store. To get to the store you have to drive a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Driving a car is the fastest way to get to the fruit section at the store.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> <radical>request</radical>s a <kanji>sphere</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>sphere</kanji> is a <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう) sphere. A strange sphere shaped cucumber.

kanji.kunyomi: き・める, き・まる
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You have at your disposal a <radical>tsunami</radical> to assassinate this <radical>person</radical>, or a <radical>hook</radical>. Which method will you choose? <kanji>Decide</kanji> now!
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
To remember the けつ reading, we always use the word "ketsup." It's a special mix of ketchup and catsup (yum):

You finally <kanji>decide</kanji>. You're going to go with the tsunami... but not just any tsunami. You'll kill him with a tsunami of <reading>ketsu</reading>p (けつ).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> grants a <radical>gladiator</radical> its <radical>power</radical> so he will <kanji>win</kanji>! <kanji>Victory</kanji> will be his!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: He <kanji>win</kanji>s over and over again, and soon the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) is even rooting for him. In fact, the Shougun claims him as his personal gladiator of choice.

compounds.meaning: a score of one to two

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Writing</radical> and <radical>measurement</radical> stand <kanji>versus</kanji> one another. Writing is all about feeling and expression. Measurement is about cold hard numbers. Yep, in this world writing people are basically the <kanji>opposite</kanji> of measurement people. Which side are you on?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Whenever it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else, you wear a <reading>tie</reading> (たい). Naturally, your tie is always the <kanji>opposite</kanji> color of your opponent's tie. Kinda like how political rivals wear different color ties when they debate. It's pretty silly, but at least your tie makes it clear that it's you versus them.

kanji.kunyomi: なが・れる, なが・す
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> lifts all the <radical>trash</radical> out of the <radical>river</radical> and it <kanji>stream</kanji>s out onto the shores.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Next to the trash <kanji>stream</kanji> you suddenly see <reading>Ryu</reading> (りゅう) from Street Fighter and he looks pissed. He's furious that so many people throw their trash in the river and it causes streams like this.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: When you're in <radical>prison</radical>, whoever ends up with the <radical>shellfish</radical> will <kanji>lose</kanji>. It's the game all prisoners play. It's like keep away from the shellfish. And if you end up with the shellfish BZZZZTT that's it, you're the loser.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If you <kanji>lose</kanji>, you're a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). All you had to do was not hold the prison shellfish. It really shouldn't have been that hard to not lose, ya fool.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: In your <radical>fingers</radical> is a <radical>weapon</radical>, so you <kanji>throw</kanji> it. Maybe you're angry and you threw the weapon at a person you don't like. Maybe you're a pacifist and you threw it away so no one else could use it. Either way, when you have a weapon in your fingers you have to throw it.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>throw</kanji> your weapon away because you're about to enter <reading>とう</reading>きょう and there are no weapons allowed there. There is, however, a big pile of thrown away weapons by the border, which is where you're throwing yours right now.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fruit</radical> radical and the <kanji>fruit</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Bodacious!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: They sell <kanji>fruit</kanji> at the store, and you need to drive your <reading>ca</reading>r (か) to get there. A car is the fastest way to fruit.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>simple</radical> <radical>drunkard</radical> starting a <kanji>war</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The simple drunkard started a <kanji>war</kanji> with the <reading>cen</reading>taurs (せん)! This is especially unfortunate, because the centaurs are really good at <kanji>battle</kanji>s because they're all automatically cavalry troops.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Tying a <radical>thread</radical> to a <radical>tombstone</radical> each year will help you <kanji>manage</kanji> the <kanji>passage of time</kanji>. That way you’ll know how many years you <kanji>pass through</kanji>, since you’ll have one thread for each year to count.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Dealing with the <kanji>passage of time</kanji> can be tough, so after you tie the thread to the tombstone, each year you eat a piece of <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい). You already eat cake to mark the passage of time on your birthday, so why not here as well?

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You see a <radical>tsunami</radical> that's <radical>simultaneous</radical> (with another tsunami, I assume) and you know the world is about to <kanji>come to an end</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Just as the world is about to <kanji>come to an end</kanji>, your <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい) appears and blocks it with its cyborg body!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: After being thrown in <radical>prison</radical>, a <radical>drunkard</radical> thinks, "What have I <kanji>become</kanji>?" It's then they resolve to become a better person.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Determined to <kanji>become</kanji> a better human, you take up a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). With this saber in hand, you'll turn your life around and become a new person… a hero… an ally of justice!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You send your <radical>private</radical> <radical>sword</radical> man out with your <radical>shellfish</radical> so he can <kanji>trade</kanji> them. Shellfish were used as currency back in the olden days. And you aren't going to go out trading and dirty your own hands, no no. Trading your shellfish is the job for the private sword you hired!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: While he's out making the <kanji>trade</kanji> for you, you decide to relax and do some <reading>bow</reading>ling (ぼう). In fact, you can't wait for the trade to be done because you're hoping he's going to come back with a new bowling ball for you.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>easy</radical> radical and the <kanji>easy</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What would be an <kanji>easy</kanji> reading for this kanji? <reading>い</reading>! The sound easy starts with!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What does a <radical>car</radical> and the <radical>Death Star</radical> have in common? They're both used to <kanji>transport</kanji> people and things.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Right now you and the Death Star are <kanji>transport</kanji>ing <reading>yu</reading>rts (ゆ). They're the universe's #1 best transportable homes!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: You need to look a <radical>tree</radical> in the <radical>eye</radical> to gain a <kanji>mutual</kanji> respect for each other. Stand up straight, look the tree directly in its eye(s). If it looks right back, you know things are mutual.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: If your respect for the tree is <kanji>mutual</kanji> with the respect the tree feels for you, you'll be able to see the tree's <reading>sou</reading>l (そう). Right now its soul looks pretty sad, like it's trying to say, "Why are your people cutting down all my friends? I thought we had a mutual understanding."

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>change</radical> radical and <kanji>change</kanji> kanji are exactly the same. Except this kanji can also mean <kanji>transform</kanji>. But that's just another kind of change, isn't it?
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Imagine your country's leader taking this spoon and whispering some magic words to it to <kanji>change</kanji>it into a <reading>car</kanji> (か).

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>compare</radical> radical and the <kanji>compare</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Huzzah!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Compare</kanji> the <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) today with the heat yesterday. Is it hotter today? It's up to you to compare.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>original</radical> radical and the <kanji>original</kanji> kanji are the same!

This kanji can also mean <kanji>field</kanji>, probably because that's what everything originally looked like before humans: just a bunch of fields.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> Japanese hero was <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん), from "The Tale of Genji."

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>mouth</radical> is so <radical>big</radical> that it's the <kanji>cause</kanji> of all your problems.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Your big mouth is the <kanji>cause</kanji> behind all your friends and family moving to an <reading>inn</reading> (いん). They move to the inn so they don't have to live with you and hear you talk anymore.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Building</radical>s hold <radical>festival</radical>s on special <kanji>occasion</kanji>s.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>occasion</kanji> this time is to celebrate your wonderful <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい). It's about time you did something nice for it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> is <radical>righteousness</radical>, at least that's what you believe. You keep talking and saying these things, and you don't listen to anyone else's words. This is your style of <kanji>deliberation</kanji> and <kanji>discussion</kanji>.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: What are you in <kanji>deliberation</kanji> about? Whether or not to send some poor soul to the <reading>gui</reading>llotine (ぎ). "I think he should go," you say. "I don't think he should," says another. This <kanji>deliberation</kanji> is going nowhere...

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> of <radical>tongue</radical>s is coming at you. As it washes over you, you feel each individual tongue moving around on your body, licking you. They make you feel so... <kanji>lively</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>lively</kanji> feeling isn't just happening to you, the tongue tsunami is licking it into all of the <reading>cats</reading> (かつ) in your neighborhood too!

kanji.kunyomi: か・わる, か・える
kanji.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Again</radical> and again, <radical>winter</radical> <kanji>change</kanji>s you each year.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You know what else <kanji>change</kanji>s each winter? <reading>Hen</reading>s (へん)! They're constantly laying eggs, which then (possibly) turn into new hens.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: It's <radical>correct</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> to focus on <kanji>politics</kanji> and the <kanji>government</kanji>. Elections are happening, in the new year politicians are being sworn in. Winter is government time!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Everyone involved in <kanji>politics</kanji> and <kanji>government</kanji> wields a special <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). If two political parties are arguing, they'll whip out their sabers and start slashing away!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>canopy</radical> <radical>attach</radical>ing your entire country is the <kanji>government</kanji>. They loom over you all and try to keep you all organized and together under their control.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Try to get out from under this <kanji>government</kanji> canopy and you'll be labeled a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). Unless... you can fool them!

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: It's important to focus <radical>oneself</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> so that one can emerge <kanji>renew</kanji>ed! You can't really go outside in winter without getting cold or sick, so spend winter focusing on YOU.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Winter ends and, <kanji>renew</kanji>ed, you come out ready to start a new hobby: <reading>kay</reading>aking (かい)! Nothing says renewal like a brand new kayak and sense of purpose in life.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>Not</radical> <radical>Mouth</radical> says “<kanji>no</kanji>”. What else would you expect from something named the “Not Mouth”? The Not Mouth will always say “no”, regardless of the question.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: You ask the Not Mouth if it is afraid of <reading>he</reading>at (ひ). The Not Mouth says, “<kanji>no</kanji>”. So you set the Not Mouth on fire. The Not Mouth then screams, “NONONONONONONONONONOOOOOO~!” Looks like someone can’t handle the heat.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic:
A <radical>white</radical> guy jumps into a <radical>pool</radical> with a <kanji>target</kanji> painted on the bottom. He's aiming for the target, of course.

This kanji can also mean <kanji>-al</kanji>, as in the endings you get on some English adjectives. You know, like the pool is artifici-al. Or painting a target down there is not practic-al. That kind of -al.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: This white dude is a huge <reading>techie</reading> (てき) so he has electronic enhancements that make sure he hits the <kanji>target</kanji>. Being a techie has its advantages.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Go up on the <radical>roof</radical> in <radical>spring</radical> to see the <kanji>truth</kanji>. The <kanji>reality</kanji> of the world is being revealed as winter ends and the trees bear <kanji>fruit</kanji> once again.
kanji.reading_mnemonic: As the snow melts and reveals the <kanji>truth</kanji> and <kanji>reality</kanji> of the world to you, you notice one of the trees you were looking at has already borne two piece of <kanji>fruit</kanji>. <reading>Gee, two</reading> (じつ)?! That's a lot of fruit for this early in the spring.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical it comes from. <radical>Lack</radical> becomes <kanji>Lack</kanji>!
kanji.reading_mnemonic:
To remember けつ, we use the word "ketsup." It's the perfect blend of ketchup and catsup!

You're <kanji>lack</kanji>ing something in your fridge. You look around, trying to find the <reading>ketsu</reading>p (けつ) you lack. You can't find it, because you lack it.

kanji.meaning_mnemonic: Sticking a <radical>cross</radical> into a <radical>rice paddy</radical> to get its <radical>measurement</radical>s is your <kanji>specialty</kanji>. Most people get really confused when they have to measure their rice paddies, but that's where you come in. You plant a cross right in the middle, look down it from one end to the other, and voila! You know the measurements immediately. That's why it's your specialty!
kanji.reading_mnemonic: Hearing of your amazing <kanji>specialty</kanji> and cross measurement abilities, a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん) from a far off land recruits you for a job. The centaur’s father has just passed away and the centaur wants you to measure the rice paddies that have been left to him.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>lack</kanji> of <kanji>point</kanji>s. These are things about yourself you wish were better. These are your <vocabulary>shortcoming</vocabulary>s.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out because けつ is being shortened to けっ here!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the same as the reading for this vocab word. Enjoy the snow!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>change</kanji> so you'd think the verb version is "to change," but it's a bit more specific. This word means <vocabulary>to change form</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to transform</vocabulary>.

化ける means to change into something else, usually in a surprising and magical way. It's often used in stories where animals or spirits take on human forms. It can also describe transformations in real life that are so dramatic they feel unreal.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You try to transform. You want to turn into something awesome, like a dinosaur, but then *poof* you turn into a sheep. "<reading>Ba</reading>aaa," you say. "Baaa."

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When you do (する) <kanji>versus</kanji>, you choose <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> an opponent. It’s where your attention and efforts are going to <vocabulary>be directed toward</vocabulary>. Alternatively, you can use this word <vocabulary>to contrast</vocabulary> one thing with another.

This word is used to help point out the relationship between two things in a sentence, where one thing is focusing on another thing. This is all a little vague and perhaps confusing, so check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this word no problem.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
When it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else to <kanji>decide</kanji> it all, you know this is a <vocabulary>showdown</vocabulary>. It's a decisive <vocabulary>confrontation</vocabulary>!

対決 is when two sides go head-to-head in a serious match or showdown. Think rivals <vocabulary>facing off</vocabulary> in a big game or the final battle in an anime. It's tense and dramatic, but also exciting — like, "Alright, this is it. Time to settle things. Who's gonna come out on top?"
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>throw</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to throw</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached, so you can bet it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn this reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're at a baseball game watching people <vocabulary>throw</vocabulary> balls around. But you're hungry so you call for a snack from a vendor. You raise your hand and they throw some <reading>na</reading>chos (な) at you. Oh no! Oh ouch! The nachos are hot and they hit you in the face. The vendor just threw a bunch of hot, sauced nachos at you! WHY?!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading because it's a single kanji on its own. Luckily, that's the reading you learned with the kanji already, so you should be able to read this.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>win</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to win</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

What did you just <vocabulary>win</vocabulary>? You won a new <reading>ca</reading>r (か)!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Win</kanji>, <kanji>lose</kanji>... both will happen in tonight's <vocabulary>match</vocabulary>! What a <vocabulary>showdown</vocabulary> it will be!

Note that 勝負 can also describe situations where one takes a significant risk or makes a bold move— <vocabulary>a gamble </vocabulary>—with high stakes involved.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that ふ becomes ぶ because of rendaku here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading, same like you learned with the kanji. That is the truth, I promise.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: When you look at something <kanji>versus</kanji> something else, you <kanji>compare</kanji> them with one another. You look at the <vocabulary>contrast</vocabulary> between them and make a <vocabulary>comparison</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>win</kanji> sounds like a great thing. When these two kanji are put together, a <vocabulary>certain victory</vocabulary> is inevitable.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Take note that the つ in ひつ is turned into a small っ, though.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>lack</kanji>, and this verb has a few meanings related to that. You'll often see it meaning <vocabulary>to get chipped</vocabulary>, like when talking about a teacup or your teeth. I guess a chipped teacup is lacking... a piece of itself?

欠ける can also literally mean <vocabulary>to be lacking</vocabulary>, as in "a good goalie is lacking from their team." You can use it like this when you're short of something, or when something is missing that would complete a set. In these situations, you'll usually see it as 欠けている!
vocab.reading_mnemonic:

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>come to an end</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is also about something ending: it means <vocabulary>to be finished</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be done</vocabulary>.

済む is used when something finishes or is resolved, often without further trouble, like 支払いが済む (the payment is completed). From this core idea of resolution, it also pops up in various other expressions about things coming to a close or being "enough."

For example, 気が済む means to feel satisfied with something such that you can get some issue out of your system, as in 気が済むまで泣く (cry till you feel better). Likewise, 〜で済む expresses that something on its own is sufficient, like 電話一本で済む (a single phone call is all it takes).

果たして is a word used to express skepticism or uncertainty about an outcome. For example, you might hear a soccer announcer say 果たしてゴールできるのか？(will they indeed be able to score?) as a player runs down the field, or an anime character say 果たしてそうなのかな？(I wonder if that's really the case?) when they're doubting something they've been told. It sounds a bit dramatic and theatrical, so you'll run into it more in entertainment media than in casual conversation.

In some cases, it can also mean <vocabulary>as was expected</vocabulary>, as in 果たして失敗した (as expected, they failed), but this meaning is mostly limited to either older or quite literary writing.

Depending on the context, you'll also see it used to mean "<vocabulary>economical</vocabulary>" as in cost-efficient, where the focus is on saving money or using resources wisely.

果てる is used to describe something reaching its limit or completely running out such that nothing more remains, like 望みが果てる(all hope is lost) or 命が果てる (one's life comes to an end).

When combined with other verbs, it describes a state taken to its extreme, like 困り果てる (to be at a complete loss). You'll also see it in expressions like 果てしない (endless), which flips the idea — something that never reaches an end.

You can remember this because you like to finish things en <reading>masse</reading> (ます). It's always best get lots of things done all at once.

済ます describes actively bringing something to completion, as in 仕事を済ます (finish your work) or 食事を済ます (finish a meal). Unlike 終わらせる, which simply means "to bring something to an end," 済ます focuses more on dealing with something like it's a task on your to do list — you're getting it out of the way so you can move on.

Because of this, it's also often used in the pattern 〜で済ます to mean you're handling something in a way that goes no further than necessary, like 簡単な食事で済ます (just eat something quick and simple) or 電話で済ます (just deal with something by phone).

vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. よく goes to よっ, so be careful not to want the wrong reading.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Warm</kanji> <kanji>warm</kanji> is <vocabulary>warm</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Note that 否 (いな) is very formal and somewhat archaic. Today, it's most commonly used in the expression 〜か否か (whether… or <vocabulary>not</vocabulary>).
vocab.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Instead of saying "no" you say "na," and instead of saying "na" you say <reading>いな</reading>. 

Note that 否 can also be read いや, which is a common way to say “no” in modern Japanese, but that reading is almost always written in kana.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: "No" is what you have determined to be the answer when you are making a denial. You are denying the truth or validity of something and working towards its negation. 否定 is a broad word that can be used in a wide variety of situations: denying an accusation, rejecting a theory, shooting down someone's opinion, invalidating someone's experience, and so on. You'll also see it used in grammar contexts to describe negating a sentence, like changing "Spot runs" to "Spot does not run."
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: "<kanji>No</kanji>" is the <kanji>decision</kanji> I've made. Sorry, but this is <vocabulary>rejection</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: It has <kanji>simplicity</kanji> and is <kanji>easy</kanji>. Whatever it is, it is <vocabulary>simple</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>throw</kanji> and <kanji>throw away</kanji> something. That's why this means <vocabulary>to throw away</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 投げる and 捨てる, combined into one garbage inducing dump of a word.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> <kanji>oil</kanji> is oil in its original state. That is <vocabulary>crude oil</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: If 否定 is "denial," then the verb version would be <vocabulary>to deny</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the word 否定 as well.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: 否定 is denial. Remember how 形 sometimes refers to grammar tense / type? Well, with a denial type grammar, you have a <vocabulary>negative form</vocabulary>, making it a <vocabulary>negative sentence</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>change</kanji> something then <kanji>exchange</kanji> it, you are making a <vocabulary>conversion</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>change</vocabulary>.

変換 generally refers to converting something from one form to another, like data conversion, energy transformation, or even converting hiragana to kanji.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Trade</kanji> is <kanji>easy</kanji> if you like <vocabulary>trade</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>commerce</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The 貿 reading is okay, but the 易 reading is different from what you're used to. Just think about how a lot of the trade that comes in will come into the train <reading>station</reading> (駅). So if you want good trade, you'll want to be at the えき.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>recruit</kanji>, so this verb vocab version can also mean <vocabulary>to recruit</vocabulary>. However, its primary meaning is <vocabulary>to appeal for something</vocabulary>, like a job position or donations.

This verb can also be intransitive (oh my!) and mean <vocabulary>to grow stronger</vocabulary>, usually in reference to some sort of feelings or emotions. Make sure to check out the common word combinations for some example usages!
vocab.reading_mnemonic: You'd like <vocabulary>to appeal for</vocabulary> <reading>two, no</reading> (つの), three things! Three!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: Being in the <kanji>versus</kanji> <kanji>yonder</kanji> (the opposite side) means you are in one yonder and someone is in the other yonder, and you are coming towards each other. So this means <vocabulary>to be oncoming</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come towards</vocabulary>.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>All</kanji> <kanji>general</kanji>-<kanji>al</kanji>! It's super general. It's <vocabulary>general</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>overall</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>across the board</vocabulary>. Nothing specific going on here.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>blow</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to blow</vocabulary>.

This word can be either intransitive or transitive. So, something can be blowing on its own, as in 風が吹く (the wind blows), or you can blow something, like 笛を吹く (to blow a whistle).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You have a <kanji>cause</kanji>, and you have the <kanji>fruit</kanji> (aka result) that it has created. Put them together and you get <vocabulary>cause and effect</vocabulary>. Some might even call this <vocabulary>karma</vocabulary>.

因果 refers to the relationship of one thing leading to another. You'll see it in phrases like 因果関係 (causal relationship) or 因果応報 (you reap what you sow).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know these readings already, so you should be fine here — just look out for the rendaku on 果 changing it from か to が.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 吹く is "to blow" and the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>. So this word means <vocabulary>to blow in</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to breathe into</vocabulary>, and it can be used both transitively and intransitively.

It can also be used figuratively to mean to breathe into or<vocabulary>to imbue</vocabulary>, like breathing new life into something, or imbuing someone’s mind with hatred.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 吹く and the kanji 込む.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 吹く is "to blow" and that 飛ばす is "To let fly." So, if you use your blowing to let something fly, you are going <vocabulary>to blow away</vocabulary> it.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 吹く and 飛ばす, put together.

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>lack</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to lack something</vocabulary>. 

欠く is often used for intangible qualities someone lacks, like flexibility or consideration. But it can also be used for physical things, especially in the context of basic necessities. It sounds kind of advanced and formal, so it tends to pop up more in writing than in casual speech.

Note that this is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object — someone is actively lacking something, like あの人の行動は常識を欠いている (their behavior lacks common sense).
vocab.reading_mnemonic: If your life seems <vocabulary>to lack something</vocabulary>, like excitement or meaning, the best thing you can do is hop in your <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Take your car out on the open road and go search for whatever it is you're lacking. You'll find it — we believe in you!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
Noun version of <kanji>decide</kanji>? It's a <vocabulary>decision</vocabulary>.

決 is a formal word that refers to a decisive <vocabulary>verdict</vocabulary>. It's used in formal phrases like 決を採る (to take a vote) or 決を下す (to pass a judgment), both of which are about making decisions or delivering verdicts.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the kanji!

vocab.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>inside</kanji> <kanji>cause</kanji> is an <vocabulary>internal cause</vocabulary>. Internal causes are usually the nastiest causes, if you ask me.

This word is mostly used in the fields of medicine and psychology. You’ll often see it as 内因性, which is a technical term used to talk about factors that originate within a person or an organism.
vocab.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
